17-def Aexp.Equiv (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : Prop :=
18-  ∀ (st : State),
19-    a₁.eval st = a₂.eval st
20-

22-    a₁.Equiv a₂ ↔ ∀ (st : State), a₁.eval st = a₂.eval st := by rfl

1-import LF.CustomTactics
2-import HL.Imp
3-
4-import SFLCompat
5-
6---  # Hoare: Hoare Logic, Part I
7-
8---  Our goal in this chapter is to develop the tools to work
9---  through some simple examples of *program verification*
10---  -- i.e., to use the precise definition of Imp to prove
11---  formally that particular programs satisfy particular
12---  specifications of their behavior.
13---
14---  We'll develop a reasoning system called *Floyd-Hoare
15---  Logic* -- often shortened to just *Hoare Logic* -- in
16---  which each of the syntactic constructs of Imp is
17---  equipped with a generic "proof rule" that can be used to
18---  reason compositionally about the correctness of programs
19---  involving this construct.
20-
21---  Hoare Logic combines two beautiful ideas: a natural way
22---  of writing down *specifications* of programs, and a
23---  *structured proof technique* for proving that programs
24---  are correct with respect to such specifications -- where
25---  by "structured" we mean that the structure of proofs
26---  directly mirrors the structure of the programs that they
27---  are about.
28-
29---  ## Assertions
30-
31---  An *assertion* is a logical claim about the state of a
32---  program's memory -- formally, a predicate of `State`s.
33-
34-open scoped Com MyGetElem
35-
36-abbrev Assertion := State → Prop
37-
38---  For example,
39---
40---  - `fun st => st[X] = 3` holds for states `st` in which
41---    value of `X` is `3`,
42---
43---  - `fun st => True` hold for all states, and
44---
45---  - `fun st => False` holds for no states.
46-
47---   ----------------------------------------
48-
49---  _Quiz:_
50-
51---  Paraphrase the following assertions in English (i.e.,
52---  say which states satisfy them)
53---
54---  (A) `fun st => st[X] ≤ st[Y]`
55---
56---  (B) `fun st => st[X] = 3 ∨ st[X] ≤ st[Y]`
57---
58---  (C)
59---  `fun st => st[Z] * st[Z] ≤ st[X] ∧ ¬ ((st[Z] + 1) * (st[Z] + 1) ≤ st[X])`
60-
61---   ----------------------------------------
62-
63---  ### Notations for Assertions
64-
65---  We'll use Lean's notation features to make assertions
66---  look as much like informal math as possible.
67---
68---  For example, instead of writing
69---
70---      fun st => st[X] = m
71---
72---  we'll usually write just
73---
74---      {{ X = m }}
75-
76---  Here, the `{{ A }}` brackets delimit the scope of the
77---  assertion notation.
78-
79---  THE FOLLOWING DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation: Assertions)
80-namespace Assertion
81-
82-section
83-open Lean Elab Term
84-
85-scoped syntax:max (name := assn) "assn(" ident "; " term ")" : term
86-scoped syntax:lead "{{" term "}}" : term
87-
88-@[term_elab assn]
89-def assnElab : TermElab := fun stx _type? => do
90-  match stx with
91-  | `(assn($st; $t:term)) =>
92-    let t ← elabTerm t none
93-    let ty ← Meta.inferType t
94-    -- if (← Meta.isDefEq ty (mkConst ``_root_.Ident)) then -- this incorrectly assigns metavariables
95-    if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Ident) then
96-      return mkApp6 (mkConst ``_root_.MyGetElem.getElem)
97-        (mkApp2 (mkConst ``TotalMap) (mkConst ``String) (mkConst ``Nat))
98-        (mkConst ``String)
99-        (mkConst ``Nat)
100-        (← Meta.synthInstance <| mkApp3 (mkConst ``_root_.MyGetElem)
101-          (mkApp2 (mkConst ``TotalMap) (mkConst ``String) (mkConst ``Nat))
102-          (mkConst ``String)
103-          (mkConst ``Nat))
104-        (← elabTerm st none) t
105-    if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Aexp) then -- Detect an embedded `Aexp` and turn it into `Aexp.eval st t`
106-      return (mkApp2 (mkConst ``Aexp.eval) (← elabTerm st none) t)
107-    else if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Bexp) then  -- Detect an embedded `Bexp` and turn it into `Bexp.eval st t`
108-      return (mkApp2 (mkConst ``Bexp.eval) (← elabTerm st none) t)
109-    else if ty.isMVar then -- This is a hack to guard against `Meta.isDefEq` assigning the type to be an `Assertion`
110-      return t
111-    else if (← Meta.isDefEq ty (mkConst ``_root_.Assertion)) then
112-      return mkApp t (← elabTerm st none)
113-    else
114-      return t
115-  | _ => throwUnsupportedSyntax
116-
117--- `: Assertion` guards that the resulting type is `State → Prop`.
118-macro_rules
119-  | `({{ $t }}) => `((fun st : _root_.State => assn(st; $t) : Assertion))
120-
121-macro_rules
122-  | `(assn($st; ($P))) => ``((assn($st; $P)))
123-  | `(assn($st; $l = $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) = assn($st; $r))
124-  | `(assn($st; $l + $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) + assn($st; $r))
125-  | `(assn($st; $l - $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) - assn($st; $r))
126-  | `(assn($st; $l * $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) * assn($st; $r))
127-  | `(assn($st; $l ≤ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ≤ assn($st; $r))
128-  | `(assn($st; $l < $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) < assn($st; $r))
129-  | `(assn($st; $l ≥ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ≥ assn($st; $r))
130-  | `(assn($st; $l > $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) > assn($st; $r))
131-  | `(assn($st; $l ∧ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ∧ assn($st; $r))
132-  | `(assn($st; $l ∨ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ∨ assn($st; $r))
133-  | `(assn($st; $l → $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) → assn($st; $r))
134-  | `(assn($st; $l ↔ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ↔ assn($st; $r))
135-  | `(assn($st; ¬ $t)) => ``(¬ assn($st; $t))
136-  | `(assn($st; $f $args*)) => do
137-    let mut result := f
138-    for arg in args do
139-      result ← `($result assn($st; $arg))
140-    return result
141-end
142-
143-#check {{ 1 = 2 }}
144-#check {{ X = X }}
145-#check {{ X = 2 * X }} -- X is the constant "X" defined in Imp
146-#check_failure {{ X }} -- fails as expected
147-#check {{ True }}
148-
149-#check {{ fun st => st[X] = st[Y] }}
150-
151-variable (a : Aexp)
152-#check {{ X = a }}
153-
154-variable (b : Bexp)
155-#check {{ b }}
156-#check {{ ¬ b }}
157-#check {{ b ∧ b }}
158-
159-variable (P Q : Assertion)
160-#check {{ P ∧ Q }}
161-
162-variable (f : Nat → Nat → Nat → Nat)
163-#check {{ f X Y X = 0 }}
164-
165-end Assertion
166-open scoped Assertion
167---  END DETAILS
168-
169---  Function applications inside assertions automatically
170---  interpret their arguments in the current state:
171---
172---  `{{ f e1 ... en }}` stands for
173---  `(fun st => f (e1 st) ... (en st))`.
174-
175---  We can place a raw Lean function directly inside
176---  assertion notation:
177---
178---  For example: `{{ fun st => ∀ x, st[x] = 0 }}`
179-
180---  ### Example Assertions
181-
182-namespace ExamplePrettyAssertions
183-
184-def assertion1 : Assertion := {{ X = 3 }}
185-def assertion2 : Assertion := {{ True }}
186-def assertion3 : Assertion := {{ False }}
187-def assertion4 : Assertion := {{ True ∨ False }}
188-def assertion5 : Assertion := {{ X ≤ Y }}
189-def assertion6 : Assertion := {{ X = 3 ∨ X ≤ Y }}
190-def assertion7 : Assertion := {{ Z = max X Y }}
191-def assertion8 : Assertion := {{ Z * Z ≤ X
192-                                 ∧ ¬ (((Nat.succ Z) * (Nat.succ Z)) ≤ X) }}
193-def assertion9 : Assertion := {{ Nat.add X Y > max Y X }}
194-variable {xs : List Nat}
195--- #check {{ xs = X }}

197-info: def ExamplePrettyAssertions.assertion8 : Assertion :=
198-fun st => st[Z] * st[Z] ≤ st[X] ∧ ¬st[Z].succ * st[Z].succ ≤ st[X]
199--/
200-#guard_msgs in
201-#print assertion8
202-
203-end ExamplePrettyAssertions

205---  ### Printing Assertions
206-
207---  THE FOLLOWING DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: printing assertions back)
208-namespace Assertion.Delab
209-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Imp.Delab
210-
211-/-- Rebuild the surface form of an assertion body, undoing the state
212-threading the `assn` elaborator performs: `st[X]` prints as `X`,
213-`Aexp.eval st a` as `a`, `Bexp.eval st b = true` as `b`, an applied
214-assertion `P st` as `P`, and a subterm that does not mention the state
215-prints as itself. -/
216-partial def delabBody (stId : FVarId) : DelabM Term := do
217-  let e ← getExpr
218-  if !e.containsFVar stId then
219-    delab
220-  else
221-    match_expr e with
222-    | MyGetElem.getElem _ _ _ _ st _ =>
223-      guard (st == .fvar stId)
224-      withNaryArg 5 delab
225-    | Aexp.eval st _ =>
226-      guard (st == .fvar stId)
227-      withAppArg delab
228-    | HAdd.hAdd _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
229-      `($(← withNaryArg 4 (delabBody stId)) + $(← withNaryArg 5 (delabBody stId)))
230-    | HSub.hSub _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
231-      `($(← withNaryArg 4 (delabBody stId)) - $(← withNaryArg 5 (delabBody stId)))
232-    | HMul.hMul _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
233-      `($(← withNaryArg 4 (delabBody stId)) * $(← withNaryArg 5 (delabBody stId)))
234-    | Eq _ l r =>
235-      -- `Bexp.eval st b = true` is the threaded form of a bare boolean `b`
236-      if r.isConstOf ``Bool.true && l.isAppOfArity ``Bexp.eval 2
237-          && l.appFn!.appArg! == .fvar stId then
238-        withNaryArg 1 <| withAppArg delab
239-      else
240-        `($(← withNaryArg 1 (delabBody stId)) = $(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)))
241-    | Ne _ _ _ =>
242-      `($(← withNaryArg 1 (delabBody stId)) ≠ $(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)))
243-    | LE.le _ _ _ _ =>
244-      `($(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)) ≤ $(← withNaryArg 3 (delabBody stId)))
245-    | LT.lt _ _ _ _ =>
246-      `($(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)) < $(← withNaryArg 3 (delabBody stId)))
247-    | GE.ge _ _ _ _ =>
248-      `($(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)) ≥ $(← withNaryArg 3 (delabBody stId)))
249-    | GT.gt _ _ _ _ =>
250-      `($(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)) > $(← withNaryArg 3 (delabBody stId)))
251-    | And _ _ =>
252-      `($(← withNaryArg 0 (delabBody stId)) ∧ $(← withNaryArg 1 (delabBody stId)))
253-    | Or _ _ =>
254-      `($(← withNaryArg 0 (delabBody stId)) ∨ $(← withNaryArg 1 (delabBody stId)))
255-    | Iff _ _ =>
256-      `($(← withNaryArg 0 (delabBody stId)) ↔ $(← withNaryArg 1 (delabBody stId)))
257-    | Not _ =>
258-      `(¬ $(← withAppArg (delabBody stId)))
259-    | _ =>
260-      if e.isArrow then
261-        `($(← withBindingDomain (delabBody stId)) →
262-          $(← withBindingBody `h (delabBody stId)))
263-      else if let .app f v := e then
264-        -- an applied assertion `P st` (or an applied escape lambda)
265-        guard (v == .fvar stId)
266-        guard !(f.containsFVar stId)
267-        withAppFn delab
268-      else
269-        failure
270-
271-/-- Print an `Assertion`-valued term as it appears inside `{{ … }}`: a
272-state lambda is un-threaded; a term the printer cannot rebuild falls back
273-to the raw lambda, which is exactly this notation's escape form. -/
274-partial def delabAssn : DelabM Term := do
275-  if (← getExpr).isLambda then
276-    (withBindingBody' `st (pure ·.fvarId!) fun stId => delabBody stId)
277-      <|> Delaborator.delab
278-  else
279-    delab
280-
281-/-- Print an assertion-position argument: a state lambda gets the
282-`{{ … }}` notation; any other term (a named assertion, a substitution)
283-already reads well bare. -/
284-def delabAssnArg (i : Nat) : DelabM Term := do
285-  if (← withNaryArg i getExpr).isLambda then
286-    `({{ $(← withNaryArg i delabAssn) }})
287-  else
288-    withNaryArg i Delaborator.delab
289-
290-/-- Print a bare assertion lambda in `{{ … }}` notation.  Keyed on lambdas
291-at large, so the guards bail out cheaply unless the binder is a `State`
292-and the body is a proposition the printer can rebuild. -/
293-@[delab lam]
294-def delabAssertion : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
295-  let e ← getExpr
296-  guard <| e.isLambda && e.bindingDomain!.isConstOf ``_root_.State
297-  let P ← withBindingBody' `st (pure ·.fvarId!) fun stId => do
298-    guard (← Meta.inferType (← getExpr)).isProp
299-    delabBody stId
300-  `({{ $P }})
301-
302-end Assertion.Delab

305---  ### Assertion Implication
306-
307---  Given two assertions `P` and `Q`, we say that `P`
308---  *implies* `Q`, written `P ->> Q`, if, whenever `P` holds
309---  in some state `st`, `Q` also holds.
310-
311-def AssertImplies (P Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
312-  ∀ st, P st → Q st
313-
314---  Note that the notation for *assertion implication* is
315---  analogous to the "usual" Lean implication `→`.
316-
317-notation:26 P:27 " ->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q
318-
319-theorem assertImplies_def {P Q : Assertion} : P ->> Q ↔ ∀ st, P st → Q st := by rfl
320-
321---  We'll also want the "iff" variant of implication between
322---  assertions:
323-
324-notation:26 P:27 " <<->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q ∧ AssertImplies Q P
325-
326-theorem assertIff_def {P Q : Assertion} : P <<->> Q ↔ AssertImplies P Q ∧ AssertImplies Q P
327-    := by rfl
328-
329---  THE FOLLOWING DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: printing implications back)
330-namespace Assertion.Delab
331-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr
332-
333-@[delab app.AssertImplies]
334-def delabAssertImplies : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
335-  guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``AssertImplies 2
336-  `($(← delabAssnArg 0) ->> $(← delabAssnArg 1))
337-
338-/-- `<<->>` abbreviates a conjunction of two `AssertImplies`, so its
339-delaborator is keyed on `∧` and bails out unless the two conjuncts mirror
340-each other. -/
341-@[delab app.And]
342-def delabAssertIff : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
343-  let e ← getExpr
344-  guard <| e.isAppOfArity ``And 2
345-  let l := e.appFn!.appArg!
346-  let r := e.appArg!
347-  guard <| l.isAppOfArity ``AssertImplies 2 && r.isAppOfArity ``AssertImplies 2
348-  guard <| l.appFn!.appArg! == r.appArg! && l.appArg! == r.appFn!.appArg!
349-  `($(← withNaryArg 0 <| delabAssnArg 0) <<->> $(← withNaryArg 0 <| delabAssnArg 1))
350-
351-end Assertion.Delab

353-
354---  ## Hoare Triples, Informally
355-
356---  A *Hoare triple* is a claim about the state before and
357---  after executing a command. A commond notation for Hoare
358---  triples, and the one we use in this book, is
359---
360---      {{P}} c {{Q}}
361---
362---  meaning:
363---
364---  - If command `c` begins execution in a state satisfying
365---    assertion `P`,
366---
367---  - and if `c` eventually terminates in some final state,
368---
369---  - then that final state will satisfy the assertion `Q`.
370---
371---  Assertion `P` is called the *precondition* of the
372---  triple, and `Q` is the *postcondition*.
373-
374---  For example,
375---
376---  - The Hoare triple
377---
378---      {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
379---
380---  states that command `X := X + 1` will transform a state
381---  in which `X = 0` to a state in which `X = 1`.
382---
383---  - On the other hand,
384---
385---      ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
386---
387---  is a *proposition* stating that the Hoare triple
388---  `{{X = m}} X :=
389---  X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}` is valid for any
390---  choice of `m`. Note that `m` in the two assertions is a
391---  reference to the *Lean* variable `m`, which is bound
392---  outside the Hoare triple.
393-
394---   ----------------------------------------
395-
396---  _Quiz:_
397-
398---  Paraphrase the following in English.
399---
400---      1) {{True}} c {{X = 5}}
401---
402---      2) ∀ m, {{X = m}} c {{X = m + 5}}
403---
404---      3) {{X ≤ Y}} c {{Y ≤ X}}
405---
406---      4) {{True}} c {{False}}
407---
408---      5) ∀ m,
409---           {{X = m}}
410---           c
411---           {{Y = real_fact m}}
412---
413---      6) ∀ m,
414---           {{X = m}}
415---           c
416---           {{(Z * Z) ≤ m ∧ ¬ ((Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ m)}}
417-
418---   ----------------------------------------
419-

423---  claimed relation between `P`, `c`, and `Q` true?
424---
425---      {{True}} X := 5 {{X = 5}}
426---
427---  (A) Yes
428---
429---  (B) No
430-

436---

438---
439---  (A) Yes
440---
441---  (B) No

462---
463---  (A) Yes
464---
465---  (B) No

533---  ## Hoare Triples, Formally
534-
535---  We formalize valid Hoare triples in Lean as follows:
536-
537-open scoped HasEval
538-
539-def ValidHoareTriple
540-    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
541-  ∀ {st st' : State},
542-    (st =[ ~c ]=> st') →
543-    P st →
544-    Q st'
545-
546-class HasTriple (Com : Type) where
547-  Triple : Assertion → Com → Assertion → Prop
548-
549-namespace HasTriple
550-
551-/-- Hoare triple: `{{ P }} c {{ Q }}` with `imp_com` command syntax -/
552-scoped syntax:lead "{{" term "}} " imp_com:lead " {{" term "}}" : term
553-scoped macro_rules
554-  | `({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }}) =>
555-      ``(HasTriple.Triple ({{ $P }}) (imp { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))
556-end HasTriple
557-
558-instance : HasTriple Com where
559-  Triple := ValidHoareTriple
560-
561---  We make `ValidHoareTriple` irreducible for "technical
562---  reasons", and use it only via `validHoareTriple_def` in
563---  proofs.
564-
565-open scoped HasTriple
566-
567-theorem validHoareTriple_def {P : Assertion} {c : Com} {Q : Assertion} :
568-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} ↔ ∀ {st st' : State},
569-      (st =[ ~c ]=> st') →
570-      P st →
571-      Q st' := by rfl
572-
573-attribute [irreducible] ValidHoareTriple
574-
575---  THE FOLLOWING DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: printing triples back)
576---  The delaborator is agnostic to the command type: it
577---  prints the command with whatever printer is registered
578---  for its constructors and splices the result into the
579---  triple, so a language-extension chapter only has to
580---  register a printer for its own `Com`.
581-
582-namespace HasTriple.Delab
583-
584-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Assertion.Delab Imp.Delab
585-@[delab app.HasTriple.Triple]
586-def delabTriple : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
587-  guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``HasTriple.Triple 5
588-  let P ← withNaryArg 2 delabAssn
589-  let c ← withNaryArg 3 delab
590-  let Q ← withNaryArg 4 delabAssn
591-  match c with
592-  | `(imp { $c:imp_com }) => ``({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }})
593-  | c => ``({{ $P }} ~$c {{ $Q }})
594-
595-end HasTriple.Delab

604-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by

615-
616---  ## Proof Rules
617-
618---  We want to be able to *prove* Hoare triples formally.
619---
620---  Here's our plan:
621---
622---  - introduce one "proof rule" for each Imp syntactic form
623---
624---  - plus a couple of "structural rules" that help glue
625---    proofs together
626---
627---  - prove these rules correct in terms of the definition
628---    of `ValidHoareTriple`
629---
630---  - prove programs correct using these proof rules,
631---    without ever unfolding the definition of
632---    `ValidHoareTriple`
633-
634---  ### Skip
635-
636---  Since `skip` doesn't change the state, it preserves any
637---  assertion `P`:
638---
639---      --------------------  (hoare_skip)
640---      {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
641-
642-theorem hoare_skip {P : Assertion} :
643-    {{ P }} skip {{ P }} := by
644-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
645-  intro st st' h hpre
646-  inversion h
647-  exact hpre
648-
649---  ### Sequencing
650-
651---  If command `c1` takes any state where `P` holds to a
652---  state where `Q` holds, and if `c2` takes any state where
653---  `Q` holds to one where `R` holds, then doing `c1`
654---  followed by `c2` will take any state where `P` holds to
655---  one where `R` holds:
656---
657---       {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
658---       {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
659---      ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
660---      {{ P }} c1; c2 {{ R }}
661-
662-theorem hoare_seq {P Q R : Assertion} {c1 c2 : Com}
663-    (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{ R }}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
664-    {{ P }} ~c1; ~c2 {{ R }} := by
665-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
666-  intro st st' h hpre
667-  inversion h with
668-  | seq st'' hc1 hc2 =>
669-    rw [validHoareTriple_def] at h1 h2
670-    exact h1 hc2 (h2 hc1 hpre)
671-
672---  ### Assignment
673-
674---  How can we complete this triple?
675---
676---      {{ ??? }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
677---
678---  One natural possibility is:
679---
680---      {{ Y = 1 }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
681---
682---  The precondition is just the postcondition, but with `X`
683---  replaced by `Y`.
684-
685---  How about this one?
686---
687---      {{ ??? }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
688---
689---  Replace `X` with `X + Y`:
690---
691---      {{ X + Y = 1 }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
692---
693---  This works because "equals 1" holding of `X` is
694---  guaranteed by the property "equals 1" holding of
695---  whatever is being assigned to `X`.
696-
697---  In general, the postcondition could be some arbitrary
698---  assertion `Q`, and the right-hand side of the assignment
699---  could be some arbitrary arithmetic expression `a`:
700---
701---      {{ ??? }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
702---
703---  The precondition would then be `Q`, but with any
704---  occurrences of `X` in it replaced by `a`.
705-
706---  Let's introduce a notation for this idea of replacing
707---  occurrences: Define `Q \[X ↦ a`] to mean "`Q` where `a`
708---  is substituted in place of `X`".
709---
710---  This yields the Hoare logic rule for assignment:
711---
712---      {{ Q [X ↦ a] }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
713---
714---  One way of reading this rule is: If you want statement
715---  `X := a` to terminate in a state that satisfies
716---  assertion `Q`, then it suffices to start in a state that
717---  also satisfies `Q`, except where `a` is substituted for
718---  every occurrence of `X`.
719-
720---  Here are some valid instances of the assignment rule:
721---
722---      {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }}         (that is, X + 1 ≤ 5)
723---        X := X + 1
724---      {{ X ≤ 5 }}
725---
726---      {{ (X = 3) [X ↦ 3] }}              (that is, 3 = 3)
727---        X := 3
728---      {{ X = 3 }}
729---
730---      {{ (0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3] }}.  (that is, 0 ≤ 3 ∧ 3 ≤ 5)
731---        X := 3
732---      {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }}
733-
734---  To formalize the rule, we must first formalize the idea
735---  of "substituting an expression for an Imp variable in an
736---  assertion", which we refer to as assertion substitution,
737---  or `Assertion.subst`.
738---
739---  Intuitively, given a proposition `P`, a variable `X`,
740---  and an arithmetic expression `a`, we want to derive
741---  another proposition `P'` that is just the same as `P`
742---  except that `P'` should mention `a` wherever `P`
743---  mentions `X`.
744-
745---  This operation is related to the idea of substituting
746---  Imp expressions for Imp variables that we saw in *Equiv*
747---  (`subst_aexp` and friends). The difference is that,
748---  here, `P` is an arbitrary Lean assertion, so we can't
749---  directly "edit" its text.
750-
751---  However, we can achieve the same effect by evaluating
752---  `P` in an updated state, defined as follows:
753-
754-def Assertion.subst (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) : Assertion :=
755-  fun (st : State) => P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
756-
757-namespace Assertion
758-
759-/-- Assertion substitution, written inside the braces: `{{ (P) [X ↦ a] }}`.
760-The substituted assertion is re-read with the same notation, so Imp
761-variables in it mean state lookups as usual; a named assertion is passed
762-through directly. -/
763-scoped syntax:max term:arg " [" ident " ↦ " imp_aexp "]" : term
764-
765-macro_rules
766-  | `(assn($st; $P [$x ↦ $a:imp_aexp])) =>
767-    match P with
768-    | `($_:ident) => ``(Assertion.subst $x (aexp { $a }) $P $st)
769-    | _ => ``(Assertion.subst $x (aexp { $a }) ({{ $P }}) $st)
770-
771-theorem subst_def {x : Ident} {a : Aexp} {P : Assertion} :
772-    Assertion.subst x a P = fun (st : State) => P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st) := by rfl
773-
774-@[simp]
775-theorem subst_apply {x : Ident} {a : Aexp} {P : Assertion} {st : State} :
776-    Assertion.subst x a P st ↔ P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st) := by rfl
777-
778-end Assertion
779-
780---  This notation allows us to write this operation as:
781---
782---      P [ X ↦ a ]
783-
784-#check (fun st => Assertion.subst X (aexp { 2 * X }) ({{ X ≤ 10 }}) st)
785-#check {{ (X ≤ 10) [X ↦ 2 * X] }}
786-#check (∀ st, ({{ (X ≤ 10) [X ↦ 2 * X] }}) st)
787-
788---  THE FOLLOWING DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: printing substitutions back)
789-namespace Assertion.Delab
790-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Imp.Delab
791-
792-/-- Print an `Assertion.subst` back in `P [x ↦ a]` notation.  Emits the
793-bare inside-the-braces form: the generic application case of `delabBody`
794-picks it up inside an assertion body, and the enclosing printer supplies
795-the single pair of braces. -/
796-@[delab app.Assertion.subst]
797-def delabSub : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
798-  guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``Assertion.subst 3
799-  let `($x:ident) ← withNaryArg 0 delab | failure
800-  let a ← withNaryArg 1 delabAexpInner
801-  if (← withNaryArg 2 getExpr).isLambda then
802-    `(($(← withNaryArg 2 delabAssn)) [$x:ident ↦ $a:imp_aexp])
803-  else
804-    match ← withNaryArg 2 delab with
805-    | `($P:ident) => `($P:ident [$x:ident ↦ $a:imp_aexp])
806-    | P => `(($P) [$x:ident ↦ $a:imp_aexp])
807-
808-end Assertion.Delab
809---  END DETAILS
810-
811---  That is, `P [X ↦ a]` stands for an assertion -- let's
812---  call it `P'` -- that behaves just like `P` except that,
813---  wherever `P` looks up the variable `X` in the current
814---  state, `P'` instead uses the value of the expression
815---  `a`.
816-
817---  We can demonstrate formally that we have captured
818---  intuitive meaning of "assertion subsitution" by proving
819---  some example logical equivalences:
820-
821-namespace ExampleAssertionSub
822-example :
823-    {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3] }} <<->> {{ 3 ≤ 5 }} := by
824-  rw [assertIff_def]
825-  rw [assertImplies_def]
826-  constructor
827-  · intro st _
828-    simp
829-  · intro st h
830-    simp
831-
832-example :
833-    {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }} <<->> {{ (X + 1) ≤ 5 }} := by
834-  rw [assertIff_def]
835-  constructor
836-  · rw [assertImplies_def]
837-    intro st
838-    simp
839-  · rw [assertImplies_def]
840-    intro st
841-    simp
842-
843-end ExampleAssertionSub
844-
845---  Most of the `simp` calls rely on
846---  `Assertion.subst_apply`, `TotalMap.update_eq` plus some
847---  `Aexp` characterizing lemmas like `Aexp.eval_num`.
848-
849---  Now, using the substitution operation we've just
850---  defined, we can give the precise proof rule for
851---  assignment:
852---
853---      ---------------------------- (hoare_asgn)
854---      {{Q [X ↦ a]}} X := a {{Q}}
855---
856---  We can prove formally that this rule is indeed valid.
857-
858-theorem hoare_asgn {Q : Assertion} {x : Ident} {a : Aexp} :
859-    {{ Q [x ↦ ~a] }} x := ~a {{ Q }} := by
860-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
861-  intro st st' hE hQ
862-  inversion hE with
863-  | asgn n h =>
864-    subst h
865-    rw [Assertion.subst_def] at hQ
866-    exact hQ
867-
868---  Here's a first formal proof of a Hoare triple using this
869---  rule.
870-
871-theorem assertion_sub_example :
872-    {{ (X < 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }}
873-      X := X + 1
874-    {{ X < 5 }} := by
875-  exact hoare_asgn
876-
877---  Of course, we'd probably prefer to work with this
878---  simpler triple:
879---
880---      {{X < 4}} X := X + 1 {{X < 5}}
881---
882---  We will see how to do so in the next section.
883---
884---  Several proofs below use the facts about total-map
885---  updates proved in the *Typeclasses* chapter --
886---  `TotalMap.update_eq`, `TotalMap.update_neq`,
887---  `TotalMap.update_shadow`, `TotalMap.update_same`, and
888---  `TotalMap.update_permute`. Make sure you understand
889---  their statements.
890-
891---  ### Consequence
892-
893---  Sometimes the preconditions and postconditions we get
894---  from the Hoare rules won't quite be the ones we want in
895---  the particular situation at hand -- they may be
896---  logically equivalent but have a different syntactic form
897---  that fails to unify with the goal we are trying to
898---  prove, or they actually may be logically weaker (for
899---  preconditions) or stronger (for postconditions) than
900---  what we need.
901-
902---  For instance,
903---
904---      {{(X = 3) [X ↦ 3]}} X := 3 {{X = 3}},
905---
906---  follows directly from the assignment rule, but
907---
908---      {{True}} X := 3 {{X = 3}}
909---
910---  does not. This triple is valid, but it is not an
911---  instance of `hoare_asgn` because `True` and
912---  `(X = 3) \[X ↦ 3`] are not syntactically equal
913---  assertions.
914---
915---  However, they are logically *equivalent*, so if one
916---  triple is valid, then the other must certainly be as
917---  well. We can capture this observation with the following
918---  rule:
919---
920---         {{P'}} c {{Q}}
921---           P <<->> P'
922---      ---------------------
923---         {{P}} c {{Q}}
924-
925---  Taking this line of thought a bit further, we can see
926---  that strengthening the precondition or weakening the
927---  postcondition of a valid triple always produces another
928---  valid triple. This observation is captured by two *Rules
929---  of Consequence*.
930---
931---             {{P'}} c {{Q}}
932---                P ->> P'
933---      -----------------------------   (hoare_consequence_pre)
934---             {{P}} c {{Q}}
935---
936---             {{P}} c {{Q'}}
937---               Q' ->> Q
938---      -----------------------------    (hoare_consequence_post)
939---             {{P}} c {{Q}}
940-
941---  Here are the formal versions:
942-
943-theorem hoare_consequence_pre {P P' Q : Assertion} {c : Com}
944-    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
945-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
946-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
947-  intro st st' heval hpre
948-  apply hhoare heval
949-  rw [assertImplies_def] at himp
950-  exact himp _ hpre
951-
952-theorem hoare_consequence_post {P Q Q' : Assertion} {c : Com}
953-    (hhoare : {{ P }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (himp : Q' ->> Q) :
954-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by

956-  intro st st' heval hpre
957-  rw [assertImplies_def] at himp
958-  apply himp
959-  exact hhoare heval hpre

991---  Finally, here is a combined rule of consequence that
992---  allows us to vary both the precondition and the
993---  postcondition.

996---                P ->> P'
997---                Q' ->> Q

1001-theorem hoare_consequence {P P' Q Q' : Assertion} {c : Com}
1002-    (htriple : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (hpre : P ->> P') (hpost : Q' ->> Q) :
1003-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1004-  apply hoare_consequence_pre (P' := P')
1005-  · exact hoare_consequence_post htriple hpost
1006-  · exact hpre

1008---  ### Automation
1009-
1010---  Many of the proofs we have done so far with Hoare
1011---  triples can be streamlined using the automation
1012---  techniques that we introduced in the *Automation*
1013---  chapter of *Logical Foundations*.
1014---
1015---  Recall that `simp` rewrites with any lemmas we pass it.
1016---  The definitions whose meaning we keep needing to expose
1017---  in this chapter -- `ValidHoareTriple`, `AssertImplies`,
1018---  and `Assertion.subst` -- each come with a characterizing
1019---  lemma (`validHoareTriple_def`, `assertImplies_def`,
1020---  `Assertion.subst_def`) restating the definition as an
1021---  equation. Passing these lemmas to `simp` replaces the
1022---  defined notions by their meanings wherever they appear.
1023---  We'll do that explicitly below (and shortly package the
1024---  recipe up as a tactic of our own).
1025-
1026---  Here's a good candidate for automation:
1027-
1028---      theorem hoare_consequence_pre (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1029---          (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1030---          {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1031---        rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
1032---        intro st st' heval hpre
1033---        apply hhoare heval
1034---        rw [assertImplies_def] at himp
1035---        exact himp _ hpre
1036-
1037---  Since `AssertImplies` is not marked `irreducible`, and
1038---  `assertImplies_def` is a proof by definitional equality,
1039---  we can skip the `rw [assertImplies_def] at himp` and use
1040---  `P ->> P'` like an implication directly.
1041-
1042-theorem hoare_consequence_pre' (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1043-    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1044-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1045-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
1046-  intro st st' heval hpre
1047-  apply hhoare heval
1048-  exact himp _ hpre
1049-
1050---  From now on, we will not usually rewrite
1051---  `assertImplies_def` explicitly.
1052---
1053---  Since, after the `rw` and `intro`, the remaining steps
1054---  just apply hypotheses to the goal (and each other), the
1055---  remaining proof can be compressed into a single tactic:
1056---  `apply_rules`.
1057-
1058-theorem hoare_consequence_pre'' (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1059-    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1060-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1061-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
1062-  intro st st' heval hpre
1063-  apply_rules
1064-
1065---  The same trick works for `hoare_consequence_post`.
1066-
1067-theorem hoare_consequence_post' (P Q Q' : Assertion) (c : Com)
1068-    (hhoare : {{ P }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (himp : Q' ->> Q) :
1069-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1070-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
1071-  intro st st' heval hpre
1072-  apply_rules

1081-  · -- The goal is `{{?P'}} X := 1 {{X = 1}}`
1082-    exact hoare_asgn -- Assigns `?P'` to `{{ (X = 1) [X ↦ 1] }}` (automatically closing `case P'`)
1083-  · intro st _ -- Since `->>` is an implication, we can just use `intro` directly.
1084-    simp

1122-                                Assertion.subst_def] at *

1139---  Again, we have quite a nice proof script. All the
1140---  low-level details of proofs about assertions have been

1142---  isn't able to prove everything we could possibly want to

1146---  ### Sequencing + Assignment
1147-
1148---  Here's an example of a program involving both sequencing
1149---  and assignment. Note the use of `hoare_seq` in
1150---  conjunction with `hoare_consequence_pre` and `apply`'s
1151---  metavariables.
1152-
1153-theorem hoare_asgn_example3 (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
1154-    {{a = n}}
1155-      X := ~a;
1156-      skip
1157-    {{X = n}} := by
1158-  apply hoare_seq
1159-  · -- right part of seq
1160-    exact hoare_skip
1161-  · -- left part of seq
1162-    apply hoare_consequence_pre
1163-    · exact hoare_asgn
1164-    · assertion_auto
1165-
1166---  Informally, a nice way of displaying a proof using the
1167---  sequencing rule is as a "decorated program" where the
1168---  intermediate assertion `Q` is written between `c1` and
1169---  `c2`:
1170---
1171---               {{ a = n }}
1172---      X := a
1173---               {{ X = n }};    <--- decoration for Q
1174---      skip
1175---               {{ X = n }}
1176---
1177---  We'll come back to the idea of decorated programs in
1178---  much more detail in the next chapter.
1179-
1180---  ### Conditionals
1181-
1182---  What sort of rule do we want for reasoning about
1183---  conditional commands?
1184---
1185---  Certainly, if the same assertion `Q` holds after
1186---  executing either of the branches, then it holds after
1187---  the whole conditional. So we might be tempted to write:
1188---
1189---              {{P}} c1 {{Q}}
1190---              {{P}} c2 {{Q}}
1191---      ---------------------------------
1192---      {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 {{Q}}
1193-
1194---  However, this is rather weak. For example, using this
1195---  rule, we cannot show
1196---
1197---      {{ True }}
1198---        if X = 0
1199---          then Y := 2
1200---          else Y := X + 1
1201---        end
1202---      {{ X ≤ Y }}
1203---
1204---  since the rule doesn't tell us enough about the state in
1205---  which the assignments take place in the "then" and
1206---  "else" branches.
1207-
1208---  Better:
1209-
1210---      {{P ∧   b}} c1 {{Q}}
1211---      {{P ∧ ¬ b}} c2 {{Q}}
1212---      ------------------------------------  (hoare_if)
1213---      {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 end {{Q}}
1214-
1215-theorem bexp_eval_false (b : Bexp) (st : State) (h : b.eval st = false) :
1216-    ¬ ({{ b }}) st := by
1217-  dsimp
1218-  simp [h]
1219-
1220---  Now we can formalize the Hoare proof rule for
1221---  conditionals and prove it correct.
1222---
1223---  The statement of the rule reads: given
1224---  `htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c1 {{Q}}` and
1225---  `hfalse : {{ P ∧ ¬b }} ~c2 {{Q}}`, we can conclude
1226---  `{{P}} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{Q}}`.
1227-
1228-theorem hoare_if {P Q : Assertion} {b : Bexp} {c1 c2 : Com}
1229-    (htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) (hfalse : {{ P ∧ ¬ b }} ~c2 {{ Q }}) :
1230-    {{ P }} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{ Q }} := by
1231-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at htrue hfalse ⊢
1232-  intro st st' hE hpre
1233-  inversion hE with
1234-  | ifTrue hb hc1 =>
1235-    exact htrue hc1 ⟨hpre, hb⟩
1236-  | ifFalse hb hc =>
1237-    rw [← Bool.not_eq_true] at hb
1238-    exact hfalse hc ⟨hpre, hb⟩
1239-
1240---  #### Example
1241-
1242-theorem if_example :
1243-    {{True}}
1244-      if (X = 0) {
1245-        Y := 2
1246-      } else {
1247-        Y := X + 1
1248-      }
1249-    {{X ≤ Y}} := by
1250-  apply hoare_if
1251-  · -- Then
1252-    apply hoare_consequence_pre
1253-    · exact hoare_asgn
1254-    · assertion_auto
1255-  · -- Else
1256-    apply hoare_consequence_pre
1257-    · exact hoare_asgn
1258-    · assertion_auto
1259-
1260---  We can even shorten it a little bit more.
1261-
1262-theorem if_example' :
1263-    {{True}}
1264-      if (X = 0) {
1265-        Y := 2
1266-      } else {
1267-        Y := X + 1
1268-      }
1269-    {{X ≤ Y}} := by
1270-  apply hoare_if <;> apply hoare_consequence_pre hoare_asgn (by assertion_auto)

1272---  ### While Loops
1273-
1274---  The Hoare rule for `while` loops is based on the idea of
1275---  a *command invariant* (or just *invariant*): an
1276---  assertion whose truth is guaranteed after executing a
1277---  command, assuming it is true before.
1278---
1279---  That is, an assertion `P` is a command invariant of `c`
1280---  if
1281---
1282---      {{P}} c {{P}}
1283---
1284---  holds. Note that the command invariant might temporarily
1285---  become false in the middle of executing `c`, but by the
1286---  end of `c` it must be restored.
1287-
1288---  The Hoare while rule combines the idea of a command
1289---  invariant with information about when guard `b` does or
1290---  does not hold.
1291---
1292---            {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
1293---      --------------------------------- (hoare_while)
1294---      {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
1295-
1296-theorem hoare_while {P : Assertion} {b : Bexp} {c : Com}
1297-    (hhoare : {{P ∧ b}} ~c {{ P }}) :
1298-    {{ P }} while (~b) { ~c } {{P ∧ ¬ b}} := by
1299-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
1300-  intro st st' heval hpre
1301-  /- We proceed by induction on `heval`, because, in the "keep
1302-  looping" case, its hypotheses talk about the whole loop instead
1303-  of just `c`. We begin by generalizing over an
1304-  arbitrary command, together with an equation remembering that the
1305-  command is the original loop. The cases for commands other than
1306-  `while` are dismissed because their equations are contradictory. -/
1307-  generalize heq : (imp { while (~b) { ~c } }) = cmd at heval
1308-  induction heval with
1309-  | @whileFalse b0 s0 c0 hb =>
1310-    injection heq with hbeq hceq
1311-    simp_all
1312-  | @whileTrue s0 s0' s0'' b0 c0 hb hc hloop ih1 ih2 =>
1313-    injection heq with hbeq hceq
1314-    subst hbeq hceq
1315-    exact ih2 (hhoare hc ⟨hpre, hb⟩) rfl
1316-  | skip | asgn | seq | ifTrue | ifFalse =>
1317-    contradiction
1318-
1319---  We call `P` a *loop invariant* of `while b do c end` if
1320---
1321---      {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
1322---
1323---  is a valid Hoare triple.
1324---
1325---  This means that `P` will be true at the end of the loop
1326---  body whenever the loop body executes. If `P` contradicts
1327---  `b`, this holds trivially since the precondition is
1328---  false.
1329---
1330---  For instance, `X = 0` is a loop invariant of
1331---
1332---      while X = 2 do X := 1 end
1333---
1334---  since the program will never enter the loop.
1335-

1450---  ## Summary
1451-
1452---  The rules of Hoare Logic are:
1453---
1454---             --------------------------- (hoare_asgn)
1455---             {{Q [X ↦ a]}} X:=a {{Q}}
1456---
1457---             --------------------  (hoare_skip)
1458---             {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
1459---
1460---               {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
1461---               {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
1462---              ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
1463---              {{ P }} c1;c2 {{ R }}
1464---
1465---              {{P ∧   b}} c1 {{Q}}
1466---              {{P ∧ ¬ b}} c2 {{Q}}
1467---      ------------------------------------  (hoare_if)
1468---      {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 end {{Q}}
1469---
1470---               {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
1471---        -----------------------------------  (hoare_while)
1472---        {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬ b}}
1473---
1474---                {{P'}} c {{Q'}}
1475---                   P ->> P'
1476---                   Q' ->> Q
1477---         -----------------------------   (hoare_consequence)
1478---                {{P}} c {{Q}}
1479-
1480---  Our main task in this chapter has been to *define* the
1481---  rules of Hoare logic, and prove that the definitions are
1482---  sound. Having done so, we can go on and work *within*
1483---  Hoare logic to prove that particular programs satisfy
1484---  particular Hoare triples. In the next chapter, we'll see
1485---  how Hoare logic is can be used to prove that more
1486---  interesting programs satisfy interesting specifications
1487---  of their behavior.
1488---
1489---  Crucially, we will do so without ever again `unfold`ing
1490---  the definition of Hoare triples -- i.e., we will take
1491---  the rules of Hoare logic as a closed world for reasoning
1492---  about programs.
1493-

68-
69---  ## Decorated Programs
70-
71---  The beauty of Hoare Logic is that it is *syntax
72---  directed*: the structure of proofs exactly follows the
73---  structure of programs.
74---
75---  We can record the essential ideas of a Hoare-logic proof
76---  — omitting low-level calculational details — by
77---  "decorating" a program with appropriate assertions on
78---  each of its commands.
79---
80---  Such a *decorated program* carries within itself an
81---  argument for its own correctness.
82-
83---  For example, consider the program:
84---
85---      X := m;
86---      Z := p;
87---      while X <> 0 do
88---        Z := Z - 1;
89---        X := X - 1
90---      end
91-
92---  Here is one possible specification for this program, in
93---  the form of a Hoare triple:
94---
95---      {{ True }}
96---      X := m;
97---      Z := p;
98---      while X <> 0 do
99---        Z := Z - 1;
100---        X := X - 1
101---      end
102---      {{ Z = p - m }}
103-
104---  Here is a decorated version of this program, embodying a
105---  proof of this specification:
106---
107---      {{ True }} ->>
108---      {{ m = m }}
109---        X := m
110---                           {{ X = m }} ->>
111---                           {{ X = m /\ p = p }};
112---        Z := p;
113---                           {{ X = m /\ Z = p }} ->>
114---                           {{ Z - X = p - m }}
115---        while X <> 0 do
116---                           {{ Z - X = p - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
117---                           {{ (Z - 1) - (X - 1) = p - m }}
118---          Z := Z - 1
119---                           {{ Z - (X - 1) = p - m }};
120---          X := X - 1
121---                           {{ Z - X = p - m }}
122---        end
123---      {{ Z - X = p - m /\ ~ (X <> 0) }} ->>
124---      {{ Z = p - m }}
125-
126---  Concretely, a decorated program consists of the
127---  program's text interleaved with assertions (sometimes
128---  multiple assertions separated by ->>).
129-
130---  A decorated program can be viewed as a compact
131---  representation of a proof in Hoare Logic: the assertions
132---  surrounding each command specify the Hoare triple to be
133---  proved for that part of the program using one of the
134---  Hoare Logic rules, and the structure of the program
135---  itself shows how to assemble all these individual steps
136---  into a proof for the whole program.
137-
138---  ### Example: Swapping
139-
140---  Consider the following program, which swaps the values
141---  of two variables using addition and subtraction, instead
142---  of by assigning to a temporary variable.
143---
144---      X := X + Y;
145---      Y := X - Y;
146---      X := X - Y
147---
148---  We can give a proof, in the form of decorations, that
149---  this program is correct — i.e., it really swaps `X` and
150---  `Y` — as follows.
151-
152---  WORK IN CLASS
153-
154---  ### Example: Simple Conditionals
155-
156---  Here's a simple program using conditionals, along with a
157---  possible specification:
158---
159---      {{ True }}
160---        if X <= Y then
161---          Z := Y - X
162---        else
163---          Z := X - Y
164---        end
165---      {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
166---
167---  Let's turn it into a decorated program...
168-
169---  WORK IN CLASS
170-
171---  ### Example: Reduce to Zero
172-
173---  Here is a very simple `while` loop with a simple
174---  specification:
175---
176---      {{ True }}
177---        while (X <> 0) do
178---          X := X - 1
179---        end
180---      {{ X = 0 }}
181-
182---  WORK IN CLASS
183-
184---  ### Example: Division
185-
186---  Let's do one more example of simple reasoning about a
187---  loop.
188---
189---  The following Imp program calculates the integer
190---  quotient and remainder of parameters `m` and `n`.
191---
192---      X := m;
193---      Y := 0;
194---      while n <= X do
195---        X := X - n;
196---        Y := Y + 1
197---      end;
198---
199---  If we replace `m` and `n` by concrete numbers and
200---  execute the program, it will terminate with the variable
201---  `X` set to the remainder when `m` is divided by `n` and
202---  `Y` set to the quotient.
203-
204---  Here's a possible specification:
205---
206---      {{ True }}
207---        X := m;
208---        Y := 0;
209---        while n <= X do
210---          X := X - n;
211---          Y := Y + 1
212---        end
213---      {{ n * Y + X = m /\ X < n }}
214-
215---  WORK IN CLASS
216-
217---  ### From Decorated Programs to Formal Proofs
218-
219---  From an informal proof in the form of a decorated
220---  program, it is "easy in principle" to read off a formal
221---  proof using the Lean theorems corresponding to the Hoare
222---  Logic rules, but these proofs can be a bit long and
223---  fiddly.
224-
225---  For example...
226-
227-def reduceToZero : Com :=
228-  imp {
229-    while (X ≠ 0) {
230-      X := X - 1
231-    }
232-  }
233-
234-theorem reduce_to_zero_correct' :
235-    {{ True }} ~reduceToZero {{ X = 0 }} := by
236-  -- First put the postcondition into the form expected by
237-  -- the while rule.
238-  sorry
239-
240---  A little more (OK, quite a bit more) tactic fanciness
241---  for helping deal with the boring parts of the process of
242---  proving assertions:
243-
244-macro "verify_assertion" : tactic =>
245-  `(tactic| assertion_auto)
246-
247---  This makes it pretty easy to verify `reduce_to_zero`:
248-
249-theorem reduce_to_zero_correct''' :
250-    {{ True }} ~reduceToZero {{ X = 0 }} := by
251-  sorry
252-
253---  This example shows that it is conceptually
254---  straightforward to read off the main elements of a
255---  formal proof from a decorated program. Indeed, the
256---  process is so straightforward that it can be automated,
257---  as we will see next.
258-
259---  ## Formal Decorated Programs
260-
261---  With a little more work, we can *formalize* the
262---  definition of well-formed decorated programs and
263---  *automate* the boring mechanical steps in proving that
264---  the decorations are correct.
265-
266---  ### Syntax
267-
268---  The first thing we need to do is to formalize a variant
269---  of the syntax of Imp commands that includes embedded
270---  assertions, which we'll call "decorations." We call the
271---  new commands *decorated commands*, or `dcom`s.
272---
273---  The choice of exactly where to put assertions in the
274---  definition of `dcom` is a bit subtle. The simplest thing
275---  to do would be to annotate every `dcom` with a
276---  precondition and postcondition — something like this...
277-
278-namespace DComFirstTry
279-
280-inductive DCom where
281-  | skip (pre : Assertion)
282-  | seq (pre : Assertion) (first : DCom)
283-      (middle : Assertion)
284-      (second : DCom) (post : Assertion)
285-  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (post : Assertion)
286-  | cond (pre : Assertion) (b : Bexp)
287-      (thenPre : Assertion) (thenBranch : DCom)
288-      (elsePre : Assertion) (elseBranch : DCom)
289-      (post : Assertion)
290-  | whileDo (pre : Assertion) (b : Bexp)
291-      (bodyPre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
292-      (bodyPost : Assertion) (post : Assertion)
293-  | strengthenPre (pre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
294-  | weakenPost (body : DCom) (post : Assertion)
295-
296-end DComFirstTry
297-
298---  But this would result in *very* verbose decorated
299---  programs with a lot of repeated annotations: a simple
300---  program like `skip;skip` would be decorated like this,
301---
302---      {{P}} ({{P}} skip {{P}}) ; ({{P}} skip {{P}}) {{P}}
303---
304---  with pre- and post-conditions around each `skip`, plus
305---  identical pre- and post-conditions on the semicolon!
306-
307---  In other words, we don't want both preconditions and
308---  postconditions on each command, because a sequence of
309---  two commands would contain redundant decorations — the
310---  postcondition of the first likely being the same as the
311---  precondition of the second.
312---
313---  Instead, our formal syntax of decorated commands will
314---  omit preconditions whenever possible and embed just
315---  postconditions.
316-
317---  - The `skip` command, for example, is decorated only
318---    with its postcondition
319---
320---      skip {{ Q }}
321---
322---  on the assumption that the precondition will be provided
323---  by somebody else.
324---
325---  We carry the same assumption through the other syntactic
326---  forms: each decorated command is assumed to carry its
327---  own postcondition within itself but take its
328---  precondition from its context in which it is used.
329-
330---  - Sequences `d1 ; d2` need no additional decorations.
331---
332---  Why?
333---
334---  Because inside `d2` there will be a postcondition, which
335---  also serves as the postcondition of `d1;d2`.
336---
337---  Similarly, inside `d1` there will also be a
338---  postcondition, which additionally serves as the
339---  *precondition* for `d2`.
340-
341---  - An assignment `X := a` is decorated only with its
342---    postcondition:
343---
344---      X := a {{ Q }}
345-
346---  - A conditional `if b then d1 else d2` is decorated with
347---    a postcondition for the entire statement, as well as
348---    preconditions for each branch:
349---
350---      if b then {{ P1 }} d1 else {{ P2 }} d2 end {{ Q }}
351-
352---  - A loop `while b do d end` is decorated with its final
353---    postcondition plus a precondition for the body:
354---
355---      while b do {{ P }} d end {{ Q }}
356---
357---  The postcondition embedded in `d` serves as the loop
358---  invariant.
359-
360---  - Implications `->>` can be added as decorations either
361---    for a precondition...
362---
363---      ->> {{ P }} d
364---
365---  ...or for a postcondition:
366---
367---      d ->> {{ Q }}
368---
369---  The former is waiting for another precondition to be
370---  supplied by the context; the latter relies on the
371---  postcondition already embedded in `d`.
372-
373---  Putting this all together gives us the formal syntax of
374---  decorated commands:
375-
376-inductive DCom where
377-  | skip (post : Assertion)
378-  | seq (first second : DCom)
379-  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (post : Assertion)
380-  | cond (b : Bexp)
381-      (thenPre : Assertion) (thenBranch : DCom)
382-      (elsePre : Assertion) (elseBranch : DCom)
383-      (post : Assertion)
384-  | whileDo (b : Bexp) (bodyPre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
385-      (post : Assertion)
386-  | pre (pre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
387-  | post (body : DCom) (post : Assertion)
388-
389---  Lean keeps decorated-command notation in its own syntax
390---  category, `dcom`, so it can coexist with the ordinary
391---  Imp command syntax.
392-
393---  THE FOLLOWING DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: decorated commands)
394-declare_syntax_cat dcom
395-
396-syntax:max "(" dcom ")" : dcom
397-syntax:max "skip" " {{" term "}}" : dcom
398-syntax:max ident " := " imp_aexp " {{" term "}}" : dcom
399-syntax:20 dcom:21 ";" ppLine dcom:20 : dcom
400-syntax:max "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "then" ppLine
401-  "{{" term "}}" ppLine dcom ppLine
402-  "else" ppLine "{{" term "}}" ppLine dcom ppLine
403-  "end" ppLine "{{" term "}}" : dcom
404-syntax:max "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "do" ppLine
405-  "{{" term "}}" ppLine dcom ppLine
406-  "end" ppLine "{{" term "}}" : dcom
407-syntax:5 "->>" " {{" term "}}" ppLine dcom:0 : dcom
408-syntax:5 dcom:6 ppLine "->>" " {{" term "}}" : dcom
409-
410-syntax:min "dcom" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine dcom
411-  ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
412-
413-macro_rules
414-  | `(dcom { ($body:dcom) }) =>
415-      `(dcom { $body })
416-  | `(dcom { skip {{ $q }} }) =>
417-      `(DCom.skip ({{ $q }}))
418-  | `(dcom { $x:ident := $a:imp_aexp {{ $q }} }) =>
419-      `(DCom.asgn $x (aexp { $a }) ({{ $q }}))
420-  | `(dcom { $d1:dcom; $d2:dcom }) =>
421-      `(DCom.seq (dcom { $d1 }) (dcom { $d2 }))
422-  | `(dcom {
423-        if ($b:imp_bexp) then
424-          {{ $p1 }}
425-          $d1:dcom
426-        else
427-          {{ $p2 }}
428-          $d2:dcom
429-        end
430-          {{ $q }}
431-      }) =>
432-      `(DCom.cond (bexp { $b })
433-        ({{ $p1 }}) (dcom { $d1 })
434-        ({{ $p2 }}) (dcom { $d2 })
435-        ({{ $q }}))
436-  | `(dcom {
437-        while ($b:imp_bexp) do
438-          {{ $p }}
439-          $body:dcom
440-        end
441-          {{ $q }}
442-      }) =>
443-      `(DCom.whileDo (bexp { $b }) ({{ $p }})
444-        (dcom { $body }) ({{ $q }}))
445-  | `(dcom { ->> {{ $p }} $body:dcom }) =>
446-      `(DCom.pre ({{ $p }}) (dcom { $body }))
447-  | `(dcom { $body:dcom ->> {{ $q }} }) =>
448-      `(DCom.post (dcom { $body }) ({{ $q }}))
449---  END DETAILS
450-
451---  (We then need to redefine all our Notations to get nice
452---  concrete syntax for `dcom`.)
453-
454---  To provide the initial precondition that goes at the
455---  very top of a decorated program, we introduce a new type
456---  `decorated`:
457-
458-structure Decorated where
459-  pre : Assertion
460-  body : DCom
461-
462-example : DCom :=
463-  .skip ({{ True }})
464-
465-example : DCom :=
466-  .whileDo (bexp {true}) ({{ True }})
467-    (.skip ({{ True }})) ({{ True }})
468-
469---  To inspect the fully elaborated term behind this
470---  notation, put `set_option pp.all true in` before a
471---  `#check` or `#print` command.
472---
473---  The formal definitions can use either constructors
474---  directly or the decorated-command notation introduced
475---  above.
476-
477---  An example `decorated` program that decrements `X` to
478---  `0`:
479-
480-def decWhile : Decorated where
481-  pre := ({{ True }})
482-  body := dcom {
483-    while (X ≠ 0) do
484-      {{ True ∧ ¬ X = 0 }}
485-      X := X - 1 {{ True }}
486-    end
487-      {{ True ∧ X = 0 }}
488-    ->> {{ X = 0 }}
489-  }
490-
491---  It is easy to go from a `dcom` to a `com` by erasing all
492---  annotations.
493-
494-def DCom.erase (d : DCom) : Com :=
495-  match d with
496-  | .skip _ => .skip
497-  | .seq d1 d2 => .seq d1.erase d2.erase
498-  | .asgn x a _ => .asgn x a
499-  | .cond b _ d1 _ d2 _ => .cond b d1.erase d2.erase
500-  | .whileDo b _ body _ => .whileDo b body.erase
501-  | .pre _ body => body.erase
502-  | .post body _ => body.erase
503-
504-def Decorated.erase (dec : Decorated) : Com :=
505-  dec.body.erase
506-
507---  It is also straightforward to extract the precondition
508---  and postcondition from a decorated program.
509-
510-def Decorated.precondition (dec : Decorated) : Assertion :=
511-  dec.pre
512-
513-def DCom.postcondition (d : DCom) : Assertion :=
514-  match d with
515-  | .skip q => q
516-  | .seq _ d2 => d2.postcondition
517-  | .asgn _ _ q => q
518-  | .cond _ _ _ _ _ q => q
519-  | .whileDo _ _ _ q => q
520-  | .pre _ body => body.postcondition
521-  | .post _ q => q
522-
523-def Decorated.postcondition (dec : Decorated) : Assertion :=
524-  dec.body.postcondition
525-
526---  We can then express what it means for a decorated
527---  program to be correct as follows:
528-
529-def Decorated.OuterTripleValid (dec : Decorated) : Prop :=
530-  ValidHoareTriple dec.precondition dec.erase
531-    dec.postcondition
532-
533---  For example:
534-
535-example :
536-    decWhile.OuterTripleValid =
537-      {{ True }}
538-        while (X ≠ 0) {
539-          X := X - 1
540-        }
541-      {{ X = 0 }} := by
542-  rfl
543-
544---  The outer Hoare triple of a decorated program is just a
545---  `Prop`; thus, to show that it is *valid*, we need to
546---  produce a proof of this proposition.
547---
548---  We will do this by extracting "proof obligations" from
549---  the decorations sprinkled throughout the program.
550---
551---  These obligations are often called *verification
552---  conditions*, because they are the facts that must be
553---  verified to see that the decorations are locally
554---  consistent and thus constitute a proof of validity of
555---  the outer triple.
556-
557---  ### Extracting Verification Conditions
558-
559---  The function `DCom.VerificationConditions` takes a
560---  decorated command `d` together with a precondition `P`
561---  and returns a *proposition* that, if it can be proved,
562---  implies that the triple
563---
564---      {{P}} d.erase {{d.postcondition}}
565---
566---  is valid.
567---
568---  It does this by walking over `d` and generating a big
569---  conjunction that includes
570---
571---  - local consistency checks for each form of command,
572---    plus
573---
574---  - uses of `->>` to bridge the gap between the assertions
575---    found inside a decorated command and the assertions
576---    imposed by the external precondition; these uses
577---    correspond to applications of the consequence rule.
578-
579---  *Local consistency* is defined as follows...
580---
581---  - The decorated command
582---
583---      skip {{Q}}
584---
585---  is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P`
586---  if `P ->> Q`.
587-
588---  - The sequential composition of `d1` and `d2` is locally
589---    consistent with respect to `P` if `d1` is locally
590---    consistent with respect to `P` and `d2` is locally
591---    consistent with respect to the postcondition of `d1`.
592-
593---  - An assignment
594---
595---      X := a {{Q}}
596---
597---  is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P`
598---  if:
599---
600---      P ->> Q [X |-> a]
601-
602---  - A conditional
603---
604---      if b then {{P1}} d1 else {{P2}} d2 end {{Q}}
605---
606---  is locally consistent with respect to precondition `P`
607---  if
608---
609---  (1) `P /\ b ->> P1`
610---
611---  (2) `P /\ ~b ->> P2`
612---
613---  (3) `d1` is locally consistent with respect to `P1`
614---
615---  (4) `d2` is locally consistent with respect to `P2`
616---
617---  (5) `d1.postcondition ->> Q`
618---
619---  (6) `d2.postcondition ->> Q`
620-
621---  - A loop
622---
623---      while b do {{Q}} d end {{R}}
624---
625---  is locally consistent with respect to precondition `P`
626---  if:
627---
628---  (1) `P ->> d.postcondition`
629---
630---  (2) `d.postcondition /\ b ->> Q`
631---
632---  (3) `d.postcondition /\ ~b ->> R`
633---
634---  (4) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `Q`
635-
636---  - A command with an extra assertion at the beginning
637---
638---      ->> {{Q}} d
639---
640---  is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P`
641---  if:
642---
643---  (1) `P ->> Q`
644---
645---  (2) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `Q`
646-
647---  - A command with an extra assertion at the end
648---
649---      d ->> {{Q}}
650---
651---  is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P`
652---  if:
653---
654---  (1) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `P`
655---
656---  (2) `d.postcondition ->> Q`
657-
658---  With all this in mind, we can write a *verification
659---  condition generator* that takes a decorated command and
660---  reads off a proposition saying that all its decorations
661---  are locally consistent.
662---
663---  Formally, since a decorated command is "waiting for its
664---  precondition" the main VC generator takes a `dcom` plus
665---  a given precondition as arguments.
666-
667-def DCom.VerificationConditions
668-    (P : Assertion) (d : DCom) : Prop :=
669-  match d with
670-  | .skip Q =>
671-      P ->> Q
672-  | .seq d1 d2 =>
673-      d1.VerificationConditions P ∧
674-      d2.VerificationConditions d1.postcondition
675-  | .asgn x a Q =>
676-      P ->> {{ Q [x ↦ ~a] }}
677-  | .cond b P1 d1 P2 d2 Q =>
678-      ({{ P ∧ b }} ->> P1) ∧
679-      ({{ P ∧ ¬ b }} ->> P2) ∧
680-      (d1.postcondition ->> Q) ∧
681-      (d2.postcondition ->> Q) ∧
682-      d1.VerificationConditions P1 ∧
683-      d2.VerificationConditions P2
684-  | .whileDo b bodyPre body q =>
685-      -- The body's postcondition is both the loop invariant
686-      -- and the precondition for the first iteration.
687-      (P ->> body.postcondition) ∧
688-      ({{ body.postcondition ∧ b }} ->> bodyPre) ∧
689-      ({{ body.postcondition ∧ ¬ b }} ->> q) ∧
690-      body.VerificationConditions bodyPre
691-  | .pre P' body =>
692-      (P ->> P') ∧ body.VerificationConditions P'
693-  | .post body Q =>
694-      body.VerificationConditions P ∧
695-      (body.postcondition ->> Q)
696-
697---  The following key theorem states that
698---  `DCom.VerificationConditions` does its job correctly.
699---  Not surprisingly, each of the Hoare Logic rules plays a
700---  critical role at some point in the proof.
701-
702-theorem verification_correct (d : DCom) (P : Assertion)
703-    (hvc : d.VerificationConditions P) :
704-    ValidHoareTriple P d.erase d.postcondition := by
705-  sorry
706-
707---  Now that all the pieces are in place, we can define what
708---  it means to verify an entire program.
709-
710-def Decorated.VerificationConditions
711-    (dec : Decorated) : Prop :=
712-  dec.body.VerificationConditions dec.pre
713-
714---  And this brings us to the main theorem of this section:
715-
716-theorem verification_conditions_correct (dec : Decorated)
717-    (hvc : dec.VerificationConditions) :
718-    dec.OuterTripleValid := by
719-  exact verification_correct dec.body dec.pre hvc
720-
721---  ### More Automation
722-
723---  The propositions generated by
724---  `DCom.VerificationConditions` are fairly big and contain
725---  many conjuncts that are essentially trivial.
726-
727-example : decWhile.VerificationConditions := by
728-  unfold Decorated.VerificationConditions decWhile
729-  simp only [DCom.VerificationConditions,
730-    DCom.postcondition]
731-  sorry
732-
733---  Fortunately, our `verify_assertion` tactic can generally
734---  take care of most (or sometimes all) of them.
735-
736-example : decWhile.VerificationConditions := by
737-  sorry
738-
739---  To automate the overall process of verification, we can
740---  use `verification_correct` to extract the verification
741---  conditions, use `verify_assertion` to verify them as
742---  much as it can, and finally tidy up any remaining bits
743---  by hand.
744-
745-macro "verify" : tactic =>
746-  `(tactic|
747-    (apply verification_conditions_correct;
748-     verify_assertion))
749-
750---  Here's the final, formal proof that `decWhile` is
751---  correct.
752-
753-theorem dec_while_correct :
754-    decWhile.OuterTripleValid := by
755-  sorry
756-
757---  ## Finding Loop Invariants
758-
759---  Once the outer pre- and postcondition are chosen, the
760---  only creative part in verifying programs using Hoare
761---  Logic is finding the right loop invariants...
762-
763---  ### Example: Slow Subtraction
764-
765---  The following program subtracts the value of `X` from
766---  the value of `Y` by repeatedly decrementing both `X` and
767---  `Y`. We want to verify its correctness with respect to
768---  the pre- and postconditions shown:
769---
770---      {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}
771---        while X <> 0 do
772---          Y := Y - 1;
773---          X := X - 1
774---        end
775---      {{ Y = n - m }}
776-
777---  To verify this program, we need to find an invariant
778---  `Inv` for the loop. As a first step we can leave `Inv`
779---  as an unknown and build a *skeleton* for the proof by
780---  applying the rules for local consistency, working from
781---  the end of the program to the beginning, as usual, and
782---  without doing any thinking at all yet.
783-
784---  This leads to the following skeleton:
785---
786---      (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}  ->>                   (a)
787---      (2)    {{ Inv }}
788---               while X <> 0 do
789---      (3)              {{ Inv /\ X <> 0 }}  ->>          (c)
790---      (4)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] [Y |-> Y-1] }}
791---                 Y := Y - 1;
792---      (5)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] }}
793---                 X := X - 1
794---      (6)              {{ Inv }}
795---               end
796---      (7)    {{ Inv /\ ~ (X <> 0) }}  ->>                (b)
797---      (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
798-
799---  Examining this skeleton, we can see that any valid `Inv`
800---  will have to respect three conditions:
801---
802---  - (a) it must be *weak* enough to be implied by the
803---    loop's precondition, i.e., (1) must imply (2);
804---
805---  - (b) it must be *strong* enough to imply the program's
806---    postcondition, i.e., (7) must imply (8);
807---
808---  - (c) it must be *preserved* by a single iteration of
809---    the loop, assuming that the loop guard also evaluates
810---    to true, i.e., (3) must imply (4).
811-
812---  WORK IN CLASS (by filling in the previous template)
813-
814---  ## Weakest Preconditions (Optional)
815-
816---  A useless (though valid) Hoare triple:
817---
818---      {{ False }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
819---
820---  A better precondition:
821---
822---      {{ Y <= 4 /\ Z = 0 }}  X := Y + 1 {{ X <= 5 }}
823---
824---  The *best* precondition:
825---
826---      {{ Y <= 4 }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
827-
828---  Assertion `Y <= 4` is a *weakest precondition* of
829---  command `X := Y + 1` with respect to postcondition
830---  `X <= 5`. Think of *weakest* here as meaning "easiest to
831---  satisfy": a weakest precondition is one that as many
832---  states as possible can satisfy.
833-
834---  `P` is a weakest precondition of command `c` for
835---  postcondition `Q` if
836---
837---  - `P` is a precondition, that is, `{{P}} c {{Q}}`; and
838---
839---  - `P` is at least as weak as all other preconditions,
840---    that is, if `{{P'}} c {{Q}}` then `P' ->> P`.
841---
842---  Note that weakest preconditions need not be unique. For
843---  example, `Y <= 4` was a weakest precondition above, but
844---  so are the logically equivalent assertions `Y < 5`,
845---  `Y <= 2 * 2`, etc. It is easy to show that any two
846---  weakest preconditions `P` and `P'` of a command `c` with
847---  respect to postcondition `Q` are logically equivalent;
848---  that is, `P <<->> P'`.
849-
850-def IsWp (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
851-  ValidHoareTriple P c Q ∧
852-  ∀ P' : Assertion, {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }} → P' ->> P
853-

855-

857---  for the following postconditions?

859---      1) {{ ? }}  skip  {{ X = 5 }}
860---
861---      2) {{ ? }}  X := Y + Z {{ X = 5 }}
862---
863---      3) {{ ? }}  X := Y  {{ X = Y }}
864---
865---      4) {{ ? }}
866---       if X = 0 then Y := Z + 1 else Y := W + 2 end
867---       {{ Y = 5 }}
868---
869---      5) {{ ? }}
870---       X := 5
871---       {{ X = 0 }}
872---
873---      6) {{ ? }}
874---       while true do X := 0 end
875---       {{ X = 0 }}

8---  # Imp: Simple Imperative Programs
9-
10---  We concentrate here on defining the *syntax* and
11---  *semantics* of Imp; later in this volume we develop a
12---  theory of *program equivalence* and introduce *Hoare
13---  Logic*, a popular logic for reasoning about imperative
14---  programs.
15-
16---  ## Expressions With Variables
17-
18---  ### States
19-
20---  Since we'll want to look variables up to find out their
21---  current values, we'll use total maps from the `Maps`
22---  chapter. A *machine state* (or just *state*) represents
23---  the current values of all variables at some point in the
24---  execution of a program.
25---
26---  We give the type of variable identifiers a name,
27---  `Ident`. For now it is just `String`; naming it makes
28---  the intent clearer.
29-
30-open scoped MyGetElem
31-
32-abbrev Ident := String
33-abbrev State := TotalMap Ident Nat
34-
35---  ### Syntax
36-
37---  We can add variables to the arithmetic expressions we
38---  had before simply by including one more constructor.
39---  (This is a fresh `Aexp`, replacing the variable-free one
40---  from the *Slang* chapter.)
41-
42-inductive Aexp where
43-  | num (n : Nat)
44-  | id (x : Ident)                -- NEW
45-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
46-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
47-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
48-
49---  The `Bexp` definition is unchanged, except that it now
50---  refers to the new `Aexp`.
51-
52-inductive Bexp where
53-  | bool (b : Bool)
54-  | eq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
55-  | neq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
56-  | le (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
57-  | gt (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
58-  | not (b : Bexp)
59-  | and (b₁ b₂ : Bexp)
60-
61---  Defining a few variable names as shorthands will make
62---  examples easier to read.
63-
64-def W : Ident := "W"
65-def X : Ident := "X"
66-def Y : Ident := "Y"
67-def Z : Ident := "Z"
68-

136-    | _      => Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'true' or 'false', got '{x.getId}'"
137-  | `(bexp { ~$e }) => pure e

153-namespace Imp.Delab

156-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `imp_aexp` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
157-@[category_parenthesizer imp_aexp]
158-def imp_aexp.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
159-  maybeParenthesize `imp_aexp true wrapParens prec <|
160-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `imp_aexp prec
161-where
162-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
163-    let pstx ← `(($(⟨stx⟩)))
164-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
165-
166-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `imp_bexp` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
167-@[category_parenthesizer imp_bexp]
168-def imp_bexp.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
169-  maybeParenthesize `imp_bexp true wrapParens prec <|
170-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `imp_bexp prec
171-where
172-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
173-    let pstx ← `(($(⟨stx⟩)))
174-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)

176-/-- Tag freshly built syntax with the term info that Lean's pretty printer expects. -/
177-def annAsTerm {any} (stx : TSyntax any) : DelabM (TSyntax any) :=
178-  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
179-
180-/-- Rebuild `imp_aexp` concrete syntax from an `Aexp` term. -/
181-partial def delabAexpInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_aexp) := do
182-  let e ← getExpr
183-  let stx ←
184-    match_expr e with
185-    | Aexp.num _ =>
186-      match (← withAppArg getExpr).nat? with
187-      | some v => pure ⟨Syntax.mkNumLit (toString v) |>.raw⟩
188-      | none   => `(imp_aexp| ~$(← withAppArg delab))
189-    | Aexp.id _ =>
190-      -- A variable reference like aexp { X } elaborates to Aexp.id X where X is the
191-      -- declared Ident constant, so the delaborators print the constant's name as a
192-      -- bare identifier (and also handle the .id "X" string-literal form).
193-      match ← withAppArg getExpr with
194-      | .const nm _      => `(imp_aexp| $(mkIdent nm):ident)
195-      | .lit (.strVal s) => `(imp_aexp| $(mkIdent (.mkSimple s)):ident)
196-      | _                => `(imp_aexp| ~$(← withAppArg delab))
197-    | Aexp.plus _ _ =>
198-      let s₁ ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
199-      let s₂ ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
200-      `(imp_aexp| $s₁ + $s₂)
201-    | Aexp.minus _ _ =>
202-      let s₁ ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
203-      let s₂ ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
204-      `(imp_aexp| $s₁ - $s₂)
205-    | Aexp.mult _ _ =>
206-      let s₁ ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
207-      let s₂ ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
208-      `(imp_aexp| $s₁ * $s₂)
209-    | _ => `(imp_aexp| ~$(← delab))
210-  annAsTerm stx
211-
212-/-- Rebuild `imp_bexp` concrete syntax from a `Bexp` term. -/
213-partial def delabBexpInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_bexp) := do
214-  let e ← getExpr
215-  let stx ←
216-    match_expr e with
217-    | Bexp.bool _ =>
218-      match ← withAppArg getExpr with
219-      | .const ``Bool.true _  => `(imp_bexp| $(mkIdent `true):ident)
220-      | .const ``Bool.false _ => `(imp_bexp| $(mkIdent `false):ident)
221-      | _                     => `(imp_bexp| ~$(← withAppArg delab))
222-    | Bexp.eq _ _ =>
223-      let s₁ ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
224-      let s₂ ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
225-      `(imp_bexp| $s₁:imp_aexp = $s₂:imp_aexp)
226-    | Bexp.neq _ _ =>
227-      let s₁ ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
228-      let s₂ ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
229-      `(imp_bexp| $s₁:imp_aexp ≠ $s₂:imp_aexp)
230-    | Bexp.le _ _ =>
231-      let s₁ ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
232-      let s₂ ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
233-      `(imp_bexp| $s₁:imp_aexp ≤ $s₂:imp_aexp)
234-    | Bexp.gt _ _ =>
235-      let s₁ ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
236-      let s₂ ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
237-      `(imp_bexp| $s₁:imp_aexp > $s₂:imp_aexp)
238-    | Bexp.not _ =>
239-      let s ← withAppArg delabBexpInner
240-      `(imp_bexp| ¬ $s)
241-    | Bexp.and _ _ =>
242-      let s₁ ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
243-      let s₂ ← withAppArg delabBexpInner
244-      `(imp_bexp| $s₁ ∧ $s₂)
245-    | _ => `(imp_bexp| ~$(← delab))
246-  annAsTerm stx
247---  END DETAILS

249---  The `whenPPOption getPPNotation` wrapper lets
250---  `set_option pp.notation false` switch this delaborator
251---  off, revealing the raw constructors (see the "Desugaring
252---  Notations" discussion, after the commands are
253---  introduced).

255---  THE FOLLOWING DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: registering the delaborators)
256-@[delab app.Aexp.num, delab app.Aexp.id, delab app.Aexp.plus,
257-  delab app.Aexp.minus, delab app.Aexp.mult]
258-partial def delabAexp : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
259-  -- This delaborator only understands `Aexp`'s constructors -- bail otherwise.
260-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
261-    | Aexp.num _ => true
262-    | Aexp.id _ => true
263-    | Aexp.plus _ _ => true
264-    | Aexp.minus _ _ => true
265-    | Aexp.mult _ _ => true
266-    | _ => false
267-  match ← delabAexpInner with
268-  | `(imp_aexp| ~$e) => pure e
269-  | e => `(term| aexp { $e })
270-
271-@[delab app.Bexp.bool, delab app.Bexp.eq, delab app.Bexp.neq, delab app.Bexp.le,
272-  delab app.Bexp.gt, delab app.Bexp.not, delab app.Bexp.and]
273-partial def delabBexp : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
274-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
275-    | Bexp.bool _ => true
276-    | Bexp.eq _ _ => true
277-    | Bexp.neq _ _ => true
278-    | Bexp.le _ _ => true
279-    | Bexp.gt _ _ => true
280-    | Bexp.not _ => true
281-    | Bexp.and _ _ => true
282-    | _ => false
283-  match ← delabBexpInner with
284-  | `(imp_bexp| ~$e) => pure e
285-  | e => `(term| bexp { $e })

287-end Imp.Delab

298---  ### Evaluation
299-
300---  Now we need to add an `st` parameter to both evaluation
301---  functions:
302-
303-def Aexp.eval (st : State) (a : Aexp) : Nat :=
304-  match a with
305-  | num   n     =>  n
306-  | id    x     =>  st[x]                    -- NEW
307-  | plus  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval st + a₂.eval st
308-  | minus a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval st - a₂.eval st
309-  | mult  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval st * a₂.eval st
310-
311-def Bexp.eval (st : State) (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
312-  match b with
313-  | bool b      =>  b
314-  | eq   a₁ a₂  =>  a₁.eval st == a₂.eval st
315-  | neq  a₁ a₂  =>  a₁.eval st != a₂.eval st
316-  | le   a₁ a₂  =>  a₁.eval st ≤  a₂.eval st
317-  | gt   a₁ a₂  =>  a₁.eval st >  a₂.eval st
318-  | not  b₁     =>  !b₁.eval st
319-  | and  b₁ b₂  =>  b₁.eval st && b₂.eval st
320-
321-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_num (st : State) (n : Nat) : (num n).eval st = n := rfl
322-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_id (st : State) (x : Ident) : (Aexp.id x).eval st = st[x] := rfl
323-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_plus (st : State) (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) :
324-    (plus a₁ a₂).eval st = a₁.eval st + a₂.eval st := rfl
325-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_minus (st : State) (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) :
326-    (minus a₁ a₂).eval st = a₁.eval st - a₂.eval st := rfl
327-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_mult (st : State) (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) :
328-    (mult a₁ a₂).eval st = a₁.eval st * a₂.eval st := rfl
329-
330-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_bool (st : State) (b : Bool) : (bool b).eval st = b := rfl
331-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_eq (st : State) (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) :
332-    (eq a₁ a₂).eval st = (a₁.eval st == a₂.eval st) := rfl
333-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_neq (st : State) (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) :
334-    (neq a₁ a₂).eval st = (a₁.eval st != a₂.eval st) := rfl
335-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_le (st : State) (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) :
336-    (le a₁ a₂).eval st = (a₁.eval st ≤ a₂.eval st : Bool) := rfl
337-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_gt (st : State) (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) :
338-    (gt a₁ a₂).eval st = (a₁.eval st > a₂.eval st : Bool) := rfl
339-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_not (st : State) (b : Bexp) : (not b).eval st = !b.eval st := rfl
340-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_and (st : State) (b₁ b₂ : Bexp) :
341-    (and b₁ b₂).eval st = (b₁.eval st && b₂.eval st) := rfl
342-
343---  We reuse the total-map notation (`x →ₜ v ; ∅` etc.) for
344---  states.
345-
346-example : aexp { 3 + (X * 2) }.eval (X →ₜ 5 ; ∅) = 13 := by rfl
347-
348-example : aexp { Z + (X * Y) }.eval (X →ₜ 5 ; Y →ₜ 4 ; ∅) = 20 := by rfl
349-
350-example : bexp { true ∧ ¬(X ≤ 4) }.eval (X →ₜ 5 ; ∅) = true := by rfl
