352---  ## Commands
353-
354-inductive Com where
355-  | skip
356-  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp)
357-  | seq (c₁ c₂ : Com)
358-  | cond (b : Bexp) (c₁ c₂ : Com)
359-  | whileDo (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
360-
361---  THE FOLLOWING DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: commands, macro rules)
362-/-- Imp commands -/
363-declare_syntax_cat imp_com
364-/-- The command that does nothing (`skip`) -/
365-syntax ident : imp_com
366-/-- Sequencing: one command after another -/
367-syntax imp_com ";" ppDedent(ppLine imp_com) : imp_com
368-/-- Assignment -/
369-syntax ident " := " imp_aexp : imp_com
370-/-- Conditional -/
371-syntax "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}" ppHardSpace "else" ppHardSpace "{") ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : imp_com
372-/-- Loop -/
373-syntax "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : imp_com
374-/-- Escape to Lean -/
375-syntax:max "~" term:max : imp_com
376-
377-/-- Include an Imp command in Lean code -/
378-syntax:min "imp" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
379-
380-namespace Com
381-
382-open Lean in
383-scoped macro_rules
384-  | `(imp { $x:ident }) =>
385-    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
386-    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
387-  | `(imp { $c₁ ; $c₂ }) =>
388-    `(Com.seq (imp {$c₁}) (imp {$c₂}))
389-  | `(imp { $x:ident := $a }) =>
390-    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
391-  | `(imp { if ($b) {$c₁} else {$c₂} }) =>
392-    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c₁}) (imp {$c₂}))
393-  | `(imp { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
394-    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c}))
395-  | `(imp { ~$c }) =>
396-    pure c
397-
398-end Com
399-
400-open scoped Com

404-namespace Imp.Delab
405-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr
406-
407-partial def delabComInnerFor (ns : Name) (extra : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_com)) :
408-    DelabM (TSyntax `imp_com) := do
409-  let e ← getExpr
410-  let stx ←
411-    -- Using `(imp_com| skip)` would delaborate as `skip✝`. `mkIdent` fixes this.
412-    if e.isConstOf (ns ++ `skip) then
413-      `(imp_com| $(mkIdent `skip):ident)
414-    else if e.isAppOfArity (ns ++ `asgn) 2 then
415-      match ← withAppFn <| withAppArg getExpr with
416-      | .lit (.strVal s) =>
417-        let a ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
418-        `(imp_com| $(mkIdent (.mkSimple s)):ident := $a)
419-      | _ =>
420-        let `($x:ident) ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delab | failure
421-        let a ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
422-        `(imp_com| $x:ident := $a)
423-    else if e.isAppOfArity (ns ++ `seq) 2 then
424-      let s₁ ← withAppFn <| withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
425-      let s₂ ← withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
426-      `(imp_com| $s₁; $s₂)
427-    else if e.isAppOfArity (ns ++ `cond) 3 then
428-      let b  ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
429-      let c₁ ← withAppFn <| withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
430-      let c₂ ← withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
431-      `(imp_com| if ($b) {$c₁} else {$c₂})
432-    else if e.isAppOfArity (ns ++ `whileDo) 2 then
433-      let b ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
434-      let c ← withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
435-      `(imp_com| while ($b) {$c})
436-    else
437-      extra <|> `(imp_com| ~$(← delab))

441-partial def delabComInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_com) :=
442-  delabComInnerFor ``Com failure

444-@[delab app.Com.skip, delab app.Com.asgn, delab app.Com.seq,
445-  delab app.Com.cond, delab app.Com.whileDo]
446-partial def delabCom : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
447-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
448-    | Com.skip => true
449-    | Com.asgn _ _ => true
450-    | Com.seq _ _ => true
451-    | Com.cond _ _ _ => true
452-    | Com.whileDo _ _ => true
453-    | _ => false
454-  match ← delabComInner with
455-  | `(imp_com| ~$e) => pure e
456-  | e => `(term| imp { $e })

531---  ### Evaluation as a Function (Failed Attempt)
532-
533---  Here's an attempt at defining an evaluation function for
534---  commands (with a bogus `while` case).
535-
536-def Com.ceval_fun_no_while (st : State) (c : Com) : State :=
537-  match c with
538-  | imp {skip} => st
539-  | imp {x := ~a} => (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
540-  | imp {~c₁; ~c₂} =>
541-      let st' := ceval_fun_no_while st c₁
542-      ceval_fun_no_while st' c₂
543-  | imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} =>
544-      if b.eval st then ceval_fun_no_while st c₁
545-      else ceval_fun_no_while st c₂

548---  A nonterminating
549---  `def loop_false (n) : False := loop_false n` would make
550---  `False` provable, so Lean rejects it.
551-
552---  ### Evaluation as a Relation
553-
554---  Here's a better way: define `ceval` as a *relation*
555---  rather than a *function* -- i.e., make its result a
556---  `Prop` rather than a `State`, similar to what we did for
557---  `Aexp.EvalR` in the Slang chapter.
558-
559---  We'll use the notation `st =[ c ]=> st'` for the
560---  `Com.EvalR` relation: `st =[ c ]=> st'` means that
561---  executing program `c` in a starting state `st` results
562---  in an ending state `st'`. This can be pronounced "`c`
563---  takes state `st` to `st'`".
564-
565---  Operational Semantics
566-
567---  Here is an informal definition of evaluation, presented
568---  as inference rules for readability:
569---
570---                            -----------------                  (skip)
571---                            st =[ skip ]=> st
572---
573---                            a.eval st = n
574---                    --------------------------------           (asgn)
575---                    st =[ x := a ]=> (x →ₜ n ; st)
576---
577---                            st  =[ c₁ ]=> st'
578---                            st' =[ c₂ ]=> st''
579---                          ---------------------                (seq)
580---                          st =[ c₁;c₂ ]=> st''
581---
582---                           b.eval st = true
583---                            st =[ c₁ ]=> st'
584---                 --------------------------------------        (ifTrue)
585---                 st =[ if b then c₁ else c₂ end ]=> st'
586---
587---                          b.eval st = false
588---                            st =[ c₂ ]=> st'
589---                 --------------------------------------        (ifFalse)
590---                 st =[ if b then c₁ else c₂ end ]=> st'
591---
592---                          b.eval st = false
593---                     -----------------------------             (whileFalse)
594---                     st =[ while b do c end ]=> st
595---
596---                           b.eval st = true
597---                            st =[ c ]=> st'
598---                   st' =[ while b do c end ]=> st''
599---                   --------------------------------            (whileTrue)
600---                   st  =[ while b do c end ]=> st''
601---
602---  Here is the formal definition. Make sure you understand
603---  how it corresponds to the inference rules.
604-
605-inductive Com.EvalR : Com → State → State → Prop where
606-  | skip {st : State} : EvalR (imp {skip}) st st
607-  | asgn {st : State} {a : Aexp} {n : Nat} {x : Ident} (h : a.eval st = n) :
608-      EvalR (imp {x := ~a}) st (x →ₜ n ; st)
609-  | seq {c₁ c₂ : Com} {st st' st'' : State} (h₁ : EvalR c₁ st st') (h₂ : EvalR c₂ st' st'') :
610-      EvalR (imp {~c₁; ~c₂}) st st''
611-  | ifTrue {st st' : State} {b : Bexp} {c₁ c₂ : Com} (hb : b.eval st = true)
612-      (hc : EvalR c₁ st st') :
613-      EvalR (imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}}) st st'
614-  | ifFalse {st st' : State} {b : Bexp} {c₁ c₂ : Com} (hb : b.eval st = false)
615-      (hc : EvalR c₂ st st') :
616-      EvalR (imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}}) st st'
617-  | whileFalse {b : Bexp} {st : State} {c : Com} (hb : b.eval st = false) :
618-      EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) st st
619-  | whileTrue {st st' st'' : State} {b : Bexp} {c : Com} (hb : b.eval st = true)
620-      (hc : EvalR c st st') (hloop : Com.EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) st' st'') :
621-      EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) st st''
622-

625-  Eval : Com → In → Out → Prop
626-
627-namespace HasEval
628-/-- Evaluation: `st =[ c ]=> st'` with `imp_com` command syntax -/
629-scoped syntax:lead term " =[ " imp_com:lead " ]=> " term : term
630-scoped macro_rules
631-  | `($st =[ $c:imp_com ]=> $st') => ``(HasEval.Eval (imp { $c }) $st $st')
632-
633-namespace Delab
634-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Imp.Delab
635-@[delab app.HasEval.Eval]
636-def delabTriple : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
637-  guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``HasEval.Eval 7
638-  let c ← withNaryArg 4 delab

640-  let st' ← withNaryArg 6 delab
641-  match c with
642-  | `(imp { $c:imp_com }) => ``($st =[ $c ]=> $st')
643-  | c => ``($st =[ ~$c ]=> $st')

648-

658---  The cost of defining evaluation as a relation instead of
659---  a function is that we now need to construct a *proof*
660---  that some program evaluates to some result state, rather
661---  than letting Lean's computation mechanism do it for us.

665-      X := 2;
666-      if (X ≤ 1) {
667-        Y := 3
668-      } else {
669-        Z := 4
670-      }
671-    ]=> (Z →ₜ 4 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅) := by
672-  -- We must supply the intermediate state.
673-  apply Com.EvalR.seq (st' := (X →ₜ 2 ; ∅))
674-  · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl
675-  · apply Com.EvalR.ifFalse
676-    · rfl
677-    · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl

711---        st =[ ~c₁ ~c₂ ]=> st' →
712---        st =[ c₁ ]=> st →
713---        st =[ c₂ ]=> st'
714---
715---  (A) Yes (B) No (C) Not sure

723---      ∀ (b : Bexp) (c : Com) (st st' : State),
724---        st =[ if (~b) { ~c } else { ~c } ]=> st' →
725---        st =[ c ]=> st'
726---
727---  (A) Yes (B) No (C) Not sure

736---        (∀ st, b.eval st = true) →
737---        ∀ (c : Com) (st : State),

749---        (¬ ∃ st', st =[ while (~b) { ~c } ]=> st') →

756---  ### Determinism of Evaluation
757-
758---  Finally, we should pause to check that our evaluation
759---  relation really is a (partial) function...
760-
761-theorem ceval_deterministic (c : Com) (st st1 st2 : State)
762-    (e₁ : st =[ ~c ]=> st1) (e₂ : st =[ ~c ]=> st2) : st1 = st2 := by
763-  induction e₁ generalizing st2 with
764-  | @skip st =>
765-      inversion e₂
766-      rfl
767-  | @asgn st a n x h =>
768-      inversion e₂ with
769-      | asgn h' => subst h; subst h'; rfl
770-  | @seq c₁ c₂ st st' st'' h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
771-      inversion e₂ with
772-      | seq st2' h₁' h₂' =>
773-          have hst : st' = st2' := ih₁ _ h₁'
774-          subst hst
775-          exact ih₂ _ h₂'
776-  | @ifTrue st st' b c₁ c₂ hb hc ih =>
777-      inversion e₂ with
778-      | ifTrue hb' hc' => exact ih _ hc'
779-      | ifFalse hb' hc' => simp_all
780-  | @ifFalse st st' b c₁ c₂ hb hc ih =>
781-      inversion e₂ with
782-      | ifTrue hb' hc' => simp_all
783-      | ifFalse hb' hc' => exact ih _ hc'
784-  | @whileFalse b st c hb =>
785-      inversion e₂ with
786-      | whileFalse hb' => rfl
787-      | whileTrue hb' hc' hl' => simp_all
788-  | @whileTrue st st' st'' b c hb hc hloop ih₁ ih₂ =>
789-      inversion e₂ with
790-      | whileFalse hb' => simp_all
791-      | whileTrue st2' _ hc' hl' =>
792-          have hst : st' = st2' := ih₁ _ hc'
793-          subst hst
794-          exact ih₂ _ hl'

881---  ### Exercise (3 stars): stack_compiler ⭐⭐⭐
882-
883---  Old HP Calculators, programming languages like Forth and
884---  Postscript, and abstract machines like the Java Virtual
885---  Machine all evaluate arithmetic expressions using a
886---  *stack*. For instance, the expression
887---
888---      (2*3)+(3*(4-2))
889---
890---  would be written as
891---
892---            2 3 * 3 4 2 - * +
893---
894---  and evaluated like this (where we show the program being
895---  evaluated on the right and the contents of the stack on
896---  the left):
897-
898---  [ ]           |    2 3 * 3 4 2 - * +
899---        [2]           |    3 * 3 4 2 - * +
900---        [3, 2]        |    * 3 4 2 - * +
901---        [6]           |    3 4 2 - * +
902---        [3, 6]        |    4 2 - * +
903---        [4, 3, 6]     |    2 - * +
904---        [2, 4, 3, 6]  |    - * +
905---        [2, 3, 6]     |    * +
906---        [6, 6]        |    +
907---        [12]          |
908-
909---  The goal of this exercise is to write a small compiler
910---  that translates `aexp`s into stack machine instructions.
911---
912---  The instruction set for our stack language will consist
913---  of the following instructions:
914---
915---  - `sPush n`: Push the number `n` on the stack.
916---
917---  - `sLoad x`: Load the identifier `x` from the store and
918---    push it on the stack
919---
920---  - `sPlus`: Pop the two top numbers from the stack, add
921---    them, and push the result onto the stack.
922---
923---  - `sMinus`: Similar, but subtract the first number from
924---    the second.
925---
926---  - `sMult`: Similar, but multiply.
927-
928-namespace StackCompiler
929-
930-inductive Sinstr : Type where
931-| sPush (n : Nat)
932-| sLoad (x : String)
933-| sPlus
934-| sMinus
935-| sMult

937-open Sinstr

943---  of instructions, and it should return the stack after
944---  executing the program. Test your function on the
945---  examples below.
946---

948---  an `sPlus`, `sMinus`, or `sMult` instruction if the
949---  stack contains fewer than two elements. In a sense, it
950---  is immaterial what we do, since a correct compiler will
951---  never emit such a malformed program. But for sake of
952---  later exercises, it would be best to skip the offending
953---  instruction and continue with the next one.

1015---  ### Exercise (3 stars): short_circuit (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐

1017---  Most modern programming languages use a "short-circuit"
1018---  evaluation rule for boolean `and`: to evaluate
1019---  `BExp.and b₁ b₂`, first evaluate `b₁`. If it evaluates
1020---  to `false`, then the entire `and` expression evaluates
1021---  to `false` immediately, without evaluating `b₂`.
1022---  Otherwise, `b₂` is evaluated to determine the result of
1023---  the `and` expression.
1024---
1025---  Write an alternate version of `BExp.eval` that performs
1026---  short-circuit evaluation of `BAnd` in this manner, and
1027---  prove that it is equivalent to `BExp.eval`. (N.b. This
1028---  is only true because expression evaluation in Imp is
1029---  rather simple. In a bigger language where evaluating an
1030---  expression might diverge, the short-circuiting `and`
1031---  would *not* be equivalent to the original, since it
1032---  would make more programs terminate.)

1043---  ### Exercise (3 stars): break_imp (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐
1044-
1045---  Imperative languages like C and Java often include a
1046---  `break` or similar statement for interrupting the
1047---  execution of loops. In this exercise we consider how to
1048---  add `break` to Imp. First, we need to enrich the
1049---  language of commands with an additional case. Because
1050---  `break` is a reserved keyword in Lean, we will
1051---  abbreviate it as `brk`.
1052-
1053-namespace BreakImp
1054-
1055-inductive Com where
1056-  | skip
1057-  | brk                          -- <--- NEW
1058-  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp)
1059-  | seq (c₁ c₂ : Com)
1060-  | cond (b : Bexp) (c₁ c₂ : Com)
1061-  | whileDo (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
1062-
1063---  THE FOLLOWING DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: commands, macro rules)
1064-namespace Com

1069-    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
1070-    else if x.getId == `brk then `(Com.brk)
1071-    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip' or 'break', got '{x.getId}'"
1072-  | `(imp { $c₁; $c₂ }) =>
1073-    `(Com.seq (imp {$c₁}) (imp {$c₂}))
1074-  | `(imp { $x:ident := $a }) =>
1075-    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))

1077-    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c₁}) (imp {$c₂}))
1078-  | `(imp { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
1079-    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c}))
1080-  | `(imp { ~$c }) =>
1081-    pure c
1082-

1106-/--
1107-info: imp {
1108-  brk
1109-} : Com
1110--/
1111-#guard_msgs in
1112-#check imp {brk}
1113---  END DETAILS
1114-
1115---  Next, we need to define the behavior of `brk`.
1116---  Informally, whenever `brk` is executed in a sequence of
1117---  commands, it stops the execution of that sequence and
1118---  signals that the innermost enclosing loop should
1119---  terminate. (If there aren't any enclosing loops, then
1120---  the whole program simply terminates.) The final state
1121---  should be the same as the one in which the `brk`
1122---  statement was executed.
1123---
1124---  One important point is what to do when there are
1125---  multiple loops enclosing a given `brk`. In those cases,
1126---  `brk` should only terminate the *innermost* loop. Thus,
1127---  after executing the following...
1128---
1129---          X := 0;
1130---          Y := 1;
1131---          while (0 <> Y) {
1132---            while (true) {
1133---              break
1134---            };
1135---            X := 1;
1136---            Y := Y - 1
1137---          }
1138---
1139---  ... the value of `X` should be `1`, and not `0`.
1140---
1141---  One way of expressing this behavior is to add another
1142---  parameter to the evaluation relation that specifies
1143---  whether evaluation of a command executes a `brk`
1144---  statement:
1145-
1146-inductive Result : Type where
1147-  | sContinue
1148-  | sBreak
1149-
1150-open Result
1151-
1152---  We will use the syntax `st =[ c ]=> st' // s` to mean
1153---  that, if `c` is started in state `st`, then it
1154---  terminates in state `st'` and either signals that the
1155---  innermost surrounding loop (or the whole program) should
1156---  exit immediately (`s = sBreak`) or that execution should
1157---  continue normally (`s = sContinue`).
1158---
1159---  The definition of the `st =[ c ]=> st' // s` relation is
1160---  very similar to the one we gave above for the regular
1161---  evaluation relation (`st =[ c ]=> st'`) -- we just need
1162---  to handle the termination signals appropriately:
1163---
1164---  - If the command is `skip`, then the state doesn't
1165---    change and execution of any enclosing loop can
1166---    continue normally.
1167---
1168---  - If the command is `brk`, the state stays unchanged but
1169---    we signal a `sBreak`.
1170---
1171---  - If the command is an assignment, then we update the
1172---    binding for that variable in the state accordingly and
1173---    signal that execution can continue normally.
1174---
1175---  - If the command is of the form `if (b) {c₁} {c₂}`, then
1176---    the state is updated as in the original semantics of
1177---    Imp, except that we also propagate the signal from the
1178---    execution of whichever branch was taken.
1179---
1180---  - If the command is a sequence `c₁ ; c₂`, we first
1181---    execute `c₁`. If this yields a `sBreak`, we skip the
1182---    execution of `c₂` and propagate the `sBreak` signal to
1183---    the surrounding context; the resulting state is the
1184---    same as the one obtained by executing `c₁` alone.
1185---    Otherwise, we execute `c₂` on the state obtained after
1186---    executing `c₁`, and propagate the signal generated
1187---    there.
1188---
1189---  - Finally, for a loop of the form `while (b) {c}`, the
1190---    semantics is almost the same as before. The only
1191---    difference is that, when `b` evaluates to `true`, we
1192---    execute `c` and check the signal that it raises. If
1193---    that signal is `sContinue`, then the execution
1194---    proceeds as in the original semantics. Otherwise, we
1195---    stop the execution of the loop, and the resulting
1196---    state is the same as the one resulting from the
1197---    execution of the current iteration. In either case,
1198---    since `break` only terminates the innermost loop,
1199---    `while` signals `sContinue`.
1200---
1201---  Based on the above description, complete the definition
1202---  of the `Com.EvalR` relation:
1203-
1204-inductive Com.EvalR : Com → State → State → Result → Prop where
1205-  | skip {st : State} : EvalR (imp {skip}) st st sContinue
1206-  --  FILL IN HERE
1207-
1208-scoped notation:40 st0:41 " =[ " c " ]=> " st1:41 " // " s:41 => Com.EvalR c st0 st1 s
1209-
1210---  Now prove the following properties of your definition:
1211-
1212-theorem break_ignore (c : Com) (st st' : State) (s : Result) (h : st =[ imp { brk ; ~c } ]=> st' // s) :
1213-  st = st' := by
1214-  sorry
1215-
1216-theorem while_continue (b : Bexp) (c : Com) (st st' : State) (s : Result)
1217-  (h : st =[ imp { while (~b) {~c} } ]=> st' // s) :
1218-  s = sContinue := by
1219-  sorry
1220-
1221-theorem while_stops_on_break (b : Bexp) (c : Com) (st st' : State)
1222-  (h₁ : b.eval st = true)
1223-  (h₂ : st =[ imp { ~c } ]=> st' // sBreak) :
1224-  st =[ imp { while (~b) {~c} } ]=> st' // sContinue := by
1225-  sorry
1226-
1227-theorem seq_continue (c₁ c₂ : Com) (st st' st'' : State)
1228-  (h₁ : st =[ imp { ~c₁ } ]=> st' // sContinue)
1229-  (h₂ : st' =[ imp { ~c₂ } ]=> st'' // sContinue) :
1230-  st =[ imp { ~c₁ ; ~c₂ } ]=> st'' // sContinue := by
1231-  sorry
1232-
1233-theorem seq_stops_on_break (c₁ c₂ : Com) (st st' : State)
1234-  (h : st =[ imp { ~c₁ } ]=> st' // sBreak) :
1235-  st =[ imp { ~c₁ ; ~c₂ } ]=> st' // sBreak := by
1236-  sorry
1237-
1238---  ### Exercise (3 stars): while_break_true (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐
1239-

1251-  st₁ = st₂ ∧ s₁ = s₂ := by

1253-
1254-end BreakImp

1256---  ### Exercise (4 stars): add_for_loop (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1257-
1258---  Add C-style `for` loops to the language of commands,
1259---  update the `ceval` definition to define the semantics of
1260---  `for` loops, and add cases for `for` loops as needed so
1261---  that all the proofs in this file are accepted by Rocq.
1262---
1263---  A `for` loop should be parameterized by (a) a statement
1264---  executed initially, (b) a test that is run on each
1265---  iteration of the loop to determine whether the loop
1266---  should continue, (c) a statement executed at the end of
1267---  each loop iteration, and (d) a statement that makes up
1268---  the body of the loop. (You don't need to worry about
1269---  making up a concrete Notation for `for` loops, but feel

2-
3---  # Slang: Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
4-
5---  ## Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
6-
7---  ### Syntax
8-
9-namespace Slang
10-
11---  Abstract syntax trees for arithmetic and boolean
12---  expressions:
13-
14-inductive Aexp where
15-  | num (n : Nat)
16-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
17-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
18-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
19-
20-inductive Bexp where
21-  | bool (b : Bool)
22-  | eq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
23-  | neq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
24-  | le (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
25-  | gt (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
26-  | not (b : Bexp)
27-  | and (b₁ b₂ : Bexp)
28-
29---  ### Evaluation
30-
31---  *Evaluating* an arithmetic expression produces a number.
32-
33-namespace Aexp
34-def eval (a : Aexp) : Nat :=
35-  match a with
36-  | num   n     =>  n
37-  | plus  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval + a₂.eval
38-  | minus a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval - a₂.eval
39-  | mult  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval * a₂.eval
40-
41-@[simp] theorem eval_num (n : Nat) : (num n).eval = n := rfl
42-@[simp] theorem eval_plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (plus a₁ a₂).eval = a₁.eval + a₂.eval := rfl
43-@[simp] theorem eval_minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (minus a₁ a₂).eval = a₁.eval - a₂.eval := rfl
44-@[simp] theorem eval_mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (mult a₁ a₂).eval = a₁.eval * a₂.eval := rfl
45-
46-example : eval (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2)) = 4 := by simp
47-end Aexp
48-
49---  Similarly, evaluating a boolean expression yields a
50---  boolean.
51-
52-namespace Bexp
53-def eval (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
54-  match b with
55-  | bool b     =>  b
56-  | eq   a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval == a₂.eval
57-  | neq  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval != a₂.eval
58-  | le   a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval ≤ a₂.eval
59-  | gt   a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval > a₂.eval
60-  | not  b₁    =>  !eval b₁
61-  | and  b₁ b₂ =>  eval b₁ && eval b₂
62-
63-@[simp] theorem eval_bool (b : Bool) : (bool b).eval = b := rfl
64-@[simp] theorem eval_eq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (eq a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval == a₂.eval) := rfl
65-@[simp] theorem eval_neq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (neq a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval != a₂.eval) := rfl
66-@[simp] theorem eval_le (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (le a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval ≤ a₂.eval : Bool) := rfl
67-@[simp] theorem eval_gt (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (gt a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval > a₂.eval : Bool) := rfl
68-@[simp] theorem eval_not (b : Bexp) : (not b).eval = !b.eval := rfl
69-@[simp] theorem eval_and (b₁ b₂ : Bexp) : (and b₁ b₂).eval = (b₁.eval && b₂.eval) := rfl
70-end Bexp
71-
72---  It's worth noting that `≤` and `>` are `Prop`-valued,
73---  i.e. `a₁.eval st ≤ a₂.eval st` is a proposition, but
74---  `Bexp.eval` returns a `Bool`, so Lean implicitly inserts
75---  a `decide` coercion. You can observe the call to
76---  `decide` by hovering over `Bexp.eval_le` and
77---  `Bexp.eval_gt`.
78-
79---   ----------------------------------------
80-
81---  _Quiz:_
82-
83---  What does the following expression evaluate to?
84-
85---  Aexp.eval (.plus (.num 3) (.minus (.num 4) (.num 1)))
86-
87---  (A) true (B) false (C) 0 (D) 3 (E) 6
88-
89---   ----------------------------------------
90-
91---  ### Optimization
92-
93-namespace Aexp
94-
95-def optimize0plus (a : Aexp) : Aexp :=
96-  match a with
97-  | num   n          => num n
98-  | plus  (num 0) e₂ => optimize0plus e₂
99-  | plus  e₁      e₂ => plus  (optimize0plus e₁) (optimize0plus e₂)
100-  | minus e₁      e₂ => minus (optimize0plus e₁) (optimize0plus e₂)
101-  | mult  e₁      e₂ => mult  (optimize0plus e₁) (optimize0plus e₂)
102-
103-example :
104-    Aexp.optimize0plus (.plus (.num 2)
105-                               (.plus (.num 0)
106-                                      (.plus (.num 0) (.num 1))))
107-      = .plus (.num 2) (.num 1) := by rfl
108-
109-theorem optimize0plus_sound (a : Aexp) :
110-    a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
111-  induction a with
112-  | num n => rfl
113-  | plus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
114-    cases a₁ with
115-    | num n =>
116-      cases n with
117-      | zero =>
118-        simp only [optimize0plus, eval_plus, eval_num, Nat.zero_add]
119-        exact ih₂
120-      | succ n =>
121-        simp only [optimize0plus, eval_plus, eval_num]
122-        rw [ih₂]
123-    | plus b₁ b₂ =>
124-      simp only [optimize0plus, eval_plus] at ih₁ ⊢
125-      rw [ih₁, ih₂]
126-    | minus b₁ b₂ =>
127-      simp only [optimize0plus, eval_plus] at ih₁ ⊢
128-      rw [ih₁, ih₂]
129-    | mult b₁ b₂ =>
130-      simp only [optimize0plus, eval_plus] at ih₁ ⊢
131-      rw [ih₁, ih₂]
132-  | minus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
133-    simp only [optimize0plus, eval_minus]
134-    rw [ih₁, ih₂]
135-  | mult a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
136-    simp only [optimize0plus, eval_mult]
137-    rw [ih₁, ih₂]
138-
139---  We can use `fun_induction` to achieve a much shorter
140---  proof.
141-
142-theorem optimize0plus_sound' (a : Aexp) :
143-    a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
144-  fun_induction Aexp.optimize0plus a <;> simp_all
145-
146-end Aexp
147-
148---  ### Exercise (3 stars): optimize0plus_sound ⭐⭐⭐
149-
150---  Since the `Aexp.optimize0plus` transformation doesn't
151---  change the value of an `Aexp`, we should be able to
152---  apply it to all the `Aexp`s that appear in a `Bexp`
153---  without changing the `Bexp`'s value. Write a function
154---  that performs this transformation on `Bexp`s and prove
155---  it sound. Use the combinators we've just seen to make
156---  the proof as short and elegant as possible.
157-
158-def Bexp.optimize0plus (b : Bexp) : Bexp := sorry
159-
160-theorem Bexp.optimize0plus_test1 :
161-    Bexp.optimize0plus
162-        (.not (.gt (.plus (.num 0) (.num 4)) (.num 8)))
163-      = (.not (.gt (.num 4) (.num 8))) := sorry
164-
165-theorem Bexp.optimize0plus_test2 :
166-    Bexp.optimize0plus
167-        (.and (.le (.plus (.num 0) (.num 4)) (.num 5)) (.bool true))
168-      = (.and (.le (.num 4) (.num 5)) (.bool true)) := sorry
169-
170-theorem Bexp.optimize0plus_sound (b : Bexp) :
171-    b.optimize0plus.eval = b.eval := by
172-  sorry
173-

302---  ### Computational vs. Relational Definitions
303-
304---  Sometimes relational definitions are the only reasonable
305---  option...
306-
307-namespace Slang.AevalRDivision
308-
309---  For example, suppose that we wanted to extend the
310---  arithmetic operations with division:
311-
312-inductive Aexp where
313-  | num (n : Nat)
314-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
315-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
316-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
317-  | div (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)             -- NEW
318-
319---  Extending the definition of `Aexp.eval` to handle this
320---  new operation would not be straightforward due to
321---  division being a *partial* operation; i.e., what should
322---  we return as the result of `.div (.num 5) (.num 0)`? One
323---  option would be to lift the definition of `Aexp.eval` to
324---  return an option:
325-
326-namespace Aexp
327-
328-def eval (a : Aexp) : Option Nat :=
329-  match a with
330-  | num   n     =>  some n
331-  | plus  a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
332-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ + n₂)
333-                    | _, _ => none
334-  | minus a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
335-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ - n₂)
336-                    | _, _ => none
337-  | mult  a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
338-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ * n₂)
339-                    | _, _ => none
340-  | div   a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
341-                    | _, some 0 => none
342-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => if n₂ ∣ n₁ then some (n₁ / n₂) else none
343-                    | _, _ => none
344-end Aexp
345-
346---  This definition is a lot wordier than the earlier
347---  version. There are tools to reduce this overhead, namely
348---  monads, but we will not discuss these in Software
349---  Foundations in Lean. Curious readers can learn more
350---  about them from [Functional Programming in
351---  Lean](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monads/).
352---
353---  By contrast, partiality is no problem for the relational
354---  version of the definition.
355-
356---  What should `Aexp.eval` return for
357---  `.div (.num 1) (.num 0)`??
358-
359-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
360-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
361-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
362-      EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
363-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
364-      EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
365-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
366-      EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
367-  | div (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ n₃ : Nat)             -- NEW
368-      (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) (hpos : n₂ > 0) (hdiv : n₂ * n₃ = n₁) :
369-      EvalR (.div a₁ a₂) n₃
370-
371---  Notice that there are some inputs (those with a divisor
372---  of 0) for which this relation does not specify an
373---  output.
374-
375-end Slang.AevalRDivision
376-
377-namespace Slang.AevalRExtended
378-
379---  Another example: a *nondeterministic* number generator:
380-
381---  As another example, suppose that we want to extend the
382---  arithmetic operations by a nondeterministic number
383---  generator `any` that, when evaluated, may yield any
384---  number. (This is not the same as making a
385---  *probabilistic* choice among all numbers -- we only say
386---  which results are *possible*.)
387-
388-inductive Aexp where
389-  | any                            -- NEW
390-  | num (n : Nat)
391-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
392-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
393-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
394-
395---  Again, extending `Aexp.eval` would be tricky, since
396---  evaluation is now *not* a deterministic function from
397---  expressions to numbers; but extending the relation is no
398---  problem.
399-
400---  What should `Aexp.eval` do with nondeterminism??
401-
402-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
403-  | any (n : Nat) : EvalR .any n                   -- NEW
404-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
405-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
406-      EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
407-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
408-      EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
409-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
410-      EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
411-
412-end Slang.AevalRExtended

13-/-- Internal syntactic representation of a single inversion alternative. -/
14-declare_syntax_cat invAlt

16-
17-/-- An inversion alternative matching one or more goal tags,
18-  expanding to multiple single [invAlt]s. -/

20-syntax (" | " caseArg)+ " => " tacticSeq : invAlts

22-/--
23-  `inversion h` behaves like `cases h` except that where `cases` would fail with
24-  > "Dependent elimination failed: Failed to solve equation ...",
25-
26-  `inversion` instead leaves behind those unsolveable equations in the context.
27-  These equations arise from generalizing the indices of `h`'s type.
28-  In such cases, `h` itself is generalized with a heterogenenous equality `heq`
29-  to the corresponding constructor in each branch.
30-
31-  For instance, given a hypothesis `h : f n ≤ 0`,
32-  `inversion h` will produce one goal for the case `Nat.le.refl {n} : n ≤ n`
33-  with the equations `eq : f n = 0` and `heq : h ≍ Nat.le.refl`,
34-  rather than failing to solve `f n = 0`.
35-
36-  * If `inversion +clear h` is set, then `heq` will be `clear`ed from the context if present,
37-    along with `h` if there are no dependencies on it.
38-    This is the usual behavior of `cases`.
39-  * The form `inversion t with (tac ...) | tag₁ x ... => tac ... | ... | tagₙ z ... => tac ...`
40-    is supported, similar to that of `cases` and `induction`.
41--/
42-syntax (name := inversion)
43-  "inversion " optConfig ident (" with " (tacticSeq)? (colGe invAlts)*)? : tactic
44-
45-end Lean.Parser

60-/--
61-  This function is similar to `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`: Given `e` of the
62-  form `forall ..xs, A`, this combinator will create a new metavariable for
63-  each `x` in `xs` until it reaches an `x` whose type is defeq to `t`,
64-  and instantiate `A` with these, while also reducing `A` if needed.
65-  It uses `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`.
66-
67-  This function returns a triple `(mvs, bis, out)` where
68-  - `mvs` is an array containing the new metavariables.
69-  - `bis` is an array containing the binder infos for the `mvs`.
70-  - `out` is `e` but instantiated with the `mvs`.
71-
72-  Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Lean/Meta/Basic.lean#L41].
73--/
74-def forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq
75-    (e t : Expr) (kind : MetavarKind := MetavarKind.natural) :
76-    MetaM (Array Expr × Array BinderInfo × Expr) := do
77-  let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing e (some 1) kind
78-  unless ms.size == 1 do
79-    if ms.size == 0 then throwError m!"Failed: {← ppExpr e} is not the type of a function."
80-    else throwError m!"Failed"
81-  let mut mvs := ms
82-  let mut bis := bs
83-  let mut out : Expr := tp
84-  while !(← isDefEq (← inferType mvs.toList.getLast!) t) do
85-    let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing out (some 1) kind
86-    unless ms.size == 1 do
87-      throwError m!"Failed to find {← ppExpr t} as the type of a parameter of {← ppExpr e}."
88-    mvs := mvs ++ ms
89-    bis := bis ++ bs
90-    out := tp
91-  return (mvs, bis, out)
92-
93-/-- Given equations `eqs` in the local context of `mvarId`,
94-  unify them using [Lean.Meta.unifyEq?],
95-  but if unification fails, leave the equation in the context.
96-  This means we should never get a "Dependent elimination failed" error.
97-  While marked partial, this _should_ always terminate,
98-  decreasing on the sum of the sizes of the terms of each equation.
99-
100-  Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyEqs]. -/
101-partial def unifyEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (mvarId : MVarId) (subst : FVarSubst) (caseName? : Option Name) : MetaM (MVarId × FVarSubst) := withIncRecDepth do
102-  match eqs with
103-  | [] => return (mvarId, subst)
104-  | eq :: eqs =>
105-    let some { mvarId, subst, numNewEqs } ← Option.join <$> (observing? $ unifyEq? mvarId eq subst MVarId.acyclic caseName?)
106-      | unifyEqs eqs mvarId subst caseName?
107-    let (newEqs, mvarId) ← mvarId.introN numNewEqs
108-    let eqs := eqs.map (Expr.fvarId! ∘ subst.get)
109-    unifyEqs (newEqs.toList ++ eqs) mvarId subst caseName?
110-
111-/-- Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyCasesEqs]. -/
112-def unifyCasesEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
113-  subgoals.filterMapM fun s => do
114-    let eqs := eqs.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
115-    let (mvarId, subst) ← unifyEqs eqs s.mvarId s.subst s.ctorName
116-    if (← mvarId.isAssignedOrDelayedAssigned) then return none
117-    else return some { s with
118-      mvarId := mvarId,
119-      subst  := subst,
120-      fields := s.fields.map (subst.apply ·)
121-    }
122-
123-/-- Try to clear the given fvars from the local context of each subgoal,
124-  using the subgoals' substitution mappings to find the fvars.
125-
126-  As with [MVarId.tryClearMany], the fvars must be in the order they appear in the context.  -/
127-def casesClearMany (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) (fvarIds : Array FVarId) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
128-  subgoals.mapM fun s => do
129-    let fvarIds := fvarIds.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
130-    let mvarId ← s.mvarId.tryClearMany fvarIds
131-    return { s with mvarId }

143-/--
144-  `apply t at i` uses forward reasoning with `t` at the hypothesis `i`.
145-  Explicitly, if `t : α₁ → ⋯ → αᵢ → ⋯ → αₙ` and `i` has type `αᵢ`, then this tactic adds
146-  metavariables/goals for any terms of `αⱼ` for `j = 1, …, i-1`,
147-  then replaces the type of `i` with `αᵢ₊₁ → ⋯ → αₙ` by applying those metavariables and the
148-  original `i`.

153-  let f ← elabTermForApply t

163-  let mainGoal ← mainGoal.tryClear ldecl.fvarId

166-structure InversionConfig where

171-open Cases in
172-/-- Perform inversion on the given variable in the context of the given goal.
173-  Behaves like [Lean.Meta.Cases.cases] and generalizes indices if they aren't independent,
174-  except instead of calling [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyEqs], which may fail
175-  if the generalizing equations can't all be destructed and substituted away,
176-  it calls our [unifyCasesEqs] above, which keeps unsolvable equations in the context. -/
177-def _root_.Lean.MVarId.inversion (mvarId : MVarId) (h : FVarId) (config : InversionConfig)
178-    (givenNames : Array AltVarNames := #[]) (interestingCtors? : Option (Array Name) := none) :
179-    TacticM (Array CasesSubgoal) := mvarId.withContext do
180-  let goal ← getMainGoal
181-  goal.withContext do
182-    let some ctx ← mkCasesContext? h
183-    | throwTacticEx `inversion goal "Target {Expr.fvar h} does not belong to an inductive type"
184-    -- If the target's type isn't a predicate with indices, behave like `cases`
185-    if ← hasIndepIndices ctx then
186-      let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn goal h givenNames ctx (interestingCtors? := interestingCtors?)
187-      let subgoals ← if config.clear
188-        then casesClearMany subgoals #[h]
189-        else pure subgoals
190-      return subgoals
191-    -- Otherwise, use custom [unifyEqs] to not fail on unifying HEqs
192-    else
193-      let gis@⟨newGoal, _, newTarget, numEqs⟩ ← generalizeIndices goal h
194-      let (newEqs, newGoal) ← newGoal.introN numEqs
195-      let some targetEq := newEqs.back?
196-      | throwTacticEx `inversion newGoal "Failed to generalize target"
197-      let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn newGoal newTarget givenNames ctx (interestingCtors? := interestingCtors?)
198-      let subgoals ← elimAuxIndices gis subgoals
199-      let subgoals ← unifyCasesEqs newEqs.toList subgoals
200-      let subgoals ← if config.clear
201-        then casesClearMany subgoals #[h, targetEq]
202-        else pure subgoals
203-      return subgoals

205-/-- Given an inversion alternative and a list of goals,
206-  solve the tagged goal with the provided tactics,
207-  throwing an error if the goal cannot be found or solved. -/
208-def evalInvAlt (goals : List MVarId) (alt : TSyntax `invAlt) : TacticM (List MVarId) :=
209-  match alt with
210-  | `(invAlt| | $tag:ident $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
211-    if let some goal ← goals.findM? (matchTag tag.getId <$> ·.getUserName) then
212-      return [← trySolveGoal vars tactics goal]
213-    else throwError m!"Invalid alternative name `{tag.getId}`: {← errorMsg}"
214-  | `(invAlt| | _ $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
215-    if !goals.isEmpty then
216-      goals.mapM (trySolveGoal vars tactics)
217-    else throwErrorAt alt m!"Invalid wildcard alternative: {← errorMsg}"
218-  | _ => throwErrorAt alt "Could not parse inversion alternative"
219-where
220-  matchTag tag name : Bool :=
221-    tag == name || tag.isPrefixOf name || tag.isSuffixOf name
222-  trySolveGoal vars tactics goal : TacticM MVarId := do
223-    let goals ← renameInaccessibles goal vars >>= evalTacticAt tactics
224-    unless goals.isEmpty do
225-      reportUnsolvedGoals goals
226-    return goal
227-  errorMsg : TacticM MessageData := do
228-    let goalMsgs ← goals.mapM (.ofName <$> ·.getUserName)
229-    return if goals.isEmpty
230-      then m!"There are no unhandled alternatives"
231-      else m!"Expected {.orList goalMsgs}"
232-
233-@[tactic Lean.Parser.inversion, inherit_doc Lean.Parser.inversion]
234-public meta def evalInversion : Tactic
235-  | `(tactic| inversion $config $h:ident $[with $[$tactics?:tacticSeq]? $[$alts?:invAlts]*]?) => do
236-    let casesSubgoals ← (← getMainGoal).inversion (← getFVarId h) (← elabInversionConfig config)
237-    let mut goals ← casesSubgoals.toList.mapM setUserName
238-    if let some tactics := tactics?.join then
239-      let subgoals ← goals.mapM (evalTacticAt tactics)
240-      goals ← subgoals.flatten.filterM (not <$> ·.isAssignedOrDelayedAssigned)
241-    if let some alts := alts? then
242-      let expandedAlts ← Array.flatten <$> alts.mapM expandInvAlts
243-      for alt in expandedAlts do
244-        let solvedGoals ← evalInvAlt goals alt
245-        goals := goals.removeAll solvedGoals
246-      unless goals.isEmpty do
247-        reportUnsolvedGoals goals
248-    replaceMainGoal goals
249-  | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion tactic"
250-where
251-  setUserName subgoal : TacticM MVarId := do
252-    if let some name := subgoal.ctorName then
253-      subgoal.mvarId.setUserName name.getSuffix
254-    return subgoal.mvarId
255-  expandInvAlts
256-    | `(invAlts| $[| $args:caseArg]* => $tactics:tacticSeq) =>
257-      args.mapM (`(invAlt| | $(·) => $tactics))
258-    | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion alternatives"
259-
260-end Lean.Elab.Tactic
261-
262-end -- meta section

264-namespace Tests
265-open Nat
266-
267-set_option autoImplicit false
268-set_option pp.proofs true
269-set_option pp.fieldNotation false
270-
271-/-! # `inversion` tests -/
272-
273-/-- In Lean, "inversion" on `leq : f n ≤ 0`, where `f : Nat → Nat`,
274-  requires `generalizing e : f n = m`, since Lean does not perform
275-  the dependent case analysis automatically. `cases leq` will fail here.
276-  We want to keep the style of reasoning familiar to PL:
277-  "I know `h`; what must have been true for `h` to be true?"
278-  The technicality of needing to generalize hinders teaching and learning
279-  this style of reasoning for audiences new to proof assistants and logic.
280-  To solve this, we introduce and use the `inversion` tactic,
281-  which automatically generalizes varaibles, performs case analysis,
282-  and eliminates impossible subcases. -/
283-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
284-  -- cases leq /- Dependent elimination failed: Failed to solve equation 0 = f n -/
285-  inversion leq; assumption
286-
287-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
288-  inversion +clear leq; assumption
289-
290-/-- error: Unknown identifier `leq` -/
291-#guard_msgs(error) in
292-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
293-  inversion +clear leq
294-  guard_hyp leq
295-
296-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
297-  inversion leq with
298-  | refl heq eq =>
299-    guard_hyp heq : leq ≍ le.refl
300-    guard_hyp eq : 0 = f n
301-    assumption
302-
303-/-- warning: declaration uses `sorry` -/
304-#guard_msgs(warning) in
305-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n m : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ f m) : f n = 0 := by
306-  inversion leq with
307-  | refl e _ | step k _ e _ =>
308-    try rw [← e]
309-    sorry
310-
311-/-- error: Invalid wildcard alternative: There are no unhandled alternatives -/
312-#guard_msgs(error) in
313-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n m : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ f m) : f n = 0 := by
314-  inversion +clear leq with
315-  | refl e | step k _ e =>
316-    try rw [← e]
317-    sorry
318-  | _ => sorry
319-
320-/-- error: Invalid alternative name `step`: There are no unhandled alternatives -/
321-#guard_msgs(error) in
322-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n m : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ f m) : f n = 0 := by
323-  inversion +clear leq with
324-  | _ e | step k _ e =>
325-    try rw [← e]
326-    sorry
327-
328-inductive The : ∀ {α}, α → Prop where
329-  | mk : The zero
330-
331-/-- sfl#40: Case names should be the constructors' names -/
332-example {x : Nat} (h : The x) : x = zero := by
333-  inversion h with
334-  | mk => rfl
335-
336-example {α} {n m k : α} : [n, m] = [k, k] → [n] = [m] := by
337-  intro h
338-  inversion h; rfl
339-
340-example {n : Nat} : n + 1 = 1 + n := by
341-  induction n with try rfl
342-  | succ => lia
343-
344-inductive NoStutter {α : Type} : List α → Prop where
345-  | nostutter0: NoStutter []
346-  | nostutter1 {n} : NoStutter (n :: [])
347-  | nostutter2 {x y l} (hneq : x ≠ y) (h : NoStutter (y :: l)) : NoStutter (x :: y :: l)
348-
349-/-- The last (only) case name need not be provided -/
350-example : ¬ (NoStutter [3, 1, 1, 4]) := by
351-  intro contra
352-  inversion contra with | _ contra =>
353-  inversion contra with | _ h _ =>
354-  apply h
355-  rfl
356-
357-/-- Inversion may optionally take a sequence of tactics on all goals -/
358-example {α x y} {l : List α} (h : NoStutter l) (hl : l = x :: y :: []) : x ≠ y := by
359-  inversion h with
360-    injections
361-    try subst_vars
362-  | nostutter2 => assumption
363-
364-/-- `with` acts similarly to `<;>` on the optional sequence of tactics -/
365-example {α x y} {l : List α} (h : NoStutter l) (hl : l = x :: y :: []) : x ≠ y := by
366-  inversion h with
367-    injections
368-    try (subst_vars; assumption)
369-
370-example {x y} {l : List Nat} (h : NoStutter l) (hl : l = x :: y :: []) : x ≠ y := by
371-  inversion h with
372-    injections
373-    try cases x
374-  | nostutter2.zero => subst_vars; assumption
375-  | nostutter2.succ => subst_vars; assumption
376-
377-inductive Vec α : Nat → Type where
378-  | nil : Vec α 0
379-  | cons {n} : α → Vec α n → Vec α (n + 1)
380-
381-/-- Inversion should work on indexed `Type`s as well -/
382-example {α} (n : Nat) (v : Vec α (n + 1)) : ∃ hd tl, v = Vec.cons hd tl := by
383-  inversion v with
384-  | cons hd tl => exists hd, tl
385-
386-inductive Wec α : Nat → Type where
387-  | nil : Wec α 0
388-  | cons {n} (f : Nat → Nat) : α → Wec α n → Wec α (f n)
389-
390-/-- warning: declaration uses `sorry` -/
391-#guard_msgs(warning) in
392-example {α} (n : Nat) (v : Wec α (succ n)) :
393-    ∃ hd tl, v = Wec.cons succ hd tl := by
394-  inversion v with
395-  | cons m f hd tl eq heq =>
396-    guard_hyp eq : succ n = f m
397-    guard_hyp heq : v ≍ Wec.cons f hd tl
398-    sorry
399-
400-inductive EmptyRelation : Nat → Nat → Prop where
401-
402-/-- sfl#52: Inversion should still work on nonindexed `Prop`s -/
403-example n m : ¬ EmptyRelation n m := by
404-  intro contra; inversion contra
405-
406-/-- With `inductive.autoPromoteIndices` true (the default),
407-  this is also a nonindexed `Prop`... -/
408-inductive silly : Nat → Prop where
409-| silly1 n (h : n > 1) : silly n
410-| silly2 n (h : exists m, m * 2 = n) : silly n
411-| silly3 n (h : exists m, n = m + 2) : silly n
412-
413-/-- ...and inversion should continue to work -/
414-example {n} (h : silly n) : n ≠ 1 := by
415-  inversion h <;> omega
416-
417-/-- Inversion should also work on nonindexed `Type`s -/
418-example (n : Nat) : Nat := by
419-  inversion n with
420-  | zero => exact zero
421-  | succ n' => exact n'
422-
423-/-! # `lemma` tests -/
424-
425-lemma doubleNegation : ∀ P, P → ¬ ¬ P := by
426-  intro P p np; exact (np p)
427-
428-/-! # `apply` tests -/
429-
430-example (H : Bool → Nat → False) (n : Nat) : False := by
431-  apply H at n; apply n; exact true
432-
433-end Tests

LF/Typeclasses.lean

1-import SFLCompat
2-
3---  # Typeclasses
4-
5---  Chapter Poly introduced **parametric polymorphism**,
6---  declaring a type variable with no constraint on it.
7---
8---  This lets us work with a type like `List α`, writing
9---  functions like `List.reverse` and `List.length` and
10---  proofs like `List.length_reverse`, which use only the
11---  list's structure and never inspect any particular
12---  `a : α`.
13---
14---  Sometimes, though, we want less freedom: rather than
15---  leaving `α` completely generic, we want to partially
16---  specify its behavior. In Lean, this is done through a
17---  form of "ad hoc polymorphism" called **typeclasses**.
18---  The concept originated in Haskell and is analogous to
19---  features you may know from other languages, such as
20---  traits in Rust.
21-
22---  ## Why We Need Typeclasses
23-
24---  Consider the following function, which checks whether a
25---  natural number occurs in a list:
26-
27-def List.elemNat (n : Nat) (ms : List Nat) : Bool :=
28-  match ms with
29-  | [] => false
30-  | m :: ms' => bif n == m then true else elemNat n ms'
31-
32-theorem List.elem_nat_nil (n : Nat) : [].elemNat n = false := rfl
33-
34-theorem List.elem_nat_cons (n m : Nat) (ms : List Nat) :
35-    (m :: ms).elemNat n = bif n == m then true else elemNat n ms := rfl
36-
37-#eval [0, 1].elemNat 0
38-#eval [0, 1].elemNat 1
39-#eval [0, 1].elemNat 2
40-
41---  What if we want this to work for lists of *any* element
42---  type, not just `Nat`? Parametric polymorphism suggests
43---  simply replacing `Nat` with a type variable `α`, but
44---  that produces a puzzling error:
45-
46-sf_expect_failure_in
47-  def List.elemPoly {α : Type} (x : α) (ys : List α) : Bool :=
48-    match ys with
49-    | [] => false
50-    | y :: ys' => bif x == y then true else elemPoly x ys'
51-
52---  Output:
53---    failed to synthesize instance of type class
54---      BEq α
55---
56---    Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
57-
58---  Lean is trying to use typeclasses to work out how `==`
59---  should behave on a value of type `α`. We'll see exactly
60---  why shortly; for now, here's one way to sidestep the
61---  problem: have the caller supply the equality test to
62---  use.
63-
64-def List.elemPolyEq {α : Type} (eq : α → α → Bool) (x : α) (ys : List α) : Bool :=
65-  match ys with
66-  | [] => false
67-  | y :: ys' => bif eq x y then true else elemPolyEq eq x ys'
68-
69-#eval [0, 1].elemPolyEq Nat.beq 0
70-
71---  This works, but it's tedious: every caller has to know,
72---  and remember to supply, the right equality function.
73---
74---  Typeclasses automate this — instead of the programmer
75---  passing the function explicitly, Lean searches for one
76---  and provides it on its own. We specify something we want
77---  Lean to search for by declaring a `class` with the
78---  needed function as a field; a `class` is like an
79---  interface in Java or a trait in Rust. Particular
80---  implementations of that class are called *instances*;
81---  each type can have its own instance of a class. For
82---  functions that would use such instances, we specify the
83---  name of the class in an *instance implicit* on the
84---  polymorphic variable that the instance's function
85---  applies to. This directs Lean to rely on the class
86---  inside the function, and to find and fill in the
87---  appropriate instance when the function is called.
88---
89---  Here is what this looks like for `List.elemPoly`:
90-
91-def List.elemPoly {α : Type} [BEq α] (x : α) (ys : List α) : Bool :=
92-  match ys with
93-  | [] => false
94-  | y :: ys' => bif x == y then true else elemPoly x ys'
95-
96-theorem List.elemPoly_nil {α : Type} [BEq α] (x : α) : [].elemPoly x = false := rfl
97-
98-theorem List.elemPoly_cons {α : Type} [BEq α] (x y : α) (ys : List α) :
99-    (y :: ys).elemPoly x = bif x == y then true else elemPoly x ys := rfl
100-
101-#eval [0, 1].elemPoly 0
102-
103---  Comparing `List.elemPolyEq` with `List.elemPoly`, we see
104---  three differences. First, `List.elemPolyEq` takes an
105---  *explicit* parameter `eq`, whereas `List.elemPoly`
106---  specifies an instance implicit `[BEq α]`. The instance
107---  implicit indicates that an instance of `BEq` must be
108---  provided at call sites for the particular type `α` that
109---  is used. Second, whereas `List.elemPolyEq` invokes
110---  parameter `eq` to test equality, `List.elemPoly` uses
111---  `==` instead. As Lists noted when we first used it, `==`
112---  on `Nat` comes from the `BEq` typeclass. Finally,
113---  whereas `[0, 1].elemPolyEq Nat.beq 0` passes the
114---  equality function `Nat.beq` explicitly, in
115---  `[0, 1].elemPoly 0` Lean fills it in automatically based
116---  on the type `Nat` of the `List`.
117-
118---  Going back to the earlier version of `List.elemPoly`,
119---  without the instance implicit, we can now understand the
120---  error message: `α` was fully generic, so the `==` in its
121---  body would have needed to work for *every* type `α`, and
122---  no single `BEq` instance can do that. So Lean's search
123---  failed.
124---
125---  Now it is time to dig into the details of what we have
126---  seen so far. We'll see exactly how `[BEq α]` gets filled
127---  in below, starting with how to define a typeclass in the
128---  first place.
129-
130---  ## Defining Your Own Typeclasses
131-
132---  `BEq` comes from Lean's standard library. Let's define a
133---  typeclass of our own, to see the mechanism — classes,
134---  instances, and synthesis — that made `==` resolve
135---  automatically above.
136---
137---  Suppose we want a function that returns the first
138---  element of a list, defaulting to a given value if the
139---  list is empty. As with `List.elemPolyEq` above, here is
140---  a version that makes the default value an explicit
141---  parameter:
142-
143-def List.headOrEx {α : Type} (defaultValue : α) (xs : List α) : α :=
144-  match xs with
145-  | [] => defaultValue
146-  | x :: _ => x
147-
148-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOrEx 0
149-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOrEx 0
150-
151---  This works, but again it's tedious: every caller has to
152---  supply an element of `α` to default to, even when
153---  there's an obvious choice based on the type of the
154---  things in the list, like `0` for `Nat`.
155---
156---  Getting Lean to fill in `defaultValue` automatically
157---  takes two things. One is marking the parameter as
158---  "searchable," rather than something the caller always
159---  supplies explicitly. The other is giving Lean some
160---  information about what it should search *for*.
161---
162---  Considering the second problem first: the way to provide
163---  this information is to *name* the data we're after — the
164---  **default value** of a type. In particular, a
165---  `structure` (chapter Lists) is a good way to give this
166---  information a name; structures can also bundle together
167---  more than one piece of data, which will come in handy
168---  later, though we only need a single field here.
169---
170---  To address the first problem, we need to mark this
171---  particular structure as one Lean should search for
172---  automatically — not every `structure`-typed argument
173---  should be.
174---
175---  Let's build up to what we want in two steps: first the
176---  naming, as a plain `structure`; then the marking, by
177---  upgrading it to a `class`. Here's the structure — we'll
178---  put it in its own namespace so we can reuse the name
179---  `DefaultValue` for the class version below:
180-
181-namespace DefaultValueScratch
182-
183-structure DefaultValue (α : Type) where
184-  value : α
185-
186---  A value of type `DefaultValue Nat` picks out a
187---  particular `Nat` to serve as the type's default: it's
188---  built the same way any structure is, by supplying a
189---  `Nat` for the `value` field:
190-
191-def natDefault : DefaultValue Nat where
192-  value := 0
193-
194-end DefaultValueScratch
195-
196---  Now for the marking: we need to tell Lean that
197---  `DefaultValue` is the sort of structure it should search
198---  for automatically, the way it needs to for
199---  `List.headOrEx`'s `defaultValue` argument. We do this by
200---  writing `class` in place of `structure`:
201-
202-class DefaultValue (α : Type) where
203-  value : α
204-
205---  We then provide values of this type a bit differently.
206---  Instead of `def`, we use `instance`:
207-
208-instance instDefaultValueNat : DefaultValue Nat where
209-  value := 0
210-
211---  Lean can now find this instance on its own, via
212---  *typeclass synthesis* (or *typeclass inference*) — the
213---  same process that found `BEq Nat` earlier. That means we
214---  can rewrite `List.headOrEx` the same way we rewrote
215---  `List.elemPolyEq` into `List.elemPoly` above, replacing
216---  the explicit `defaultValue` parameter with an instance
217---  implicit:
218-
219-def List.headOr {α : Type} [DefaultValue α] (xs : List α) : α :=
220-  match xs with
221-  | [] => DefaultValue.value
222-  | x :: _ => x
223-
224-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOr
225-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOr
226-
227-example : DefaultValue.value = (0 : Nat) := by rfl
228-
229---  Notice that we refer to `DefaultValue.value` alone, with
230---  no instance named. Because the expression equates
231---  `DefaultValue.value` with the `Nat` `0`, Lean selects
232---  `instDefaultValueNat`, the instance for
233---  `DefaultValue Nat`. We know this because we are able to
234---  prove that `DefaultValue.value` is equal to `0`.
235---
236---  Let's declare a second instance, for `Int`, the type of
237---  integers `... -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...`:
238-
239-instance instDefaultValueInt : DefaultValue Int where
240-  value := -1
241-
242---  We can also create instances for polymorphic types, like
243---  `Option α`, whose default is `none`, by giving the
244---  instance declaration a parameter:
245-
246-instance instDefaultValueOption {α : Type} : DefaultValue (Option α) where
247-  value := none
248-
249---  Now, Lean can infer instances for all these types,
250---  including inside `List.headOr`:
251-
252-example : DefaultValue.value = (0 : Nat) := by rfl
253-example : DefaultValue.value = (-1 : Int) := by rfl
254-example : DefaultValue.value = (none : Option Bool) := by rfl
255-example : DefaultValue.value = (none : Option (List Nat)) := by rfl
256-example : ([] : List Nat).headOr = 0 := by rfl
257-example : ([] : List Int).headOr = -1 := by rfl
258-example : ([] : List (Option Bool)).headOr = none := by rfl
259-example : ([] : List (Option Bool)).headOr = none := by rfl
260-
261---  Synthesis infers instances we could have specified
262---  explicitly:
263-
264-example : instDefaultValueNat.value = (0 : Nat) := by rfl
265-example : instDefaultValueInt.value = (-1 : Int) := by rfl
266-example : instDefaultValueOption.value = (none : Option Nat) := by rfl
267-
268---  The option `pp.all` shows which instance Lean picked:
269-
270-set_option pp.all true in
271-#check (DefaultValue.value : Nat)
272-
273---  Output:
274---    @DefaultValue.value Nat instDefaultValueNat : Nat
275-
276-set_option pp.all true in
277-#check (DefaultValue.value : Int)
278-
279---  Output:
280---    @DefaultValue.value Int instDefaultValueInt : Int
281-
282---  This reveals `instDefaultValueNat` and
283---  `instDefaultValueInt` as the instances Lean picked. The
284---  `#synth` command runs the same search directly:
285-
286-#synth DefaultValue Nat
287-
288---  Output:
289---    instDefaultValueNat
290-
291---  For a typeclass like `DefaultValue` that carries data —
292---  a term, such as the `1` above, rather than only proofs
293---  (which we will see below) — we expect at most one
294---  instance per type, so this search has a unique answer.
295---
296---  We'll put `DefaultValue`'s standard-library equivalent,
297---  `Inhabited`, to work later in this chapter, when we
298---  define maps that need a default value for a generic
299---  type. First, though, let's go back to `List.elemPoly`
300---  and see how its `[BEq α]` argument actually gets
301---  resolved.
302-
303---  ## Using Typeclasses
304-
305---  Let's check what `==` meant for `List.elemNat`, with
306---  notation display turned off:
307-
308-set_option pp.notation false in
309-#check 1 == 2
310-
311---  Output:
312---    BEq.beq 1 2 : Bool
313-
314---  Rather than `Nat.beq`, `==` turns out to be notation for
315---  `BEq.beq`, a field of exactly the kind of typeclass we
316---  just learned to define:
317-
318-sf_recall
319-  class BEq (α : Type) where
320-      beq : α → α → Bool
321-
322---  Writing `x == y` makes Lean search for an **instance**
323---  of `BEq` for the type of `x` and `y`, the same way it
324---  searched for a `DefaultValue` instance above. For `Nat`,
325---  that instance is:
326-
327-instance (priority := low) : BEq Nat where
328-  beq := Nat.beq
329-
330---  This is the instance Lean supplies for `[BEq α]` when
331---  `List.elemPoly` is called on a `List Nat` — no different
332---  from Lean choosing `instDefaultValueNat` for
333---  `DefaultValue.value` earlier when it was equated with
334---  `(1 : Nat)`.
335-
336---  ### Exercise (1 star): List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat ⭐
337-
338---  Prove that `List.elemPoly` agrees with `List.elemNat`
339---  when specialized to natural numbers.
340-
341-theorem List.elemPoly_eq_elemNat (ms : List Nat) (n : Nat) : ms.elemPoly n = ms.elemNat n := by
342-  sorry
343-
344---  ## Proof-Carrying Typeclasses
345-
346---  The above examples enforce no conditions on the data an
347---  instance may carry — any value of the right type will
348---  do. But sometimes enforcing constraints on data is
349---  useful. For example, suppose we want to specify that a
350---  type has not just a single element, but two. Here is a
351---  first attempt:
352-
353-sf_experiment
354-  class HasTwoIncomplete (α : Type) where
355-    one : α
356-    two : α
357-
358---  Unfortunately, this specification isn't precise because
359---  it allows `one` and `two` to refer to the same term.
360---  Fortunately, Lean's typeclasses can carry proofs along
361---  with data, so we can write the following to enforce that
362---  `one` and `two` are distinct.
363-
364-class HasTwo (α : Type) where
365-  one : α
366-  two : α
367-  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
368-
369---  Declaring instances works in much the same way as
370---  before, except that now the `HasTwo.one_neq_two` field
371---  requires a proof:
372-
373-instance : HasTwo Nat where
374-  one := 1
375-  two := 2
376-  one_neq_two := by intro contra; contradiction
377-
378---  In most languages that support typeclasses (or traits)
379---  it is not possible to formally enforce laws such as
380---  `one_neq_two`. Thus it falls to the author to check,
381---  informally, that any required invariants are satisfied,
382---  which can lead to bugs.
383-
384---  ### Exercise (1 star): HasThree ⭐
385-
386---  Following the pattern of `DefaultValue` and `HasTwo`,
387---  define a class `HasThree` that specifies a type with at
388---  least three distinct elements, and give an instance of
389---  it for `Nat`.
390-
391-class HasThree (α : Type) where
392-  one : α
393-  two : α
394-  three : α
395-  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
396-  --  FILL IN HERE

400-  two := 2
