404-
405-namespace Algebra
406-
407---  This facility is very powerful, and is used extensively
408---  in Lean to define mathematical structures that carry
409---  both operators and laws about how those operators
410---  interact. As a simple example, let's use a typeclass to
411---  define a *monoid*, a simple algebraic structure that
412---  includes four things:
413---
414---  - an underlying set of data, represented by a type `α`,
415---
416---  - an operator (which we'll write `⊗`, typed otimes) that
417---    combines two elements of type `α` into one,
418---
419---  - a particular element `id` of type `α`, which we call
420---    the "identity element", and
421---
422---  - some laws about the interaction of `⊗` and `id`,
423---    namely that:
424---
425---    - `∀ x, id ⊗ x = x = x ⊗ id`, and
426---
427---    - `∀ x y z, x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z` (i.e., that `⊗`
428---      is associative)
429---
430---  We can express these requirements in the form of a
431---  typeclass:
432-
433--- first we define a notation typeclass for our operator ⊗
434-class OpSet (α : Type) where
435-  op : α → α → α
436-
437-infixr:70 " ⊗ " => OpSet.op
438-
439-class Monoid (α : Type) extends (OpSet α) where
440-  id : α
441-  left_id  (x : α)  : id ⊗ x = x
442-  right_id (x : α)  : x ⊗ id = x
443-  assoc (x y z : α) : x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z
444-
445---  The `extends` keyword indicates that the `Monoid`
446---  typeclass extends the `OpSet` typeclass, which just
447---  defines a set with an operator and some notation for it.
448---  The `Monoid` typeclass "inherits" the fields of `OpSet`,
449---  similar to how a class would in an object-oriented
450---  language.
451---
452---  As one might expect, the `+` operator over `Nat`s forms
453---  a monoid, where `0` is the identity element. Note that
454---  we don't have to define `Nat`'s `OpSet` instance
455---  separately, we can define a single instance that
456---  implements both classes.
457-
458-instance : Monoid Nat where
459-  op := Nat.add
460-  id := 0
461-  left_id := by lia
462-  right_id := by lia
463-  assoc := by lia
464-
465---  ### Exercise (1 star): NatMonoidMul ⭐
466-
467---  However, multiplication on `Nat`s *also* forms a monoid.
468---  What is its identity element?
469-
470-instance : Monoid Nat where
471-  op := Nat.mul
472-  id := sorry
473-  left_id := sorry
474-  right_id := sorry
475-  assoc := sorry
476-
477---  ### Exercise (1 star): ListMonoidAppend ⭐
478-
479---  There are also many monoids over other types. Most
480---  usefully in computer science, lists of any type also
481---  form a monoid, with `List.append` as the operator in
482---  question:
483-
484-instance {α : Type} : Monoid (List α) where
485-  op := List.append
486-  id := sorry
487-  left_id := sorry
488-  right_id := sorry
489-  assoc := sorry
490-
491---  In addition to defining instances of `Monoid`, we can
492---  also prove some properties about monoids in general,
493---  just based on the laws defined on the typeclass. One
494---  simple theorem about monoids is that the identity
495---  element of a monoid is unique. That is, if we have two
496---  monoids over the same set with the same operator, their
497---  identity elements must also be the same:
498-
499-theorem id_unique {α : Type} {m₁ m₂ : Monoid α} (h : m₁.op = m₂.op) : m₁.id = m₂.id := by
500-  obtain @⟨op₁, id₁, left_id₁, right_id₁, assoc₁⟩ := m₁
501-  obtain @⟨op₂, id₂, left_id₂, right_id₂, assoc₂⟩ := m₂
502-  have h' : id₁ = id₂ := by
503-    -- this introduces a use of m₁'s operator
504-    rw [← left_id₁ id₂]
505-    -- we use our hypothesis to rewrite m₁'s operator into m₂'s
506-    rw [h]
507-    -- then, we can use m₂'s right id
508-    rw [right_id₂]
509-  -- the goal `m₁.id = m₂.id` is equivalent with `id₁ = id₂` even though it displays `Monoid.id = Monoid.id`
510-  exact h'
511-
512---  In the above proof, we can destructure the monoid
513---  instances `m₁` and `m₂` with the `obtain` tactic we saw
514---  in the Logic chapter. When we do so however, because
515---  these are class instances instead of normal structures,
516---  we prepend our tuple by the `@` symbol. When stepping
517---  through the above proof, if the notation is confusing to
518---  you, remember that you can set `set_option pp.all true`
519---  or `set_option pp.explicit true` to make Lean show you
520---  more clearly what is going on. For example, the goal is
521---  displayed as `Monoid.id = Monoid.id` since the instances
522---  `m₁` and `m₂` are implicit arguments to `Monoid.id`.
523---  Setting `pp.explicit true` displays the goal as
524---  `@Eq α (@Monoid.id α m₁) (@Monoid.id α m₂)`.
525---
526---  A *group* is a special kind of monoid with an *inverse*
527---  operation `inv`, which has the property that
528---  `∀ x, inv x ⊗ x = id = x ⊗ inv x`. We can extend the
529---  definition of a `Monoid` to capture this new feature:
530-
531-class Group (α : Type) extends (Monoid α) where
532-  inv : α → α
533-  left_inv  (x : α) : inv x ⊗ x = id
534-  right_inv (x : α) : x ⊗ inv x = id
535-
536---  Now, the monoids we described earlier are not groups:
537---  there is no inverse operation on the natural numbers
538---  such that `∀ x, x + inv x = 0 = inv x + x`, for example.
539---  However, addition does form a group over the integers:
540-
541---  ### Exercise (1 star): IntGroupAdd ⭐
542-
543-instance : Group Int where
544-  op := Int.add
545-  id := sorry
546-  inv := sorry
547-  left_id := sorry
548-  right_id := sorry
549-  assoc := sorry
550-  left_inv := sorry
551-  right_inv := sorry
552-
553---  The study of groups is called *group theory* and is a
554---  rich area of mathematics. Here, we will only prove a
555---  handful of its simplest results:
556-
557---  ### Exercise (1 star): InverseUnique ⭐
558-
559---  Two groups defined with the same operation over the same
560---  set must have the same inverse as well.
561-
562-theorem inv_unique {α : Type} {g₁ g₂ : Group α} (h : g₁.op = g₂.op) : g₁.inv = g₂.inv := by
563-  sorry
564-
565---  ### Exercise (1 star): IdentityUnique ⭐
566-
567---  If an element of a monoid satisfies just one of the the
568---  identity laws (here, we take the left), then it must be
569---  equal to the monoid's identity element.
570-
571-theorem Monoid.id_unique_left {α : Type} [Monoid α] (x : α)
572-    (hₗ : ∀ y, x ⊗ y = y) : x = id := by
573-  sorry
574-
575---  ### Exercise (2 stars): InverseInverse ⭐⭐
576-
577---  The inverse of the inverse of an element is itself; we
578---  prove this using an intermediate lemma.
579-
580-theorem inv_inv' {α : Type} {g : Group α} (x y z : α)
581-    (h₁ : g.inv x = y) (h₂ : g.inv y = z) : x = z := by
582-  sorry
583-
584-theorem inv_inv {α : Type} {g : Group α} (x : α) : g.inv (g.inv x) = x := by
585-  sorry
586-
587-end Algebra
588-
589---  ## API and Encapsulation
590-
591---  ## Maps
592-
593---  *Maps* (or "dictionaries") are ubiquitous data
594---  structures both in ordinary programming and in the
595---  theory of programming languages; we're going to need
596---  them in many places in later volumes.
597---
598---  We'll define two flavors of maps: *total maps*, which
599---  include a "default" element to be returned when a key
600---  being looked up doesn't exist, and *partial maps*, which
601---  instead return an option to indicate success or failure.
602---  Partial maps are defined in terms of total maps, using
603---  `none` as the default element.
604-
605---  ### Key and Value Types
606-
607---  To define maps, we first need a type for the keys that
608---  we will use to index into our maps and a type for the
609---  values the maps return. In this section, we'll use the
610---  type variable `α` for the type of keys and `β` for
611---  values. In addition to `BEq`, which we have already
612---  seen, our key type `α` requires instances of the
613---  `ReflBEq` and `LawfulBEq` typeclasses:
614-
615-sf_recall
616-  class ReflBEq (α : Type) [BEq α] : Prop where
617-      rfl {a : α} : a == a
618-
619-sf_recall
620-  class LawfulBEq (α : Type) [BEq α] : Prop extends ReflBEq α where
621-      eq_of_beq : {a b : α} → a == b → a = b
622-
623---  These classes refine `BEq`, specifying that (`==`) is
624---  reflexive and coincides with proposition equality `=`.
625---
626---  In general, we place no constraints on the value type
627---  `β`.
628-
629---  ### Total Maps
630-
631---  The Lists chapter introduced a partial map abstraction,
632---  `PartialMap`, with a `find` function for lookup, based
633---  on lists of key-value pairs. Here, we are going to build
634---  a map abstraction using functions instead. The advantage
635---  of this representation is that it offers a more
636---  *extensional* view of maps, as we saw with functions in
637---  the Logic chapter: two maps that respond to every query
638---  in the same way will be represented as exactly the same
639---  function, rather than just as "equivalent" list
640---  structures. This simplifies proofs that use maps.
641---
642---  Instead of using functions directly, we encapsulate them
643---  inside a `structure` which we call `TotalMap`.
644---  Intuitively, a total map just contains a function
645---  `inner` from a key of type `α` to a value of type `β`.
646-
647-structure TotalMap (α : Type) (β : Type) where
648-  inner : α → β
649-
650-namespace TotalMap
651-
652---  In order to declare a default value of `β` we will use
653---  the `Inhabited` typeclass, which is the standard
654---  library's implementation of our `DefaultValue` example
655---  from above:
656---
657---  The function `TotalMap.empty` yields an empty total map,
658---  given a default element; this map always returns the
659---  default element when applied to any key.
660-
661-def empty {α β : Type} [Inhabited β] : TotalMap α β where
662-  inner := fun _ => default
663-
664---  These types and implicit instances are now available
665---  automatically to all the definitions in this section.
666---
667---  Just as declaring `BEq`/`DefaultValue` instances above
668---  hooked `==` and `DefaultValue.value` up to our types, we
669---  can declare an instance of the standard library's
670---  `EmptyCollection` typeclass to associate `∅` with this
671---  empty map.
672-
673-instance {α β : Type} [Inhabited β] : EmptyCollection (TotalMap α β) where
674-  emptyCollection := TotalMap.empty
675-
676-theorem empty_def {α β : Type} [Inhabited β] :
677-    (∅ : TotalMap α β) = { inner := fun _ => default } := by rfl
678-
679---  Here, for example, is an empty map that takes `Nat` keys
680---  to `Nat` values:
681-
682-def emptyNatMap : TotalMap Nat Nat := ∅
683-
684---  #### Getting Elements
685-
686---  While `TotalMap`s happen to be implemented as functions
687---  under the hood, we would prefer not to expose this fact
688---  in its public interface. Accordingly, we define new
689---  operations for querying and updating mappings. We define
690---  a function `get` for getting the value associated with a
691---  key playing the role that `find` played for the Lists
692---  chapter's list-based maps,
693-
694-def get {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) := m.inner a
695-
696-/-- This exposes implementation-specific details of `TotalMap`.
697-  Avoid using this outside the `TotalMap` namespace. -/
698-theorem get_def {α β : Type} {m : TotalMap α β} {a : α} : m.get a = m.inner a := by rfl
699-
700-example : emptyNatMap.get 2 = 0 := by rfl
701-
702---  Here is an example that uses the API lemmas `empty_def`
703---  and `get_def`:
704-
705-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap.get n = 0 := by
706-  rewrite [get_def, emptyNatMap, empty_def, Nat.default_eq_zero]
707-  rfl
708-
709---  In the above example, we use `rewrite` and `rfl` instead
710---  of the usual `rw` to highlight something interesting.
711---  After the rewrites in this proof, we end up with a goal
712---  that looks like `{ inner := fun x => 0 }.inner n = 0`,
713---  which we can solve with `rfl`. This is because the
714---  projection `.inner` on a structure of the form
715---  `{ inner := x }` is definitionally equal to `x`.
716---
717---  `get` is the public API counterpart to `inner` which is
718---  an implementation-specific detail of `TotalMap`. Because
719---  `get_def` "peeks" through the abstraction, it should be
720---  used sparingly, and only inside the `TotalMap`
721---  namespace.
722---
723---  To make element-getting more convenient, let's define
724---  notation so we can write `emptyNatMap[2]` rather than
725---  `emptyNatMap.get`. We could notate `get` directly —
726---  we'll do exactly that for `update` below — but here
727---  we'll instead make "getting an element" its own
728---  typeclass, `MyGetElem`, and notate it. Doing so means
729---  `m[a]` resolves to `MyGetElem.getElem m a` for any type
730---  with a `MyGetElem` instance, not just `TotalMap`.
731---
732---  Using typeclasses to define notation is typical in Lean
733---  when the same notation is useful for many different
734---  types. We have seen the approach already with `==`:
735---  writing `x == y` is notation for `BEq.beq`, resolved by
736---  instance search for whatever type `x` and `y` have. We
737---  also just saw overloaded notation for `EmptyCollection`
738---  above, where `∅` is notation for
739---  `EmptyCollection.emptyCollection`. Our typeclass
740---  `MyGetElem` is a simpler version of the standard
741---  library's `GetElem` typeclass, which has many instances
742---  such as `Array`, `List`, and `Vector`. We develop it to
743---  illustrate the notation-as-typeclass approach.
744-
745-end TotalMap
746-
747---  The `MyGetElem` typeclass takes three type parameters:
748---  the collection implementation, its keys, and its values.
749-
750-class MyGetElem (coll : Type) (idx : Type) (elem : outParam Type) where
751-  getElem (xs : coll) (i : idx) : elem
752-
753---  (Don't worry about the `outParam` qualifier; it is a
754---  hint to Lean that helps typeclass inference.)
755---
756---  The appropriate instance of `MyGetElem` for our
757---  `TotalMap` is:
758-
759-instance {α β : Type} : MyGetElem (TotalMap α β) α β where
760-  getElem m a := m.get a
761-
762---  Now we can associate the bracket syntax with
763---  `MyGetElem.getElem`. We've defined custom notation
764---  before — `::` and `[...]` for lists (chapter Lists,
765---  including an `app_unexpander` for printing
766---  `[...]`-notation lists back out), or `+`/`*`/`==` for
767---  arithmetic — but always with `infixl`/`infixr` or
768---  `scoped macro`; this is the first time we reach for the
769---  more general `notation`/`macro_rules` forms for getting
770---  the `m[a]` syntax to work.
771---
772---  Don't worry about following the mechanism in detail —
773---  the `macro_rules` and the `app_unexpander` below are
774---  minor technicalities. However, if you do wish to learn
775---  more, Chapter 5 and 6 of [Metaprogramming in Lean
776---  4](https://leanprover-community.github.io/lean4-metaprogramming-book/)
777---  contain more detail.
778-
779-namespace MyGetElem
780-
781-scoped macro_rules | `($xs[$i]) => ``(getElem $xs $i)
782-
783-@[app_unexpander getElem]
784-def unexpandGetElem : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
785-  | `($_ $xs $i) => `($xs[$i])
786-  | _ => throw ()
787-end MyGetElem
788-
789-open scoped MyGetElem
790-
791---  Since the standard library already declares the `x[i]`
792---  syntax for `GetElem`, we only need to define the
793---  `macro_rules`, not the `notation` as we have done
794---  previously. It's scoped since we don't want to override
795---  the default `GetElem` everywhere, but only when
796---  `open scoped MyGetElem` is in force.
797-
798---  Since we provided a `MyGetElem` instance for `TotalMap`,
799---  we can now use the notation `m[a]` to access elements of
800---  a map `m`.
801-
802-namespace TotalMap
803-
804-theorem getElem_def {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m[a] = m.get a := by rfl
805-
806-example : emptyNatMap[1] = default := by rfl
807-
808-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap[n] = 0 := by
809-  rw [getElem_def, get_def, emptyNatMap, empty_def, Nat.default_eq_zero]
810-
811---  We want the public API of `TotalMap` to use the `m[a]`
812---  notation instead of `m.get a`, so we provide the reverse
813---  direction of `getElem_def` as a `simp` lemma; the `m[a]`
814---  notation is the `TotalMap` API's `simp` normal form.
815-
816-@[simp]
817-theorem get_eq_getElem {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m.get a = m[a] := rfl
818-
819-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap.get n = emptyNatMap[n] := by
820-  simp
821-
822---  This design minimizes the need to use `getElem_def`
823---  outside concrete examples (which are typically solvable
824---  with `rfl` anyways).
825-
826---  #### Updating Elements
827-
828---  Now we turn to the `update` function, which takes a map
829---  `m`, a key `a`, and a value `b`, and returns a new map
830---  that takes `a` to `b` and takes every other key to
831---  whatever `m` does. We do this by wrapping a new map
832---  function around the old one.
833-
834-def update {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) [BEq α] (a : α) (b : β) : TotalMap α β where
835-  inner := fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a']
836-
837---  For example, we can build a map taking `String` to
838---  `Bool`, where `"foo"` and `"bar"` are mapped to `true`
839---  and every other key is mapped to `false`, like this:
840-
841-def exampleMap :=
842-  (∅ : TotalMap String Bool)
843-    |>.update "foo" true
844-    |>.update "bar" true
845-
846---  Here `|>` is Lean's **pipe** notation: `x |>.f y` means
847---  `x.f y`, letting us chain a sequence of function or
848---  method calls left to right without nested parentheses.
849-
850---  We also introduce a notation for updating maps — this
851---  time, rather than going through a typeclass and its own
852---  `notation`/`macro_rules` machinery as we did for
853---  `MyGetElem`, we write a `notation` that references
854---  `TotalMap.update` directly. Unlike indexing, `update`
855---  doesn't need to work generically across container types
856---  (there's no standard-library operation like `GetElem`
857---  that we're mirroring here), so the simpler, direct route
858---  suffices.
859-
860-notation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 " ; " m:55 => TotalMap.update m a b
861-
862-/-- This exposes implementation-specific details of `TotalMap`.
863-  Avoid using this outside the `TotalMap` namespace.
864-  Prefer `update_apply` if possible. -/
865-theorem update_def {α β : Type} [BEq α] (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) :
866-  a →ₜ b ; m = { inner := fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a'] } := by rfl
867-
868-theorem update_apply {α β : Type} [BEq α] (m : TotalMap α β) (a a' : α) (b : β) :
869-  (a →ₜ b ; m)[a'] = bif a == a' then b else m[a'] := by rfl
870-
871---  We can omit the map from the notation when we want it to
872---  be empty:
873-
874-notation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 => TotalMap.update ∅ a b
875-
876---  The `examplemap` above can now be defined as follows:
877-
878-def exampleMap' : TotalMap String Bool := "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true ; ∅
879-def exampleMap'' : TotalMap String Bool := "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true
880-
881-example : exampleMap = exampleMap' := by rfl
882-example : exampleMap' = exampleMap'' := by rfl
883-
884-example : exampleMap'["bar"] = true := by rfl
885-example : exampleMap'["foo"] = true := by rfl
886-example : exampleMap'["quux"] = false := by rfl
887-
888---  Let's also see a couple of examples of working with
889---  updated maps using rewrites:
890-
891-example : exampleMap'["bar"] = true := by
892-  rw [exampleMap', update_apply, BEq.rfl, cond_true]
893-
894-example : exampleMap'["foo"] = true := by
895-  rw [exampleMap', update_apply, show ("bar" == "foo") = false by simp, cond_false]
896-  rw [update_apply, BEq.rfl, cond_true]
897-
898-example : exampleMap'["quux"] = false := by
899-  rw [exampleMap', update_apply, show ("bar" == "quux") = false by simp, cond_false]
900-  rw [update_apply, show ("foo" == "quux") = false by rfl, cond_false]
901-  rw [empty_def, getElem_def, get_def, Bool.default_bool]
902-
903---  When we use maps in later volumes, we'll need several
904---  fundamental facts about how they behave.
905---
906---  Even if you don't work the following exercises, make
907---  sure you thoroughly understand the statements of the
908---  lemmas!
909---
910---  (Some of the proofs require the extensionality tactic
911---  `ext`, discussed in the Logic chapter.)
912---
913---  First, the empty map returns its default element for all
914---  keys:
915-
916-@[simp]
917-theorem getElem_empty {α β : Type} [BEq α] [Inhabited β] (a : α) : (∅ : TotalMap α β)[a] = default := by
918-  rw [empty_def, getElem_def, get_def]
919-
920---  Notice that in the example `exampleMap'["quux"] = false`
921---  the last rewrite is effectively just `getElem_empty`.
922---
923---  Next, if we update a map `m` at a key `a` with a new
924---  value `b` and then look up `a` in the map resulting from
925---  the `update`, we get back `b`:
926-
927-@[simp]
928-theorem update_eq {α β : Type} [BEq α] [ReflBEq α] (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : (a →ₜ b ; m)[a] = b := by
929-  rw [update_def, getElem_def, get_def]
930-  dsimp only -- reduces `{ inner := ... }.inner` so that we get a subterm that looks like `a == a`
931-  rw [BEq.rfl, cond_true]
932-
933---  On the other hand, if we update a map `m` at a key `a₁`

1020---  ### Notation for Concrete Maps
1021-
1022---  Wouldn't it be nice if we could use a more natural
1023---  notation for concrete maps like
1024---  `{ "bar" ↦ true, "foo" ↦ true }`? To accomplish this we
1025---  define a simple structure that consists of a key and a
1026---  value along with `↦` notation for it.
1027-
1028-/--
1029-A key-value pair with `↦` syntax.
1030--/
1031-@[ext]
1032-structure KVPair (K : Type) (V : Type) where
1033-  key : K
1034-  value : V
1035-
1036-namespace KVPair
1037-scoped notation k " ↦ " v => KVPair.mk k v
1038-end KVPair
1039-
1040-open scoped KVPair
1041-
1042---  Next, we declare `Insert` and `Singleton` instances —
1043---  the standard-library typeclasses behind the
1044---  `{x, y, ...}` and `{x}` collection-literal notation that
1045---  `List`, `Finset`, and other stdlib containers already
1046---  support — so that `TotalMap` can use it too.
1047-
1048-namespace TotalMap
1049-
1050-instance {α β : Type} [BEq α] : Insert (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
1051-  insert kv m := kv.key →ₜ kv.value ; m
1052-
1053-instance {α β : Type} [BEq α] [Inhabited β] : Singleton (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
1054-  singleton kv := insert kv ∅
1055-
1056-instance {α β : Type} [BEq α] [Inhabited β] : LawfulSingleton (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
1057-  insert_empty_eq _ := rfl
1058-
1059-end TotalMap

1061---  Here are a couple of examples using the new notation:
1062-
1063-example : ({ "bar" ↦ true, "foo" ↦ true }) = "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true ; ∅ := rfl
1064-
1065-example : ({ "foo" ↦ true } : TotalMap String Bool)["foo"] = true := rfl
1066-
1067-example : ({ 1 ↦ 2, 1 ↦ 3 } : TotalMap Nat Nat)[1] = 2 := rfl

1070---  map is that Lean doesn't know what type of collection
1071---  `{ "foo" ↦ true }` is without type hints, as we can see
1072---  with `#check`:
1073-
1074-#check { "foo" ↦ true }
1075-
1076---  Output:
1077---    {"foo" ↦ true} : ?m.4
1078-
1079---  The type shows a `?m.4`, which indicates that Lean can't
1080---  infer the type. A type which can't be inferred doesn't
1081---  have any type classes like `MyGetElem`, so typeclass
1082---  resolution gets stuck in the following example:

1084-sf_expect_failure_in
1085-  example : ({ "foo" ↦ true })["foo"] = true := by rfl

1087---  ### Partial Maps
1088-
1089---  Lastly, we define *partial maps* on top of total maps. A
1090---  partial map with elements of type `β` is simply a total
1091---  map with elements of type `Option β`, whose default
1092---  element is `none`.
1093-
1094-structure PartialMap (α : Type) (β : Type) where
1095-  /-- The underlying total map. Lean always generates a public projection for a structure
1096-    field, so `inner` is technically accessible, but it isn't part of the intended interface:
1097-    use `PartialMap.toTotal` instead, so there's exactly one sanctioned way to get at it. -/
1098-  inner : TotalMap α (Option β)
1099-
1100-/- Note that this definition of `EmptyCollection` doesn't need `β` to have an `Inhabited`
1101-  instance like `TotalMap` did. This is because `Option β` has its own `Inhabited` instance:
1102-  `none` is a value of every `Option` type. -/
1103-instance {α β : Type} : EmptyCollection (PartialMap α β) where
1104-  emptyCollection := { inner := ∅ }
1105-
1106-namespace PartialMap
1107-
1108-def toTotal {α β : Type} (m : PartialMap α β) : TotalMap α (Option β) := m.inner
1109-
1110-/-- This exposes implementation-specific details of `PartialMap`.
1111-  Avoid using this outside the `PartialMap` namespace. -/
1112-theorem toTotal_def {α β : Type} (m : PartialMap α β) : m.toTotal = m.inner := by rfl
1113-
1114-instance {α β : Type} : MyGetElem (PartialMap α β) α (Option β) where
1115-  getElem m a := m.toTotal[a]
1116-
1117-theorem getElem_def {α β : Type} (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) : m[a] = m.toTotal[a] := rfl
1118-
1119-def emptyNatMap : PartialMap Nat Nat where
1120-  inner := ∅
1121-
1122-example : emptyNatMap[1] = default := by rfl
1123-
1124-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap[n] = none := by
1125-  rw [getElem_def, toTotal_def, emptyNatMap]
1126-  dsimp only
1127-  rw [TotalMap.getElem_def, TotalMap.get_def, TotalMap.empty_def, Option.default_eq_none]
1128-
1129-@[simp]
1130-theorem toTotal_eq_getElem {α β : Type} (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) :
1131-    m.toTotal[a] = m[a] := rfl

1133---  We previously defined `TotalMap.get` so that users can
1134---  retrieve elements from a `TotalMap` in a manner
1135---  independent of its actual implementation, which is a
1136---  function stored in `TotalMap.inner`. We follow a similar
1137---  principle with `PartialMap`s, and define
1138---  `PartialMap.toTotal` to be the public API counterpart to
1139---  `PartialMap.inner`.
1140---
1141---  We again want the public API to use the `m[a]` notation
1142---  instead of `m.toTotal[a]`, so we provide the reverse
1143---  direction of `getElem_def` as a `simp` lemma to specify
1144---  that the `simp` normal form is `m[a]`.
1145---
1146---  Updating a partial map at a key means storing a `some`
1147---  value there. To update, we create a new partial map from
1148---  `a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal` by wrapping it in angle
1149---  brackets, i.e. using the anonymous constructor syntax.
1150---  This is equivalent to writing
1151---  `{ inner := a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal }`. We also
1152---  introduce a similar notation for it as for total maps.
1153-
1154-def update {α β : Type} [BEq α] (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : PartialMap α β :=
1155-  ⟨a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal⟩
1156-
1157-notation a:55 " →ₚ " b:55 " ; " m:55 => PartialMap.update m a b
1158-
1159-notation a:55 " →ₚ " b:55 => PartialMap.update ∅ a b
1160-
1161-def examplePmap : PartialMap String Bool := "Church" →ₚ true ; "Turing" →ₚ false

1167-theorem toTotal_empty {α β : Type} : (∅ : PartialMap α β).toTotal = (∅ : TotalMap α (Option β)) := rfl

1208-    (a →ₚ b ; m)[a] = some b := by

1248-  insert kv m := kv.key →ₚ kv.value ; m

1258---  One last thing: for partial maps, it's convenient to
1259---  introduce a notion of map inclusion, stating that all
1260---  the entries in one map are also present in another. Lean
1261---  already has notation for this — `m₁ ⊆ m₂` — which we get
1262---  by supplying a `HasSubset` instance.
1263-
1264-def Subset {α β : Type} (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) : Prop :=
1265-  ∀ {a : α} {b : β}, m₁[a] = some b → m₂[a] = some b
1266-
1267-instance {α β : Type} : HasSubset (PartialMap α β) where
1268-  Subset := PartialMap.Subset
1269-
1270-theorem subset_def {α β : Type} (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) :
1271-    m₁ ⊆ m₂ ↔ (∀ {a : α} {b : β}, m₁[a] = some b → m₂[a] = some b) := .rfl
1272-
1273---  We can then show that map update preserves map
1274---  inclusion, that is:
1275-
1276-theorem update_subset {α β : Type} [BEq α] [LawfulBEq α] (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β)
1277-    (h : m₁ ⊆ m₂) : (a →ₚ b ; m₁) ⊆ (a →ₚ b ; m₂) := by
1278-  rw [subset_def] at h ⊢
1279-  intro a' b' hb
1280-  by_cases ha : a = a'
1281-  · subst ha
1282-    rw [update_eq] at hb ⊢
1283-    exact hb
1284-  · rw [update_neq ha] at hb ⊢
1285-    exact h hb
1286-
1287-end PartialMap

1291---  Lambda Calculus, which we will see in *Type Systems*,

1295---  ## Reflection
1296-
1297-namespace Reflection
1298-
1299---  In this section, we will make use of some definitions
1300---  and theorems about natural numbers that we discussed and
1301---  proved in previous chapters; copy your solutions to
1302---  those problems here:
1303-
1304-namespace Nat
1305-
1306-def even (n : Nat) :=
1307-  match n with
1308-  | 0     => true
1309-  | 1     => false
1310-  | n + 2 => even n
1311-
1312-theorem even_zero : even 0 = true := by rfl
1313-
1314-theorem even_succ (n : Nat) :
1315-    even (n + 1) = !(even n) := by
1316-  sorry
1317-
1318-def double (n : Nat) : Nat :=
1319-  match n with
1320-  | 0    => 0
1321-  | n' + 1 => double n' + 2
1322-
1323-theorem double_zero : double 0 = 0 := by rfl
1324-
1325-theorem double_succ (n : Nat) : double (n + 1) = double n + 2 := by rfl
1326-
1327-def Even x := ∃ n : Nat, x = Nat.double n
1328-
1329---  We've seen two different ways of expressing logical
1330---  claims in Lean: with booleans (of type `Bool`), and with
1331---  propositions (of type `Prop`).
1332---
1333---  Here are the key differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
1334-
1335---  |                       | `Bool` | `Prop` |
1336---  | --------------------- | ------ | ------ |
1337---  | decidable?            |  yes   |   no   |
1338---  | useable with `match`? |  yes   |   no   |
1339---  | works with `rewrite`? |   no   |   yes  |
1340-
1341---  The crucial difference between the two worlds is
1342---  decidability. Every (closed) Lean expression of type
1343---  `Bool` can be simplified in a finite number of steps to
1344---  either `true` or `false` — i.e., there is a terminating
1345---  mechanical procedure for deciding whether or not it is
1346---  true.
1347---
1348---  This means that, for example, the type `Nat → Bool` is
1349---  inhabited only by functions that, given a `Nat`, always
1350---  yield either `true` or `false` in finite time; and this,
1351---  in turn, means (by a standard computability argument)
1352---  that there is no function in `Nat → Bool` that checks
1353---  whether a given number is the code of a terminating
1354---  Turing machine.
1355---
1356---  By contrast, the type `Prop` includes both decidable and
1357---  undecidable mathematical propositions; in particular,
1358---  the type `Nat → Prop` does contain functions
1359---  representing properties like "the nth Turing machine
1360---  halts." The second row in the table follows directly
1361---  from this essential difference. To evaluate a pattern
1362---  match (or conditional) on a boolean, we need to know
1363---  whether the scrutinee evaluates to `true` or `false`;
1364---  this only works for `Bool`, not `Prop`.
1365---
1366---  The third row highlights an important practical
1367---  difference: equality functions like `Nat.beq` that
1368---  return a boolean cannot be used directly to justify
1369---  rewriting with the rewrite tactic; propositional
1370---  equality is required for this. Since `Prop` includes
1371---  both decidable and undecidable properties, we have two
1372---  options when we want to formalize a property that
1373---  happens to be decidable: we can express it either as a
1374---  boolean computation or as a function into Prop.
1375---
1376---  As an example, we can write
1377-
1378-example : even 42 := rfl
1379-
1380---  or that there exists some `k` such that `42 = double k`.
1381-
1382-example : Even 42 := by exists 21
1383-
1384---  Of course, it would be deeply strange if these two
1385---  characterizations of evenness did not describe the same
1386---  set of natural numbers!
1387---
1388---  Fortunately, they do! To prove this, we first need two
1389---  helper lemmas.
1390-
1391-theorem even_double (k : Nat) : even (double k) = true := by
1392-  induction k with
1393-  | zero =>
1394-    rw [double_zero, even_zero]
1395-  | succ n ih =>
1396-    rw [double_succ, even_succ, even_succ, Bool.not_not]
1397-    exact ih
1398-
1399---  ### Exercise (3 stars): even_double_exists ⭐⭐⭐
1400-
1401-theorem even_double_exists (n : Nat) :
1402-    ∃ (k : Nat), n = bif even n then double k else double k + 1 := by
1403-  sorry
1404-
1405---  Now the main theorem:
1406-
1407-theorem even_iff_Even {n : Nat} : even n = true ↔ Even n where
1408-  mp h := by
1409-    have ⟨k, hk⟩ := even_double_exists n
1410-    rw [h, cond_true] at hk
1411-    subst hk
1412-    exists k
1413-  mpr h := by
1414-    obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := h
1415-    subst hk
1416-    exact even_double k
1417-
1418-end Nat
1419-
1420---  In view of this theorem, we can say that the boolean
1421---  computation `Nat.even n` is reflected in the truth of
1422---  the proposition `∃ (k : Nat), n = Nat.double k`.
1423---
1424---  Similarly, to state that two numbers n and m are equal,
1425---  we can say either
1426---
1427---  - that `n == m` returns `true`, or
1428---  - that `n = m`
1429---
1430---  Again, these two notions are equivalent:
1431-
1432-example (n₁ n₂ : Nat) : n₁ == n₂ ↔ n₁ = n₂ := beq_iff_eq
1433-
1434---  So what should we do in situations where some claim
1435---  could be formalized as either a proposition or a boolean
1436---  computation? Which should we choose?
1437---
1438---  In general, both can be useful. Which we choose has to
1439---  do with the *computational* nature of Lean's core
1440---  language, which is designed so that every function it
1441---  expresses is total, and by default computable unless we
1442---  explicit indicate otherwise. As an example, consider
1443---  trying to write a function `α → α → Bool` checking for
1444---  equality on an arbitrary type:
1445-
1446---  Lean will complain here that it cannot find an instance
1447---  of `Decidable`. This typeclass
1448-
1449-sf_recall
1450-  class inductive Decidable (p : Prop) where
1451-    /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `¬ p` -/
1452-    | isFalse (h : Not p) : Decidable p
1453-    /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `p` -/
1454-    | isTrue (h : p) : Decidable p
1455-
1456---  is the way that we express in Lean that a given
1457---  proposition is decidable. This is the generalization of
1458---  our observation that `Nat.even_iff_Even` was reflecting
1459---  a proof between boolean and propositional equality. In
1460---  fact, we can use this theorem to directly construct a
1461---  `Decidable` instance.
1462-
1463-instance (n : Nat) : Decidable (Nat.Even n) :=
1464-  decidable_of_decidable_of_iff Nat.even_iff_Even
1465-
1466---  Now we are able to complete such proofs by computation
1467---  using the `decide` tactic:
1468-
1469-example : Nat.Even 2 := by decide
1470-example : Nat.Even 4 := by decide
1471-example : Nat.Even 6 := by decide
1472-example : Nat.Even 100 := by decide
1473-example : ¬ Nat.Even 101 := by decide
1474-example : ∀ n < 10, Nat.Even (2 * n) := by decide
1475-example : ∀ n < 10, Nat.Even (2 * n) ∧ ¬ Nat.Even (2 * n + 1) := by decide
1476-
1477---  In general, Lean will try to use typeclass synthesis
1478---  with `Decidable` in order to determine when it is
1479---  appropriate to use `Prop` and `Bool` interchangeably.
1480---  For instance, while our example `eq` failed above while
1481---  trying to use propositional equality `=` in the
1482---  condition of an `if` statement, we are allowed to write
1483-
1484-def nat_eq (m n : Nat) : Bool := if m = n then true else false
1485-
1486---  Why is this allowed? It is precisely because equality of
1487---  natural numbers is decidable, and Lean makes use of this
1488---  fact. If we print this definition with notation unset,
1489---  we would find that it is using `instDecidableEqNat`:

1491-set_option pp.all true in
1492-#print nat_eq
1493-
1494---  which proves that this equality is decidable.
1495---
1496---  This is only half the story however: while Lean's core
1497---  theory enables this computation, Lean is also often used
1498---  in applications where we don't care about computability,
1499---  such as pure mathematics. In particular, it is possible
1500---  to write a function for arbitrary equality:

1502-sf_experiment

4-
5-namespace SFLCompat.Experiment
6-
7-open Lean Elab Command
8-
9-meta section
10-
11--- Copied from `SubVerso.Compat` to avoid making generated projects depend on verso.
12--- We want to have info state and messages available right after the elaboration,
13--- so we need to disable `Elab.async` which would let diagnostics produced asynchronously
14--- through spanshot tasks.
15-private def commandWithoutAsync (act : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
16-  match (← get).scopes with
17-  | [] => act
18-  | h :: t =>
19-    let mut orig : Option Bool := none
20-    try
21-      orig := h.opts.get? `Elab.async
22-      modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := h.opts.setBool `Elab.async false } :: t }
23-      act
24-    finally
25-      if let h :: t := (← get).scopes then
26-        let opts := orig.map (h.opts.setBool `Elab.async) |>.getD (h.opts.erase `Elab.async)
27-        modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := opts } :: t }
28-
29-private def withRestoringState (keepMsgs : Bool) (m : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
30-  let savedState ← get
31-  try
32-    m
33-  finally
34-    let state ← get
35-    set { savedState with
36-      -- Preserve the info tree
37-      infoState := state.infoState
38-      messages := if keepMsgs then state.messages else savedState.messages }
39-
40-namespace IndentedCommands
41-
42-/-! # Block Commands Parser
43-  Parse an indented command block. Commands are separated by new lines.
44-  Since we want to capture parsing errors in `sf_expect_failure_in`,
45-  we can't use Lean command parser directly in our command's syntax,
46-  because any parsing error occurred would fail `sf_expect_failure_in` itself.
47-  One possible solution is to first parse the whole indented body as raw syntax,
48-  and then run Lean's command parser followed by command elaboration.
49--/
50-
51-open Parser
52-
53-private def rawLineEndFn : ParserFn :=
54-  eoiFn <|> satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break"
55-
56-/-- Consumes everything until the next newline and then consumes the newline itself. -/
57-private def rawLineFn : ParserFn :=
58-  takeUntilFn (· == '\n') >> rawLineEndFn
59-
60-/- For each line after the first body line, consumes leading whitespaces.
61-  If it's blank, consumes the newline; otherwise consumes the line
62-  requiring the indentation.
63--/
64-private def rawIndentedLineFn : ParserFn := atomicFn <|
65-  takeWhileFn (· == ' ') >>
66-  (satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break" <|>
67-    (checkColGeFn "indented command sequence" >> rawLineFn))
68-
69-private def rawCommandBlockFn : ParserFn :=
70-  rawFn (rawLineFn >> manyFn rawIndentedLineFn) (trailingWs := true)
71-
72-private def rawCommandBlock : Parser := { fn := rawCommandBlockFn }
73-
74-@[combinator_parenthesizer rawCommandBlock]
75-private def rawCommandBlock.parenthesizer := PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer.visitToken
76-
77-@[combinator_formatter rawCommandBlock]
78-private def rawCommandBlock.formatter := PrettyPrinter.Formatter.visitAtom Name.anonymous
79-
80-private partial def runRawCmdsAux
81-    (ictx : InputContext) (pstate : ModuleParserState) : CommandElabM Unit := do
82-  let state ← get
83-  let scope := state.scopes.head!
84-  let pctx :=  {
85-      env := state.env
86-      options := scope.opts
87-      currNamespace := scope.currNamespace
88-      openDecls := scope.openDecls : ParserModuleContext
89-    }
90-  let (cmd, pstate, messages) := parseCommand ictx pctx pstate state.messages
91-  modify fun state => { state with messages }
92-  unless cmd.isOfKind ``Command.eoi do
93-    elabCommand cmd
94-    runLinters cmd
95-    unless isTerminalCommand cmd do
96-      runRawCmdsAux ictx pstate
97-
98-/- Recovers the source info and elaborates the commands -/
99-private def runRawCmds (body : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
100-  let some source := body.getSubstring? (withLeading := false) (withTrailing := false)
101-    | throwErrorAt body "command sequence has no source range"
102-  let fileName ← getFileName
103-  let fileMap ← getFileMap
104-  -- Recall that `rawIndentedLineFn` may consume whitespaces after the newline.
105-  -- Here we move the ending back to the last non-whitespace character to produce
106-  -- correctly positioned diagnostics.
107-  let stopPos := source.trimRight.stopPos
108-  if h : stopPos ≤ fileMap.source.rawEndPos then
109-    let ictx := InputContext.mk fileMap.source fileName
110-      (fileMap := fileMap) (endPos := stopPos) (endPos_valid := h)
111-    runRawCmdsAux ictx { pos := source.startPos, recovering := false, hasLeading := false }
112-  else
113-    throwErrorAt body "invalid command-sequence source range"
114-
115-end IndentedCommands
116-
117-end
118-
119-public meta section
120-
121-open Parser IndentedCommands
122-
123-/--
124-Elaborates the enclosed commands and reports their diagnostics,
125-but discards their effects afterwards.
126-
127-Example:
128-```lean
129-sf_experiment
130-  def hidden : Nat := 1
131-  #check hidden
132--- `hidden` is not available here.
133-```
134--/
135-def experimentTk := leading_parser
136-  "sf_experiment"
137-
138-@[command_parser] def experimentCmd := leading_parser
139-  experimentTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
140-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
141-
142-/--
143-Succeeds only if the enclosed commands fail.
144-Diagnostics from the expected failure are suppressed.
145-
146-Example:
147-```lean
148-sf_expect_failure_in
149-  example : 1 = 2 := rfl
150-```
151--/
152-def expectFailureTk := leading_parser
153-  "sf_expect_failure_in"
154-
155-/-
156-  Like `sf_expect_failure_in` but reports the diagnostics.
157--/
158-def expectFailureInfoTk := leading_parser
159-  "sf_expect_failure_in?"
160-
161-@[command_parser] def expectFailureCmd := leading_parser
162-  expectFailureTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
163-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
164-
165-@[command_parser] def expectFailureInfoCmd := leading_parser
166-  expectFailureInfoTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
167-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
168-
169-@[command_elab experimentCmd]
170-def elabExperimentCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
171-  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
172-  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState true do
173-    runRawCmds body
174-
175-@[command_elab expectFailureCmd, command_elab expectFailureInfoCmd]
176-def elabExpectFailureCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
177-  let keepMsgs := stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureInfoCmd
178-  unless keepMsgs || stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureCmd do
179-    throwUnsupportedSyntax
180-  let tk := stx[0]
181-  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
182-  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState keepMsgs do
183-    withRef tk <| failIfSucceeds <| runRawCmds body
184-
185-end
186-

1-module
2-
3--- For testing cases in this file
4-meta import all Init.Prelude
5-public meta import SFLCompat.Recall.Common
6-
7-/-!
8-# Recall, checked by elaboration
9-
10-`sf_recall` lets a chapter restate a definition from earlier in the
11-development while the build checks that the restatement means the same
12-thing. The restated declaration is elaborated for real, inside a hidden
13-namespace, and compared with the original up to definitional equality; the
14-temporary declaration is then rolled back.
15-
16-Two forms:
17-
18-```
19-sf_recall
20-  def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat := f <| f n
21-
22-sf_recall statement twice_id : twice id 3 = 3
23-```
24-
25-What is compared:
26-
27-* types, always;
28-* a `def`'s value, safety, and abbreviation status;
29-* an inductive's constructors, one by one (names, parameter and index
30-  counts, and each constructor's type);
31-* a structure's fields, field defaults, and type-class registration;
32-* a theorem's statement, never its proof.
33-
34-So a recalled definition may be reformatted or rephrased into something
35-definitionally equal, and a theorem may be reproved differently or, with
36-the `statement` form, restated without any proof. The command is global and
37-available wherever this module is imported.
38--/
39-
40-
41-namespace SFLCompat.Recall.Check
42-
43-open Lean Elab Command Meta
44-
45-meta section
46-
47-structure DeclId where
48-  /-- This could be a private name. -/
49-  actual : Name
50-  display : Name
51-
52-def DeclId.ofActual (actual : Name) : DeclId :=
53-  { actual, display := privateToUserName actual }
54-
55-/-- Look up the actual name in temp elaboration namespace -/
56-def tempDeclId (userName : Name) : CommandElabM DeclId := do
57-  let env ← getEnv
58-  let privateName := mkPrivateName env userName
59-  let actual ←
60-    if env.contains privateName then pure privateName
61-    else if env.contains userName then pure userName
62-    else throwError "the re-elaborated declaration '{userName}' was not found"
63-  return .ofActual actual
64-
65-def renameBackName (chk orig n : Name) : Name :=
66-  if chk.isPrefixOf n then n.replacePrefix chk orig
67-  else
68-    let chk := privateToUserName chk
69-    if chk.isPrefixOf n then n.replacePrefix chk orig else n
70-
71-/--
72-Replaces the name prefix `chk` with `orig` in every constant that `e`
73-mentions: `chk` itself becomes `orig`, and a longer name such as a hidden
74-constructor `chk.mk` becomes `orig.mk`. Constructor types mention the
75-hidden inductive type's name in argument and resulting positions, so this
76-rewrite is what makes a re-elaborated declaration comparable with the
77-original.
78--/
79-def renameBack (chk orig : DeclId) (e : Expr) : Expr :=
80-  e.replace fun
81-    | .const n us =>
82-      let n' := renameBackName chk.actual orig.actual n
83-      if n == n' then none else some (.const n' us)
84-    | _ => none
85-
86-/--
87-Applies `renameBack` to the expressions recorded in an info tree. The info
88-recorded while elaborating the hidden copy mentions the hidden constants,
89-so hovers over a recalled declaration would otherwise display the hidden
90-names; rewriting before the trees are stored makes them display the
91-originals, which also exist after the hidden copy is rolled back.
92--/
93-partial def renameBackInfoTree (chk orig : DeclId) (t : InfoTree) : InfoTree :=
94-  match t with
95-  | .context (.parentDeclCtx n) t' =>
96-    .context (.parentDeclCtx (renameBackName chk.actual orig.actual n))
97-      (renameBackInfoTree chk orig t')
98-  | .context ctx t' => .context ctx (renameBackInfoTree chk orig t')
99-  | .node i children =>
100-    let i := match i with
101-      | .ofTermInfo ti => .ofTermInfo (reTerm ti)
102-      | .ofDelabTermInfo dti => .ofDelabTermInfo { dti with toTermInfo := reTerm dti.toTermInfo }
103-      | other => other
104-    .node i (children.map (renameBackInfoTree chk orig))
105-  | .hole m => .hole m
106-where
107-  reTerm (ti : TermInfo) : TermInfo :=
108-    { ti with
109-      expr := renameBack chk orig ti.expr
110-      expectedType? := ti.expectedType?.map (renameBack chk orig) }
111-
112-/-- A specialization of universe parameters to a declaration.
113-  It stores level parameters of a `ConstantInfo` and mvars created from these parameters.
114--/
115-abbrev Specialization := List Name × List Level
116-
117-def renameBackS (specialization? : Option Specialization)
118-    (chk orig : DeclId) (e : Expr) : Expr :=
119-  match specialization? with
120-  | none => renameBack chk orig e
121-  | some (_params, levels) =>
122-    e.replace fun
123-      | .const n _ =>
124-        let n' := renameBackName chk.actual orig.actual n
125-        if n == n' then none else some <| .const n' levels
126-      | _ => none
127-
128-def levelsFor (specialization : Specialization) (info : ConstantInfo) :
129-    TermElabM (List Level) :=
130-  let (params, levels) := specialization
131-  info.levelParams.mapM fun param =>
132-    match params.findIdx? (· == param) with
133-    | some index => pure levels[index]!
134-    | none => throwError
135-      "universe parameter '{param}' of '{info.name}' is not a parameter of the recalled declaration"
136-
137-/--
138-Checks that the types of the original constant `x` and its re-elaborated
139-counterpart `chk` agree, definitionally. The restated type is first
140-rewritten by `renameBack renChk renOrig`; the defaults compare a
141-declaration against its own hidden copy, and the constructor check
142-overrides them with the enclosing inductive types, whose names the
143-constructor types mention. The restatement's universe parameters are
144-instantiated with the original's.
145--/
146-def checkTypesMatch (x chk : DeclId) (ref : Syntax)
147-    (specialization? : Option Specialization)
148-    (renChk : DeclId := chk) (renOrig : DeclId := x) (hint : MessageData := .nil) :
149-    TermElabM Unit := do
150-  let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
151-  let chkInfo ← getConstInfo chk.actual
152-  if specialization?.isNone then
153-    -- no specialization, do strict check first
154-    unless origInfo.levelParams.length == chkInfo.levelParams.length do
155-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"universe parameters of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)
156-  let origType ← match specialization? with
157-    | none => pure origInfo.type
158-    | some s => origInfo.instantiateTypeLevelParams <$> levelsFor s origInfo
159-  let chkType := match specialization? with
160-    | none => (renameBackS specialization? renChk renOrig chkInfo.type).instantiateLevelParams
161-        chkInfo.levelParams (origInfo.levelParams.map .param)
162-    | some _ => renameBackS specialization? renChk renOrig chkInfo.type
163-  unless ← isDefEq chkType origType do
164-    throwErrorAt ref
165-      (m!"the statement of '{x.display}' does not match.\n\
166-          Original:{indentD origInfo.type}\nRestated:{indentD chkType}" ++ hint)
167-
168-/--
169-All constructor syntax nodes of a command, in source order: an inductive
170-type's `| name : ...` alternatives and a structure's `name ::` header.
171--/
172-partial def ctorStxs (stx : Syntax) : Array Syntax :=
173-  let inner := stx.getArgs.flatMap ctorStxs
174-  if stx.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.ctor
175-      || stx.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.structCtor then
176-    #[stx] ++ inner
177-  else inner
178-
179-/-- Does the syntax contain a doc comment? -/
180-def hasDocComment (stx : Syntax) : Bool :=
181-  (stx.find? (·.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.docComment)).isSome
182-
183-/--
184-Suggestions localized to a mismatched constructor, returned as a pair of
185-hints for name errors and for type errors. An inductive type's `| name : ...` alternative is replaced
186-with the original constructor's own source. A structure's `name ::` header
187-can carry a name fix but not a field fix, so its type errors keep `outer`,
188-the suggestion that replaces the whole restatement. A constructor without
189-syntax also falls back to `outer`.
190--/
191-def ctorHints (ctorRef : Syntax) (origCtor origShort : Name) (outer : MessageData) :
192-    TermElabM (MessageData × MessageData) := do
193-  try
194-    if ctorRef.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.ctor then
195-      let origSrc := dedent (← sourceOf origCtor)
196-      -- A restatement without a doc comment gets a suggestion without one;
197-      -- the meaning check does not compare documentation.
198-      let origSrc := if hasDocComment ctorRef then origSrc
199-        else stripLeadingComments origSrc
200-      let restatedSrc ← sourceOfSyntax ctorRef
201-      let h ← replaceWithOriginalHint ctorRef origSrc restatedSrc
202-      return (h, h)
203-    if ctorRef.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.structCtor then
204-      let restatedSrc ← sourceOfSyntax ctorRef
205-      let h ← replaceWithOriginalHint ctorRef s!"{origShort} ::" restatedSrc
206-      return (h, outer)
207-    return (outer, outer)
208-  catch _ => return (outer, outer)
209-
210-/--
211-Checks a re-elaborated declaration against the original, definitionally.
212-Errors point at `ref`, the restated command, except for constructor
213-mismatches, which point at the offending constructor within it.
214--/
215-def checkMatchCore (x chk : DeclId) (ref : Syntax)
216-    (specialization? : Option (List Name × List Level))
217-    (hint : MessageData := .nil) : TermElabM Unit := do
218-  checkTypesMatch x chk ref specialization? (hint := hint)
219-  let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
220-  let chkInfo ← getConstInfo chk.actual
221-  match origInfo, chkInfo with
222-  | .defnInfo orig, .defnInfo restated =>
223-    let origVal ← match specialization? with
224-      | none => pure orig.value
225-      | some s => origInfo.instantiateValueLevelParams! <$> levelsFor s origInfo
226-    let chkVal := match specialization? with
227-      | none => (renameBackS specialization? chk x restated.value).instantiateLevelParams
228-          restated.levelParams (orig.levelParams.map .param)
229-      | some _ => renameBackS specialization? chk x restated.value
230-    unless ← isDefEq chkVal origVal do
231-      throwErrorAt ref
232-        (m!"the value of '{x.display}' does not match.\n\
233-            Original:{indentD orig.value}\nRestated:{indentD chkVal}" ++ hint)
234-  | .inductInfo orig, .inductInfo restated =>
235-    unless orig.numParams == restated.numParams && orig.numIndices == restated.numIndices do
236-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"parameters or indices of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)
237-    unless orig.ctors.length == restated.ctors.length do
238-      throwErrorAt ref
239-        (m!"'{x.display}' has {orig.ctors.length} constructors, \
240-            the restatement has {restated.ctors.length}" ++ hint)
241-    -- A `structure` that writes no `name ::` header has a constructor
242-    -- without syntax; the whole command remains the fallback position.
243-    let ctorRefs := ctorStxs ref
244-    let mut i := 0
245-    for origCtorActual in orig.ctors, chkCtorActual in restated.ctors do
246-      let origCtor := DeclId.ofActual origCtorActual
247-      let chkCtor := DeclId.ofActual chkCtorActual
248-      let ctorRef := ctorRefs[i]?.getD ref

250-      let (nameHint, typeHint) ← ctorHints ctorRef origCtor.actual origShort hint

252-        chkCtor.actual.replacePrefix chk.actual x.actual

273-      unless getOutParamPositions? env x.actual == getOutParamPositions? env chk.actual
274-          && getOutLevelParamPositions? env x.actual == getOutLevelParamPositions? env chk.actual do
275-        throwErrorAt ref (m!"the type-class metadata of '{x.display}' does not match" ++ hint)
276-    | some _, none =>
277-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"'{x.display}' is a structure, but the restatement is not" ++ hint)
278-    | none, some _ =>
279-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"'{x.display}' is not a structure, but the restatement is one" ++ hint)

291-/--
292-Run `checkpointDefEq` in `TermElabM`.
293-Note: this is only for universe level constraints solving in `isDefEq` and
294-has nothing to do with the elaborator.
295--/
296-def checkpointDefEq' (action : TermElabM Bool) : TermElabM Bool :=
297-  controlAt MetaM fun runInBase =>
298-    checkpointDefEq (mayPostpone := false) (runInBase action)
299-
300-def checkMatch (x chk : DeclId) (ref : Syntax)
301-    (strictUniverse : Bool) (hint : MessageData := .nil) : TermElabM Unit := do
302-  let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
303-  let chkInfo ← getConstInfo chk.actual
304-  if origInfo.levelParams.length == chkInfo.levelParams.length then
305-    -- if the definition being to check has exactly the same number of the parameters,
306-    -- treat it as no specialization in checking
307-    checkMatchCore x chk ref none hint
308-  else if !strictUniverse && !origInfo.levelParams.isEmpty && chkInfo.levelParams.isEmpty then
309-    -- if all parameters have been specified (monomorphic), do check with specialization
310-    let succeeded ← checkpointDefEq' do
311-      let levels ← mkFreshLevelMVarsFor origInfo
312-      checkMatchCore x chk ref (some (origInfo.levelParams, levels)) hint
313-      pure true
314-    unless succeeded do
315-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"the statement of '{x.display}' does not match" ++ hint)
316-  else
317-    throwErrorAt ref (m!"universe parameters of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)

320-/--
321-`sf_recall` restates a definition from earlier in the development and checks
322-that the restatement means the same thing. `sf_recall statement x : T` checks
323-that `T` matches the statement of the theorem `x`.
324--/
325-syntax (name := recallChk) "sf_recall " command : command
326-
327-@[inherit_doc recallChk]
328-syntax (name := recallChkStrict) "sf_recall" " +" noWs &"strictUniverse" ppSpace command : command
329-
330-@[inherit_doc recallChk]
331-syntax (name := recallChkStmt) "sf_recall " &"statement " ident " : " term : command
332-
333-
334-def elabRecallCommand (cmd : Syntax) (strictUniverse : Bool) : CommandElabM Unit := do
335-  let decl ← declaredName cmd
336-  let xActual ← liftCoreM <| withoutExporting <|
337-    realizeGlobalConstNoOverloadWithInfo decl.ident
338-  let x := DeclId.ofActual xActual
339-  -- The restatement elaborates unchanged inside a fresh hidden namespace:
340-  -- self-references (an inductive's own name in its constructor types, in
341-  -- resulting-type position included) resolve to the hidden copy, and
342-  -- every other name resolves as it would at the recall site. The
343-  -- namespace comes from the name generator: `_uniq` names cannot be
344-  -- written in source, so it is collision-free. `mkFreshId` itself returns
345-  -- a name whose last component is a `Name.num`, not a `Name.str`; appended
346-  -- onto `currNamespace` as-is, that trailing numeral breaks
347-  -- `Lean.ResolveName.resolveUsingNamespace`, which only walks up an
348-  -- enclosing-namespace chain built of `Name.str` components. The symptom
349-  -- is silent: an unqualified name inside the restatement that should
350-  -- resolve through the enclosing namespace instead falls through to a
351-  -- same-named root declaration, if one exists (e.g. `Nat` resolving to
352-  -- `_root_.Nat` instead of the local shadowing type). Converting the
353-  -- fresh id to a single `Name.str` component keeps it collision-free
354-  -- (its rendered form still can't be written in source) while keeping the
355-  -- namespace chain walkable, and `renameBack`/the constructor comparison
356-  -- only rely on structural prefix matching, which is unaffected.
357-  let ns := Name.mkStr1 (← liftCoreM (mkFreshId : CoreM Name)).toString
358-  -- Any mismatch gets a clickable fix: replace the restatement with the
359-  -- original's source text, indented like the restatement. The helpers
360-  -- for recovering and re-indenting source are shared with the
361-  -- byte-for-byte variant.
362-  -- A failed hint must not fail the check: not every constant has a
363-  -- declaration range or sources on the search path.
364-  let hint ←
365-    try
366-      let original := dedent (← sourceOf x.actual)
367-      let original := if hasDocComment cmd then original
368-        else stripLeadingComments original
369-      let restated ← sourceOfSyntax cmd
370-      liftCoreM <| replaceWithOriginalHint cmd original restated
371-    catch _ => pure .nil
372-  let envBefore ← getEnv
373-  try
374-    let chk ← withScope (fun sc => { sc with currNamespace := sc.currNamespace ++ ns }) do
375-      let saved ← getResetInfoTrees
376-      try
377-        elabCommand cmd
378-        -- this could be a private name
379-        let userName := (← getScope).currNamespace ++ decl.written
380-        let chk ← tempDeclId userName
381-        let inner ← getResetInfoTrees
382-        modifyInfoState fun s => { s with trees := saved ++ inner.map (renameBackInfoTree chk x) }
383-        return chk
384-      catch e =>
385-        let inner ← getResetInfoTrees
386-        modifyInfoState fun s => { s with trees := saved ++ inner }
387-        throw e
388-    runTermElabM fun _ => checkMatch x chk cmd strictUniverse (hint := hint)
389-  finally
390-    setEnv envBefore
391-
392-def elabRecallStatement (ident stmt : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
393-  let xActual ← liftCoreM <| withoutExporting <|
394-    realizeGlobalConstNoOverloadWithInfo ident
395-  let x := DeclId.ofActual xActual
396-  addConstInfo ident x.actual
397-  let region := mkNullNode #[ident, stmt]
398-  let restated ← sourceOfSyntax region
399-  runTermElabM fun _ => do
400-    -- The suggestion restates the original's type as the pretty-printer
401-    -- renders it. The statement cannot be carved out of the original's
402-    -- source, since finding its boundary would require parsing the
403-    -- source in the elaboration context of its declaration site.
404-    let hint ←
405-      try
406-        let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
407-        let printed ← ppExpr origInfo.type
408-        replaceWithOriginalHint region
409-          s!"{ident.getId} : {printed}" restated
410-      catch _ => pure .nil
411-    let t ← Term.elabType stmt
412-    Term.synthesizeSyntheticMVarsNoPostponing
413-    let t ← instantiateMVars (← Term.levelMVarToParam t)
414-    let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
415-    let stParams := (collectLevelParams {} t).params
416-    unless stParams.size == origInfo.levelParams.length do
417-      throwErrorAt stmt (m!"universe parameters of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)
418-    let t := t.instantiateLevelParams stParams.toList
419-      (origInfo.levelParams.map .param)
420-    unless ← isDefEq t origInfo.type do
421-      throwErrorAt stmt
422-        (m!"the restated statement of '{x.display}' does not match.\n\
423-            Original:{indentD origInfo.type}\nRestated:{indentD t}" ++ hint)
424-
425-
426-elab_rules : command
427-  | `(sf_recall $cmd:command) => elabRecallCommand cmd false
428-  | `(sf_recall +strictUniverse $cmd:command) => elabRecallCommand cmd true
429-  | `(sf_recall statement $ident:ident : $stmt:term) => elabRecallStatement ident stmt
430-
431-end

3-public meta import Lean.Elab.Command
4-
5-namespace SFLCompat.Recall
6-
7-open Lean Elab Command
8-public meta section
9-
10-/-- All `declId` nodes in a command, in source order. -/
11-partial def declIds (stx : Syntax) : Array Syntax :=
12-  let inner := stx.getArgs.flatMap declIds
13-  if stx.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.declId then #[stx] ++ inner else inner
14-
15-/-- The syntax and written name of the single declaration in a recall command. -/
16-structure DeclSyntax where
17-  ident : Syntax
18-  written : Name
19-
20-/--
21-The `declId` node of a declaration command, together with the name written
22-in it. A command that declares several names (a `mutual` block) or none (an
23-anonymous `instance`, an `example`) is rejected.
24--/
25-def declaredName (cmd : Syntax) : CommandElabM DeclSyntax := do
26-  let defined := declIds cmd
27-  match h : defined.size with
28-  | 0 => throwErrorAt cmd "the restated command does not declare a name"
29-  | 1 =>
30-    let declId := defined[0]
31-    return { ident := declId[0], written := declId[0].getId }
32-  | n + 2 =>
33-    for h : i in 0...(n + 1) do
34-      logErrorAt defined[i]
35-        "the restated command declares several names; recall one declaration at a time"
36-    throwErrorAt defined[n + 1]
37-      "the restated command declares several names; recall one declaration at a time"
38-
39-/--
40-Removes the block indentation of a declaration's source text. The first
41-line starts at the declaration's first token and has no indentation of its
42-own; each following line is stripped of the smallest indentation found
43-among the non-blank ones. Restatements of the same text at different block
44-depths dedent to identical strings, and every other difference survives
45-dedenting.
46--/
47-def dedent (s : String) : String :=
48-  match indentWidth s, s.splitOn "\n" with
49-  | some n, first :: rest =>
50-    "\n".intercalate (first :: rest.map (fun l => String.ofList (l.toList.drop n)))
51-  | _, _ => s
52-where
53-  /-- The smallest indentation among the non-blank continuation lines. -/
54-  indentWidth (s : String) : Option Nat :=
55-    s.splitOn "\n" |>.drop 1 |>.map (·.toList)
56-      |>.filter (fun l => !l.all (·.isWhitespace))
57-      |>.map (fun l => (l.takeWhile (· == ' ')).length)
58-      |>.min?
59-
60-/--
61-Indents the continuation lines of dedented source text by `n` spaces, so
62-that the text reads correctly at the block depth of a restatement.
63--/
64-def reindent (s : String) (n : Nat) : String :=
65-  match s.splitOn "\n" with
66-  | [] => s
67-  | first :: rest =>
68-    let pad := String.ofList (List.replicate n ' ')
69-    "\n".intercalate (first :: rest.map fun l =>
70-      if l.toList.all (·.isWhitespace) then l else pad ++ l)
71-
72-/--
73-Removes the comments from the front of dedented source text, together with
74-the whitespace around them, so that a suggestion offered for a restatement
75-that carries no comments does not introduce any. The text of a declaration
76-or of a constructor begins with its doc comment when it has one, possibly
77-accompanied by ordinary comments, and a leading block comment ends at its
78-depth-balanced closing delimiter, so a character scan recognizes the
79-leading run of comments exactly. A comment elsewhere in the text cannot be
80-recognized without lexing and is left in place.
81--/
82-def stripLeadingComments (s : String) : String := Id.run do
83-  let mut cs := s.toList.dropWhile (·.isWhitespace)
84-  repeat
85-    if cs.take 2 == ['/', '-'] then
86-      cs := cs.drop 2
87-      let mut depth := 1
88-      while depth > 0 do
89-        match cs with
90-        | [] => return s
91-        | '/' :: '-' :: rest => depth := depth + 1; cs := rest
92-        | '-' :: '/' :: rest => depth := depth - 1; cs := rest
93-        | _ :: rest => cs := rest
94-    else if cs.take 2 == ['-', '-'] then
95-      cs := cs.dropWhile (· != '\n')
96-    else
97-      break
98-    cs := cs.dropWhile (·.isWhitespace)
99-  return String.ofList cs
100-
101-/--
102-A clickable suggestion that replaces the restated text at `span` with
103-`original`, which must already be dedented. The original's indentation is
104-moved to match the restatement's: the restatement's own indentation width
105-when it has continuation lines, one step past the span's start column when
106-it does not.
107--/
108-def replaceWithOriginalHint [Monad m] [MonadFileMap m] [MonadLiftT CoreM m]
109-    (span : Syntax) (original restated : String) : m MessageData := do
110-  let fileMap ← getFileMap
111-  let k := match dedent.indentWidth restated, span.getRange? with
112-    | some k, _ => k
113-    | none, some r => (fileMap.toPosition r.start).column + 2
114-    | none, none => 2
115-  MessageData.hint m!"Replace the restatement with the original:"
116-    #[{ suggestion := .string (reindent original k), span? := some span }]
117-
118-/--
119-The source text of the declaration of `x`, from the file that declared it.
120-
121-The location comes from the declaration range that Lean records for every
122-constant. A declaration from the current file is read out of the file map;
123-one from an imported module is read from its source file, found on the
124-source search path. In a book build the whole project's sources are on that
125-path, so definitions can be recalled across chapters.
126--/
127-def sourceOf [Monad m] [MonadEnv m] [MonadError m] [MonadFileMap m]
128-    [MonadLiftT IO m] [MonadLiftT BaseIO m] (x : Name) : m String := do
129-  let some ranges ← findDeclarationRanges? x
130-    | throwError "no declaration range recorded for '{x}'"
131-  let env ← getEnv
132-  let text ←
133-    match env.getModuleIdxFor? x with
134-    | none => pure (← getFileMap)
135-    | some idx => do
136-      let modName := env.allImportedModuleNames[idx.toNat]!
137-      let sp ← getSrcSearchPath
138-      let some path ← sp.findModuleWithExt "lean" modName
139-        | throwError "source for module '{modName}' is not on the search path"
140-      pure (FileMap.ofString (← IO.FS.readFile path))
141-  return String.Pos.Raw.extract text.source
142-    (text.ofPosition ranges.range.pos) (text.ofPosition ranges.range.endPos)
143-
144-/-- The source text of a piece of syntax in the current file. -/
145-def sourceOfSyntax [Monad m] [MonadError m] [MonadFileMap m]
146-    (stx : Syntax) : m String := do
147-  let some r := stx.getRange?
148-    | throwErrorAt stx "no source range"
149-  return String.Pos.Raw.extract (← getFileMap).source r.start r.stop
150-
151-end
152-
153-end SFLCompat.Recall

4-
5-/-!
6-# Recall, checked byte for byte
7-
8-`sf_recall_source` lets a chapter restate a definition from earlier in the
9-development while the build checks that the restatement matches the
10-original's source text, byte for byte. The restated text is what the
11-reader already saw, and it can never drift from the original.
12-
13-```
14-sf_recall_source
15-  def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat := f (f n)
16-```
17-
18-The restated declaration is parsed but never elaborated; the check is
19-purely textual: after the block indentation is removed from each side, the
20-two texts must be equal, byte for byte. The restatement may sit at a
21-different indentation depth, but it may not be reflowed or respaced.
22-
23-The comparison covers whole declarations only. Carving a statement out of
24-the original's source would require parsing it, which is only possible in
25-the elaboration context of its declaration site; restating only a theorem
26-statement is therefore the province of `sf_recall statement`, which compares
27-elaborated types.
28--/
29-
30-namespace SFLCompat.Recall.Source
31-
32-open Lean Elab Command
33-
34-/--
35-`recall_source` restates a definition from earlier in the development and
36-checks that the restatement matches the original's source text, byte for
37-byte, modulo block indentation.
38--/
39-syntax (name := recallSrc) "sf_recall_source " command : command
40-
41-elab_rules : command
42-  | `(sf_recall_source $cmd:command) => do
43-    let decl ← declaredName cmd
44-    let x ← liftCoreM <| withoutExporting <|
45-      realizeGlobalConstNoOverloadWithInfo decl.ident
46-    -- The restatement is never elaborated, so it produces no info of its
47-    -- own. The whole compared region is one big reference to the original:
48-    -- hovering anywhere in it shows the original, and go-to-definition
49-    -- jumps to it.
50-    addConstInfo cmd x
51-    let restated ← sourceOfSyntax cmd
52-    let original ← sourceOf x
53-    unless dedent restated == dedent original do
54-      throwErrorAt cmd
55-        (m!"the restatement of '{privateToUserName x}' does not match its source.\n\
56-            Original:{indentD original}\nRestated:{indentD restated}"
57-          ++ (← liftCoreM <| replaceWithOriginalHint cmd (dedent original) restated))
58-
